areaSummaries.summary: The record is bigger than the audit's own summary reports: `judges/reads.json` holds **18 reads and 9 blind comparisons** (three subjects — msft1, azn, azn2 — × three lenses), and **all 9 chose the console**, on every dimension, with verifiability console-or-equal in 9 of 9 (§4.1's "six comparisons" counts the first round only and adds azn2's three in the following paragraph). Two framing facts kill the obvious explanations. The documents are the same size and shape — platform 13,933 words / 18 sections against console 12,756 words / 18 section headings (scorecard.md) — so this is not long-versus-short. And the console note took **longer** to read (45–60 min vs 30–45) and is **worse sourced** by the judges' own account (its load-bearing paragraph is "the least well founded", its balance sheet comes from a blog, its printed formula does not produce its own number) — yet 9 of 9 judges would act on it "with reservations" and 9 of 9 would not act on the platform's. The judges did not prefer a better-researched document. They preferred a document that **reaches a conclusion, and does not tell them not to trust it**. Running through the decisive field of each comparison ("which would you hand to a colleague and why"), four reasons do nearly all the work: the report contradicts itself and publishes severity-5 accusations against its own headline figures unresolved (7/9 and 8/9); the figures the brief turns on are absent (8/9); there is no price, so no per-share output can be positioned (8/9); and there is no view to act on (8/9). Crucially, azn2 — the post-fix run — scored `view_stated` true 3/3 and `argued` true 3/3 and still lost 3/3: **a stated view is necessary and provably not sufficient.** Almost every cause is a wiring gap, not an invariant: the scenario engine has no production caller, peer financials are never acquired, filings' financial-statement notes and exhibits are never read, focus questions never travel past the planner, the price never reaches the page, and 18 sections are drafted concurrently "on nothing another section produces". None of it requires relaxing an invariant to fix.
openQuestions: The count in the audit's §4.1 ('Twelve reads, six comparisons') is the first round only; judges/reads.json holds 18 reads and 9 comparisons once AZN #2 is included, and all 9 chose the console. Anyone quoting 'six of six' should say 'nine of nine' or scope it to the first round. Settled by reading reads.json['compares'], which has nine entries.

The judges read the exported Markdown alone. Three exhibits — the revenue-and-margin history, the football field and the sensitivity heatmap — do render in the HTML and PDF editions, so an unknown share of the 'the grid cannot be read' and 'the series exists only in footnotes' complaints is an artefact of the harness's choice of format rather than of the product. It is not all of it: the body prose independently claims 'no prior-period comparatives sit here' while the series is recorded, which is a drafting failure in any format. Settled by re-judging the PDF of the same run alongside the Markdown.

Whether a stated view moves would_act_on_it at all. AZN #2 scored view_stated 3/3 and argued 3/3 and still drew 'no' 3/3, so the record proves a view is not sufficient but does not isolate how much it contributes once contradiction, price and missing figures are fixed. Settled only by a re-run with the reconciliation pass, the price and the exhibits landed, re-judged blind.

Whether printing a market capitalisation without the closing price satisfies the operator's reading of the EODHD terms, given that capitalisation over the filed share count yields the price. This is a licence question about the operator's own subscription (ADR 0030 route 2) and only they can answer it.

How much of the per-run budget the exhibit and peer acquisition consume in wall-clock. Runs are 31–42 minutes of step time today and £7.19 average against a £10 target; the fetches are free but slow, and nothing in the record measures acquisition time separately from step time. Settled by instrumenting the acquire step on one live run.

Whether the console note's own defects would have shown up under the platform's checks — the judges found an arithmetic slip ($63bn where its printed formula gives $83bn), a global sales figure used for a US loss of exclusivity, and a balance sheet from a blog. The audit's matcher found 1 contradicted figure of 179 on the AZN baseline against 0 of 779 across five platform runs. This is the platform's genuine edge and nothing in this pass quantifies how much a reader values it, because no judge was asked to check a console figure against a filing.

areaSummaries.summary: The header line is not a judgement the platform reached — it is a hardcoded `None`. `src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3765-3766` assigns `report.rating = None` and `report.confidence = None` on every run, and all four document assemblers default `rating` to `None`, so `render/markdown.py:162` prints "no view reached" unconditionally. There is no code path anywhere that writes `reports.rating`; the column, the renderer field, the Obsidian export and the prior-research comparison all exist and read it, and nothing fills it. Underneath that cosmetic fact sits a real one: the sections that are supposed to argue the view are never shown the run's own valuation. `src/aer/sections/evidence.py:580-588` selects calculations ordered `period_end DESC NULLS LAST` with `LIMIT 40` — and `src/aer/calc/engine.py:165-169` records WACC, terminal value and value per share with `period = None`, so they sort last and are cut at the database before any budget question. That is why MSFT #1's Executive Summary says "no valuation output, no discount rate and no peer multiple" (report.md:46, 51) eleven lines under an At-a-glance block printing "WACC 9.3%" and "Value per share (base) $485.29" (report.md:39-40). It is the same defect the audit already fixed for the adversary as F-27 (§5, F-27; fix at `services/red_team.py:343-374`) and did not fix for the writers. The platform is structurally capable of stating an argued view within its invariants — it already does, in prose, in §Investment Thesis — and the machinery for the figure half (a code-owned block the model cannot contradict) exists as `SectionAugmenter` under ADR 0063. What is missing is a decision about whose view it is, and one deterministic composer.
openQuestions: Why was the market capitalisation unavailable to the cost of capital on runs where the price step succeeded? Both audited WACC blocks record "Book equity was used as the equity weight because no market capitalisation was available" (msft1/report.md:405, azn2/report.md:402), while `score-platform.json` reports `prices_acquired: true` for both — and the audit's own "market capitalisation present" row is a substring match on the report text (`audit/scoring/platform_report.py:28-38,263`), so it matches that very caveat sentence and establishes nothing. A live run's `acquire_prices` step output, or a replay of `services/price_acquisition.py:480-518` against the stored artefacts, would settle it. Any premium-to-market figure is worthless until it is settled.

Does the operator's executed EODHD agreement permit a published figure that positions a valuation against the market price — a premium, a discount, a market capitalisation — as a derived value? `src/aer/fetch/policy.py:180-186` records the operator's determination of 2026-08-09 that computed figures may be published, and ADR 0030's own table still calls a computed multiple "ambiguous". Only the operator can re-read the agreement and say whether a premium-to-value ratio falls inside their determination. The containment in `WithheldComps` and the exportable/internal chart split was built to the pre-determination posture and nobody has asked whether it is now wider than the licence requires.

Would a stated view actually flip a judge? The audit's own counter-evidence is AZN #2: three of three judges scored it "view stated and argued" and three of three still said they would not act on it, and all three blind comparisons still chose the console (§4.1). Their reasons had moved to the evidence policy and the missing content — no product-level revenue, no guidance, no named competitor, no share price. So this area is necessary and demonstrably not sufficient, and the honest expectation is that it moves "is a view stated and argued" to yes and moves "would you act on it" only in combination with the price anchor and whatever the evidence-policy area recommends. Hypothesis, not a measurement: the single change most likely to move "would act on it" is the anchor, because two of the three AZN #2 judges named the absence of a price as disqualifying in itself.

Should `investment_thesis` be required to reach a conclusion at all on a thin run? Making the view mandatory risks manufacturing one where the evidence does not support it, which is the opposite of the platform's whole posture — and the MSFT draft's refusal was, on the evidence it was shown, correct. The augmenter's `standalone` hook (`sections/deterministic.py:389-391`) is the existing mechanism for "the block is the whole truthful content", and whether an unanchored run should take that path or still be made to argue is a judgement I could not settle from the record.

How much of MSFT #1's poor showing was the evidence cap and how much was the draft? I can show the cap excludes run-level calculations by construction (`sections/evidence.py:580-588` against `calc/engine.py:165-169`) and that the resulting sentences are false about the run's own store, but I cannot show from the exports what the pack actually contained — `steps.json` carries no step outputs and no run export records the evidence units dealt to a section. A single replayed draft call with the pack logged would convert this from a strong inference into a measurement, and it is worth doing before the fix, so the regression test can be written against what was really there.

areaSummaries.summary: The platform does fetch the material the judges said was missing — it then throws it away in four places. A run's five research workers acquire, hash and store secondary and exhibit-level documents; every one of them enters at T5 (/home/user/AgeanticInvestmentPlatform/src/aer/services/research.py:81), every built-in section's ceiling is T4 (migrations 0006:38 and 0023:45,58), and the filter at /home/user/AgeanticInvestmentPlatform/src/aer/sections/evidence.py:633 drops them before any writer sees them. Even if the ceiling rose, nothing would change: a worker-fetched page gets no Extraction rows, and a citation is an extraction id (evidence.py:875, citations.py:127-147), so there would be a title and no text and nothing citable. The workers' own findings — on MSFT #2, seven of them carrying Q4 revenue, Microsoft Cloud growth, commercial RPO, the Anthropic gain, the OpenAI mark and segment direction — reach exactly one consumer, the assumptions proposer (vertical_slice_v1.py:1382,1406), and no section, no report and no page. Underneath that sit three narrower gaps: acquisition fetches only a filing's primary document, so an 8-K's substance (its Exhibit 99.1) is never acquired at T1; the issuer-IR adapter that would reach AstraZeneca's own patent-expiry schedule has no caller in src/; and the workers are never told the operator's focus questions at all. The net effect is that the run pays for research it cannot publish, and the report truthfully says "its substance is not before us" about a document it is holding.
openQuestions: Why the two MSFT exhibits missed the regulator-hit map: whether that worker node's full-text search simply never returned msft-ex99_1.htm, or whether the map being per-worker-node (built fresh in each build_executors call) is what lost it. The run export carries the findings and the recorded tier but not each node's search hit list. Settled by replaying the msft2 worker turns against the archived EDGAR responses and printing regulator_hits at the moment of each fetch.

Whether the operator wants secondary reporting in the document at all, or only regulator- and issuer-hosted material. If the answer is the latter, items 1, 6 and 7 are the whole plan and the ceiling never moves; if the former, item 2's ADR is the gate everything else waits on. Settled by the operator's own reading of check 6 in the audit's §4.4.

Whether raising the ceiling is enough to move a blind judge, or whether the withheld figures dominate. The judges cited both: 'the figures a research note is read for are withheld' (no peer multiple, no segment revenue, no market capitalisation on three runs) sits beside 'the substance is not before us'. Nothing in this area's items produces a peer multiple. Settled only by a re-run and a fresh blind pass — about £7 and one judging cycle per subject.

What a publisher-by-publisher robots and ToS determination would actually admit today. The roadmap's own check found Seeking Alpha disallowing ClaudeBot by name and ft.com unreachable; I did not re-check anything and made no network request. Settled by fetching robots.txt for each candidate publisher and recording the determination in an ADR before any first request, which is the recipe ADR 0092 already sets.

Whether a section's ceiling should be a property of the section or of the run. ADR 0111 established the per-run pattern for undated sources (work_orders.undated_sources_admissible) and the per-section pattern already exists for tiers. Item 2's options B and D are that fork, and it is a design decision the operator should take before either is built.

areaSummaries.summary: The audit's "no peer multiple on any run" is true but it names only the outermost of three independent walls, and it misdescribes the largest one. Wall 1 is the known decision: ADR 0059's first amendment stopped acquiring anything for a peer, so every peer arrives carrying a CIK and no period end and is excluded by construction (src/aer/services/comps.py:542-552). Wall 2 is undiscovered and decisive: every run already computed the subject's own multiples and threw them away — MSFT #1 recorded P/E 27.43x and EV/EBITDA 18.93x, AZN 24.49x, M&T 14.11x, all traced, all replayed — because the rendered report has no parameter that can carry a multiple (`assemble_document(..., comps: WithheldComps | None)`, src/aer/render/document.py:436) and no section writer ever sees a comps table. Wall 3 is that the multiples are persisted as six identical rows named `multiple` with `period: null`, so they sort last under the evidence cap and reach a writer unlabelled. Market capitalisation has three different root causes, none of them the peer decision: MSFT computed it and never printed it; AZN had no filed share count and the vendor fallback is an endpoint the subscription does not include; AZN #2 and M&T lost their whole price layer to a bug where "no new bars inserted" is reported as "the provider returned no prices". Separately, the WACC on every run uses book equity even when a market capitalisation exists, and the report prints a caveat saying its own discount rate is too low. Judges named every one of these.
openQuestions: Which predicate excluded AstraZeneca's filed share count. The run log proves the vendor fallback fired, which happens only when `_filed_share_count` returns nothing, and the extract log proves a `shares_outstanding` observation for 2025-12-31 was chosen. The likeliest explanation is that AZN dimensions its cover-page count by share class and the query filters `dimension_axis IS NULL` (vertical_slice_v1.py:2765). One SELECT against the audit database settles it; I did not run one, per the planning-pass constraint.

How long a peer's acquisition actually takes. My 1.5-3.5 minutes for eight peers is reasoned from the subject's 6.6 s `acquire` step and from the fact that ADR 0059 skips the two expensive parts of `extract` - 18,610 whole-document string searches for excerpts, and the segment sweep - which together dominate its 156.8 s. It is an estimate. The seeding item measures it for about GBP 7.

The fiscal year ends of the eight proposed MSFT peers. My claim that only Oracle falls within 45 days of Microsoft's 30 June is general market knowledge, not something the audit measured. Acquiring the eight and running `align_peers` once would settle it, and would settle whether the acquisition option buys a one-peer median.

Whether a peer's companyfacts aggregate, dated by `latest_filed` under ADR 0044, is quarantined on a backdated point-in-time run, and what a quarantined peer aggregate should look like on the sources page. The facts themselves are still filtered correctly by `select_point_in_time`, and a peer figure is never cited in prose, so nothing is unsound; the question is what the operator is shown.

Whether stating the premium or discount of a valuation to the last close - without quoting the close - is the right reading of ADR 0030 route 2. A ratio of two figures is derived and therefore publishable under the 2026-08-09 determination; a quoted price is the series. Judges asked for exactly this on both subjects ("the note holds a price series but never states a price, so none of $242.78 / $449.79 / $485.29 is set against anything"). MSFT's close of $492.44 sits in the run against a value per share of $485.29, and the report says neither. This is the operator's determination, and it is the cheapest single answer to the judges' loudest complaint.

Whether the peer-set basis is trailing twelve months or last fiscal year. The gate payload declares `"basis": "ttm"` (vertical_slice_v1.py:2444) and the comps build computes `MultipleBasis.LAST_FISCAL_YEAR` (comps_run.py:308, 323). Nothing notices today, because no table has ever had a peer in it.

areaSummaries.summary: The segment gap is not an extraction failure. The platform already reads dimensioned iXBRL out of the annual report, maps it and stores it: MSFT #1's own PDF carries a three-bar "Segment mix — FY2026" chart citing the 10-K at footnotes 23–25, and AZN #2's extract step reports `segment_facts_seen: 3637`. The failure is selection and presentation — `visible_facts` bars every dimensioned row from every section's evidence pack (ADR 0058), so the Segment Analysis writer truthfully writes "no segment-level dollar figures... were available to cite here" on the same page as a chart of exactly those figures; the chart prints no values on its bars and the Markdown edition the judges read drops the picture entirely; and the exhibit vanishes on every second run of a company because it joins on `job_id` while facts deduplicate to the first run's document. Guidance and the recast segment table are a different and sharper failure: the console's entire segment table and its "operating margin fell from 48.9% to 45.1% through FY26" claim came from `d291965dex991.htm` — Exhibit 99.1 inside accession 0001193125-26-380280, the very 8-K folder the platform downloaded `d291965d8k.htm` from. `Filing.url()` builds only the primary document, so the platform fetched the cover page and wrote "its substance is not before us". Named competitors are the cheapest gap of all: the run holds eight operator-confirmed peers with CIKs and written rationales in `gate-PEER_SET.json`, and the comps prose is written to count them without ever naming one.
openQuestions: Whether MSFT's FY26 Q4 results 8-K exhibit (the press release, [S1]/[S46] in the console's source table) contains written guidance, or whether Microsoft's FY27 guidance exists only in the earnings call. This decides whether the exhibit fetch alone closes the guidance gap for a domestic filer or whether the issuer-IR adapter must also be wired. Settled by reading the 8-K exhibit for the 29 July 2026 accession.

Which axis qnames AstraZeneca's 20-F actually uses for therapy area, and whether those rows were persisted by the sweep. The chart's members are country codes and region subtotals, and `min(axes)` alphabetical fallback explains that if the geographical axis sorts before the segments axis — but I have not read the artefact. Settled by listing the distinct `dimension_axis` values stored for AZN, which is one SQL query against the existing database and needs no run.

Whether MSFT's 10-K Item 1 Competition prose was excerpted at all, or scored out by Item 1A. The report's output is consistent with the latter but I did not score the stored artefact. Settled by running `_score` over the stored 10-K's blocks offline and printing the sixty that won — no network, no spend.

How many of MSFT #1's fourteen source documents were 8-Ks and how many came from research workers. The Sources table lists only the four cited documents, so five current reports may have been fetched and used uncited. This changes how much of the 'no guidance' result is acquisition and how much is citation. Settled from the run's own source_documents rows.

Whether `_EXCERPT_POOL` (200) actually binds on a large-cap run — AZN #2 recorded 165 filing excerpts, so it did not there, but a run with more filings would rank a truncated pool. Settled by counting extractions per run in the existing store.

Whether a segment figure row should carry `financial_fact_id` alone or also a rendered axis/member label in the document. ADR 0058 requires that a dimensioned row never read as the company's line; exactly how the renderer enforces that for a figure table is a design choice this pass did not settle.

areaSummaries.summary: M&T's revenue resolves to ASC 606 fee income because `Revenues` stops after FY2023 and nothing sums the two lines that are a bank's revenue. That much the audit establishes. What the code shows on top of it is that the audit's own sizing of the fix is wrong in one decisive respect: **seven of the eleven impossible relations are quarterly, and none of them is reachable from `aer.calc`**. `_figure_scenes` compares stored *facts* (`src/aer/services/evaluations.py:612`), the front page reads stored facts (`src/aer/render/glance.py:264,293`), the revenue-history chart reads stored facts (`src/aer/services/exhibits.py:198`) and the section writers' evidence pack ranks the stored `revenue` fact first (`src/aer/sections/evidence.py:135`). A derived revenue is a calculation, not a fact, so "one function in `aer.calc` and one place in the ratio inputs" clears 4 of 11 findings and gate 2 still refuses. Because `acquire` runs before `classify` (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:412-416`), a sector-gated rule cannot be applied where facts are persisted at all — which is what makes withholding a one-place fix and deriving a six-place one. Separately, the guard that is supposed to catch this has a dead third of it: `_figure_scenes` queries the concept `total_assets` and the canonical concept is `assets`, so the turnover-floor relation has never fired — the MTB run recorded asset turnover of 0.0078 and 0.0074 on a $213bn balance sheet and was never told. And the document the operator reads at the final gate is not the document that would be rendered: the review-page render omits `sector`, `comps` and `charts`, which for a bank is the entire disclosure that the DCF was refused. On legibility: the residual-income *method* is well written and better than a console note would manage; the *answer* is unusable — $184.47 per share is 0.4% above a book value per share the document never states, against a market price the document never carries, under a section headed "Valuation — Discounted Cash Flow".
openQuestions: Whether the derived definition splices. FY2021-FY2023 `Revenues` (5,992 / 8,179 / 9,643m) should equal net interest income (3,825 / 5,822 / 7,115m) plus non-interest income for the same years, but `NoninterestIncome` is not in the audit's independent truth harness (audit/scoring/facts.py:34-98) and I did not read the archived companyfacts. The artefact is addressed by sha256 31b7b199ea6bc258a238daac1215dbe0ad385cb801d7a08ec6c8bb93d57aa363 and reading it offline settles the question for nothing. Until it is read, 'revenue = NII + non-interest income' is a hypothesis with one confirmed data point (FY2025: 6,948 + 2,742 = 9,690, the audit's own figure in F-24).

How large M&T's preferred capital is, exactly. I infer it from the reconciliation between net income of $2,851m, diluted EPS of $17.00 and 158,791,000 diluted shares (report.md:146 and the run export), which implies roughly $151m of preferred dividends and other adjustments — so $1.9-2.2bn of preferred at a plausible coupon. The carrying amount is not mapped as a concept, so the run does not hold it and I could not read it. It matters because it sizes the per-share error at 5-7%.

Whether the review page's 85,366-character render logged in docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/web.log:382 is the same document as the 92,508-character report.md the scorers read. The structural evidence is conclusive either way — exactly the three blocks the review path omits (`sector`, `comps`, `charts`) are the three missing from report.md, and the three approved runs' documents carry the comps block while the two refused runs' do not — but the character and footnote counts differ, so a later render after `revise` is the likely explanation and I did not confirm it. Reproducing the review page against the run's stored record would settle it in minutes.

Whether `analyse_company` should build quarterly statements at all. Today it reads `annual_facts` only, so no quarterly ratio or derived subtotal exists, which is why the seven quarterly plausibility findings are unreachable from `aer.calc`. Making the derivation quarterly would close that route, but quarterly statements are a much larger change than the revenue question and I have not costed it.

Whether a sector-conditional derivation is the right shape at all, given `acquire` runs before `classify`. The alternative is that the taxonomy rule at the parse layer is the only place a fact's concept may be decided, and everything sector-conditional is a calculation on top. I believe the second, and it is a design position the operator should confirm before either option is built, because it determines whether `assemble` acquires a `profile` argument.

areaSummaries.summary: The platform offers "LSE" in the research request form's exchange select, accepts it through every validation rule, spends about £0.55 on the planner and its critic, asks the operator to approve a costed plan — and then dies at `acquire`, because `_acquire` resolves every subject against EDGAR's ticker file and nothing else (`vertical_slice_v1.py:2228` → `sources/sec/client.py:214`). That is audit F-04 and use case 3. The Companies House adapter is real, careful and 467 lines long; it is constructed nowhere outside its own test, and the `ServiceBundle` that carries services into a run has no field for it (`runtime.py:47-79`). The same is true of `aer.sources.issuer`, which ADR 0022 names as the other half of the UK path. Closing the gap is not one wire: the run's facts come from EDGAR's companyfacts aggregate, which has no Companies House counterpart; `upsert_company` writes a resolved identifier straight into the ten-character `cik` column, so an eight-character company number fails a check constraint before any of the interesting work begins; Companies House publishes UK SIC 2007 codes that share no prefix with the US SIC codes the sector profiles match on, which would put a UK bank back on the standard model that F-23 exists to prevent; and the date Companies House accepts a set of accounts is months later than the day the market learned the results, so a UK point-in-time run is honest and stale rather than dishonest. Two common assumptions are wrong and worth stating: the missing GBP risk-free series does *not* block a UK run (this workflow acquires no macro series at all — the rate is an operator assumption either way), and the iXBRL-to-`RawFact` machinery a UK path needs is already running in production inside the segment sweep. The cheapest honest interim is not the adapter: it is to stop selling the dead end, and to fix a refusal message that currently tells an operator asking for AstraZeneca on the LSE that AstraZeneca is "a different company".
openQuestions: What a listed plc's accounts actually are when Companies House hands them over — inline XBRL or a PDF of the annual report — and whether the document API requires an `Accept` header to choose. This is the hinge of the whole area and nothing in the repository establishes it: the fixtures in `tests/fixtures/uk/` are constructed JSON envelopes, and `docs/data-sources/companies-house.md`'s 'usually inline XBRL' is unsourced. Settled by one free-key probe against three real subjects, costing no model spend.

Whether the operator holds a Companies House API key at all. `AER_COMPANIES_HOUSE_API_KEY` is documented and optional, `runtime.py:186-200` omits the credential silently when unset, and `docs/archive/manual-acceptance.md:55` records the UK run as never having been done for want of one. Nothing in this area can be verified live until that is answered.

Whether a UK plc that reports in sterling while listed in New York — GSK and Diageo file 20-Fs in GBP — runs cleanly today on the interim route, with GBP facts against a USD ADR price through the ECB cross-rate. The audit's only 20-F subject, AstraZeneca, reports in USD, so the currency-crossing case is untested. Settled by one offline drive with stored fixtures, no live spend.

Whether Companies House's filing history reliably carries a `made_up_to` date for a listed plc's accounts. `FilingRecord.made_up_to` reads `action_date` or `made_up_date` (`companies_house.py:304`), and the fixture supplies `action_date` — but nothing establishes that the real register does so consistently, and without it a set of accounts cannot be attached to the fiscal year it reports.

Whether the operator wants a UK path at all, given its shape. On the honest reading it delivers an annual-only, months-late, peerless evidence base for a company whose US-listed compatriots already work. The alternative — closing F-04 with items 1, 2 and 12 and declaring the scope to be SEC filers — is a defensible answer that costs a session and a half in total, and §8 item 14 already puts the choice to the operator.

areaSummaries.summary: The run itself is sound; the path an operator walks through it is not. Six or seven gate stops (audit §4.2) are each survivable, but the journey has three true dead ends — a stale approval that no surface can supersede (F-16), a refused check that nothing can re-measure and a run that cannot even be superseded because a rejected gate leaves the job non-terminal, and a console that goes on saying "Waiting for you" and linking to a page that renders no form. Around those sit four demands that are too large or too raw to answer well: an unmapped-concepts gate carrying 496, 312 and 852 rows on the three subjects; an assumptions gate that makes the operator hand-type a risk-free rate and an equity risk premium on every single run, with a justification each, while a fully built, licence-cleared macro stack sits with no caller in `src/`; a citation override the gate message promises and no surface offers; and 135 distinct code identifiers on the gate pages, with metric names, module paths, tier enums and raw twelve-place decimals reaching the exported document. The terminal is still load-bearing: the console itself tells the operator to "look at the terminal running `just worker`", and `aer reseal` is named inside a user-facing pause message with no web equivalent. Two of these bear directly on issue 2: the exported footnote drops the verified excerpt the platform's whole advantage rests on, and `report.rating` is set to `None` by the only line in `src/` that writes it, so every report leads with "Non-binding view: no view reached" — the single reason all six judges gave for refusing to act.
openQuestions: The audit's §4.2 count of the unmapped-concepts page (105 items on MSFT, 51 on AZN, 304 on the bank) does not reconcile with the run exports, whose `gate-UNMAPPED_CONCEPTS.json` payloads carry 496, 312/322 and 852 rows. I tried distinct labels, rows carrying a figure, several share thresholds and a taxonomy split and reproduced none of the three. Either the driver counted something narrower than the payload, or the page collapses rows in a way the template does not show. Settled by re-rendering `/runs/{job}/financials` from a restored msft1 job and counting `<tr>` elements in `#unmapped-tags`.

Whether the risk-free rate should be acquired per run or held as a dated observation reused across runs within a window. `observation_as_at` already filters on vintage, so both work; the second is much cheaper and the difference only shows on two runs of the same subject days apart. The operator's answer decides whether the macro step belongs in the DAG or in a background refresh.

Whether a superseding decision should be admitted only when the recorded approval matches neither seal nor live page (the strictly-stranded case), or whenever the payload has moved. The narrow rule cannot be abused and cannot rescue an operator who simply changed their mind; the wide rule can do both. This is the substance of the ADR and I did not want to pre-empt it.

Whether re-running `validate` on a finished run should also re-run `red_team` and `revise`. If a late fix changes a section's content, `cited_figure_agreement` measured at `validate` is stale for the revised claims (audit F-21, §8 item 10) — so the two questions are the same question, and answering only the presentation half may leave a different check measuring the wrong text.

How much the sector gate's third answer must generalise. The decision panel is shared by all seven gates by design, and the audit's own F-26 note is about one gate. Whether the frame grows a per-gate answer set, or whether the sector gate stops sharing the frame, is a design call I could not make from the code alone.

Whether the operator wants the run console to summon them at all. Six or seven stops across 31–42 minutes of step time currently require the browser to be open and looked at; nothing else in the product notifies. I found no existing notification machinery to build on, so I have not costed it as an item.

areaSummaries.summary: The time does not go where the audit's headline suggests. Re-derived from the step records with concurrent steps merged rather than summed, a run's machine work is 26.5–36.8 minutes (azn 26.5, azn2 30.1, msft1 32.4, msft2 30.9, mtb 36.8) — the published "31–42 minutes of step time" is the *sum* of per-step elapsed times, which counts the five-wide research wave five times over (audit/report/generate.py:43). Two steps are 58–64% of it: `draft` (6.6–11.4 min) and `revise` (10.1–11.3 min), and `revise` is entirely serial — its step duration equals the sum of its model-call latencies to within a second on all three exported runs, for at most four sections, while `draft` fans the same work out four-wide. Collapsing the operator's waits, the evidence base and the valuation are complete at 7.7/9.9/11.3 minutes, the whole eighteen-section draft is finished at 16.8/16.6/22.7 minutes — and gate 2, the first moment a person is allowed to read any of it, is 13.2–14.3 minutes later. So "nothing useful exists at ten minutes" is only half a compute problem: at ten minutes the platform has struck a discounted cash flow off hashed facts and has no document-shaped surface to put it on, and two such surfaces (`/runs/{id}/preview`, `/runs/{id}/summary` — the one-page renderer from migration 0040) already exist, render from live rows, and are linked from nowhere the operator can reach while a run is running. Against a console that answers in 14.1–18.8 minutes with one prompt and no decisions, the free fixes alone (concurrent revise, a wider draft fan-out, moving the free acquisition off the plan's critical path, and the linear-in-facts extract loop) project to roughly 19–22 minutes; the ten-minute target is reachable only by publishing a first read, which is the one option here that trades something the platform exists for.
openQuestions: How long does a human actually take at each gate? The audit never measured it — §4.2 says "the audit's own stops added hours and are not the product's", and the gate waits in scorecard.md (2–86 s) are the driver's policy deciding, not a person reading. Everything in this area about operator attention is therefore inferred from page sizes and decision counts, not measured. What would settle it: one operator-driven live run with the wall clock recorded at each gate, which is also the only way to know whether batching four decisions into one sitting helps or just makes one page unbearable.

Is the console baseline's 14–19 minutes a fair comparison for time-to-first-output? The baseline was a single non-streaming API turn, and §9 says explicitly that "the console itself" is not established. A real console session streams text as it writes, so it may have something readable at two minutes; the API proxy has nothing until it returns. If the console streams, the first-read gap is larger than the end-to-end gap, and the case for publishing early is stronger than the numbers here suggest.

Is the per-fact `locate` loop really what makes `extract` cost 8.4–9.3 ms per fact? The scaling across three filers is flat and the cost tracks chosen rather than written facts, which points hard at the loop — but nothing was profiled. Thirty minutes with a profiler over the stored companyfacts artefact settles it before any code is written.

What does a quick run actually produce? Nine of eighteen sections at 0.6 of the length has never been run, scored or judged. One £4 run scored with the audit's own matcher and put to the same three judges would tell the operator whether the shortest path to console-parity on time costs anything at all in the only currency that matters, and it is the single cheapest experiment available here.

How much of `revise`'s value would a reader lose from a first read? Across the five audited runs, revise touched at most four of eighteen sections — but `executive_summary` or `investment_thesis` was among them on four of five. A first read is therefore most likely to be stale in exactly the two sections a reader opens first. Whether that matters is answerable by diffing the pre-revision and post-revision text of those sections on the exported runs, which the records support and this pass did not do.

Does the 20% overhead factor I applied to the list-scheduling projections hold at a wider bound? The model under-predicts today's four-wide draft by 8%, 11% and 26%; the spread suggests per-section retries and commit overhead rather than a constant, and at seven-wide the database becomes a larger share. The projections for a concurrent revise (200–255 s) and a seven-wide draft (259–391 s) are therefore estimates from recorded latencies, not measurements, and should be confirmed on the first live run rather than quoted as results.

areaSummaries.summary: A red-team challenge has exactly one exit in this platform — a person choosing a side at gate 3 — and that exit reaches no reader, because the appendix is written at the `validate` step and never rewritten after a settle. So every challenge prints as "Escalated for human decision at approval" whatever happens, and a reader cannot distinguish an argument nobody looked at from one the operator settled. Worse, the accusations are arithmetic ones the platform can settle in code and does not: on AZN #2 the adversary compared FY2025 draft figures against FY2021/FY2022 calculations of the same name, and six of eight published challenges rest on that void premise — while `cited_figure_agreement` (81 figures, 0 failures) and `numerical_consistency` (831 calculations, 0 failures) sit in the table immediately above them, refuting them silently. The damage is not confined to the appendix: ADR 0091's revise loop redrafted four sections in answer to those false challenges, so the published body now says both "interest is covered 8.1 times" and "Interest cover is not established by the figures available", and ADR 0095's briefer leaned "accept the challenge" on all eight. All three judges reconstructed the truth from the footnotes and all three counted it against the platform — including the sceptic, the one judge who preferred the platform on verifiability until this. The fix is a split, not a ban: arithmetic-shaped accusations must be adjudicated by code before publication, and judgement-shaped challenges — which are the platform's single clearest advantage over the console — must be published better than they are now.
openQuestions: Whether the operator wants the body to carry an adversarial paragraph at all. `two-audiences-one-surface` proposes one, and it is the item most likely to move a judge's verdict, but it adds a model-written passage near the thesis and it interacts with the wider 'Non-binding view: no view reached' framing that the audit puts in §8 as the operator's decision. Settled by the operator saying whether the body may argue the bear case in prose, under the ordinary evidence contract and the existing non-advice framing.

Whether ADR 0039's "never auto-resolved" is meant to cover a challenge's evidence premise or only its argument. I have read it as covering the argument — the ADR itself already lets code refuse a challenge citing an id the run does not hold — but the sentence "a challenge the system itself could dismiss would be worth nothing" can be read either way, and the recommended adjudicate-and-publish option was chosen partly to avoid needing the wider reading. Settled by the new ADR stating the boundary explicitly.

Whether a period adjudicator can be written conservatively enough that it can never refute a true accusation. My proposal restricts it to pairs sharing a calculation `name` and differing in `period_end`, which is narrow, but I have not checked how many recorded calculation names are period-free (the index renders "not period-specific" for those at src/aer/services/red_team.py:367-369) or how the residual-income and DCF families label their periods. Settled by a count over an existing run's `calculations` rows — no live run needed.

The exact mechanism by which AZN #2's fact index came to hold buybacks and capex but no revenue. The 40-row cap over 4,171 chosen facts is certain and sufficient to explain a starved index; which concepts survived the `period_end DESC, concept` ordering I could not reconstruct without the run's rows, so the specific list in the adversary's coverage note is reported as its testimony rather than as a verified account. Settled by replaying `_evidence_index` against the AZN #2 job's stored facts.

The token and money cost of a fact index sized to the distinct-concept count across five periods. `fact-index-shows-forty-of-four-thousand` is the one item here with a real spend consequence, and the run's red-team step cost £0.30 today. Settled by composing the input offline against an existing run and counting tokens — no model call needed.

Whether re-measuring the run-level metrics after `revise` can fail a run late in a way that strands it. `metrics-describe-a-different-document` accepts a late gate question deliberately, but F-08's stranded-run history means the failure path deserves a look before the change lands. Settled by reading the gate and escalation paths, not by a run.

areaSummaries.summary: The prose is not the disease; it is the symptom of a starved writer with nothing to argue toward. Three mechanical causes account for almost all of it. First, no run has ever produced a view: `report.rating` is assigned `None` and nothing else ever writes it (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3765`), so the header a judge reads first says "no view reached" by construction, not by judgement. Second, every section is handed a 40-row keyhole onto the run's own record — azn2 holds 831 calculations and its Executive Summary was dealt 9 of them, 12 facts and 1 excerpt, with `evidence_truncated: true` on all 48 section executions across the three logged runs — so sections contradict each other and the front page about what the run even holds. Third, the deterministic layer computes levels and almost no movements: `aer/calc/bridge.py` (a margin decomposition, unit- and mutation-tested) has zero production callers, there is no contribution-to-growth and no market-implied reverse solve, and prompt rule 1 correctly forbids the writer deriving any of them — so the one thing the console won on, decomposition, is unavailable to the platform by construction rather than by rule. On reading time the brief's framing needs correcting: the console notes are 12.7k words against the platform's 13.9–15.9k, and judges took 3.8–4.5 minutes per thousand words on the console against 2.6–2.9 on the platform. They are not defeated by length; they skim, because 44–47% of the document is apparatus (142 footnotes with 70 distinct texts on msft1) and the prose has no destination. Nothing among the fifteen evaluation metrics measures any of this, which is why every one of them passed on documents six of six judges refused to act on.
openQuestions: The brief's premise about reading time does not survive measurement, and the operator should decide what to do with that. The console notes are 12,756 and 12,699 words against the platform's 13,933-15,948, and judges took 3.8-4.5 minutes per thousand words on the console against 2.6-2.9 on the platform (reads.json reading_minutes over measured word counts). They are skimming the platform, not drowning in it. Cutting length alone will not flip a comparison; raising argument per word will. The length work still matters for ISSUE 1 - a 40-minute read is a barrier - but it belongs in the apparatus and the front door, not in the analytical prose.

Whether the audit runs' archived model replies and artefact store still exist on the operator's machine. `aer replay-draft` and `aer rehearse-section` are the difference between testing this area for pence and testing it at £7 a run, and both read the source run's rows and archived payloads. The committed audit directory carries the exports but not the store, so I could not confirm. If the databases were discarded, the first session's work is re-establishing a subject run to rehearse against.

Why the WACC used book equity on MSFT, where a market capitalisation was present. The recorded caveat 'Book equity was used as the equity weight because no market capitalisation was available... Every valuation discounted at it is correspondingly too high' appears in msft1's report at line 405, yet audit §3.4 records market capitalisation as present for MSFT. If the valuation cannot reach a market capitalisation the run holds, then the headline value per share is self-disclaimed on every run, and no stated view can rest on it. This is in another area's territory but it gates the target-price half of the stated-view item. Settled by reading `src/aer/services/valuation_run.py` against the msft1 run's price rows.

Whether the operator wants a rating at all. A stated view is the single change with the largest measured effect on the judges' verdict, and it is also the change that puts a model's opinion, or the operator's, on a shareable surface for the first time. The three options in that item differ in who authors it, and only the operator can choose. My reading of CLAUDE.md's framing - a personal research tool, one report at a time, for one investor - is that the operator authoring it at gate 2 is the most defensible, and the least useful for making the prose argue, which is why I have proposed both halves.

Whether the peer-multiple decision (audit §8 item 1) is taken before or after this work. Three of the six blind comparisons cited missing multiples, and no amount of better prose supplies them. If the operator decides to acquire peers' filings, the argument items here get materially more to argue with; if not, the stated view has to stand on a DCF alone and the document should say so in one place rather than in nine.

areaSummaries.summary: Almost nothing in this area is a bug a user meets today, and two things in it are. The two that matter are guard gaps with the platform's own name on them: a fact-backed numeric claim is never checked against its fact's value (only calculation-backed claims are, at `cited_figure_agreement`), and the reading ladder in `core/figures.py` discards the scale word, so "$331.8 million" over a stored 331,839,000,000 reads as correct at both the draft gate and the metric. The audit's "0 contradicted of 779 figures" is evidence the writers did not make that mistake on five runs, not evidence the platform would catch it — the audit's own scorer reads scale words (`audit/scoring/numerals.py:126-140, 599-609`) and the platform's guard does not. Everything else here is internal hygiene with one user-visible seam each: the model-route table is a free-text JSON textarea on the settings page whose unknown-model behaviour silently drops effort (F-05) and prices at the Fable ceiling, which can pause a run for money never spent; up to 18,706 output tokens a run of schema-rejected replies are metered but summed on no surface; the audit chain's integrity check exists only as a terminal command on the platform's single strongest use case; and the ordering defect F-03 was fixed by hand on two seeds with nothing in CI to stop it recurring. My code reading also narrows one audit claim and corrects another — the cost rows a dying step loses are lost only on a poisoned session or a killed process, not on an ordinary failure; and `agent_runs` records the requested effort only, not `effort_applied`, which the audit says it records.
openQuestions: Why AZN's `revise` attempt 0 actually lost its cost rows. The engine's ordinary failure path commits pending rows (src/aer/workflow/engine.py:830-837), so the loss requires either a poisoned session (the rollback branch at engine.py:846-855) or a process death with no commit. The audit says 'consistent with', not 'because of'. The run export at docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/azn/ should carry that step's `job_steps` row and its error detail, which would say which — and that determines whether the fix needs to survive a rollback, a kill, or both.

Whether the platform has ever written a scale word inconsistent with its own figure. The audit's matcher reads scale words and reported zero contradictions across 779 figures, which is evidence it has not happened on five runs. What is not measured is the matcher's recall (§9), and the audit's own §6 records fifteen tightenings each of which cost recall. Re-running the matcher over the five stored reports with only the scale-word rule enabled would establish whether the guard would have had anything to catch.

Whether the operator ever intends a second database role. The full answer to F-07 is the separate role migration 0001 asked for, and it sits in the same bucket as roadmap A5/A7/A8 ('before this leaves one machine'). If the answer is 'this stays a one-machine personal tool indefinitely', the trigger is the whole of the fix and the ADR should say so rather than deferring to a role that will never exist.

Whether the four Haiku routes want their effort retired or their model changed (§8 item 13). The audit records the parameter was dropped ×2 to ×3 per run with no measured quality consequence, but nothing measured what those roles would produce at a honoured low effort, so 'retire it' is the cheap answer rather than the proven one. A cheap check exists: `aer replay-draft` over an archived verdict reply is free.

Whether §4.3's 'checking the work — yes, in the interface' should be corrected in the record. The evidence walk is in the interface; the chain and artefact verification are not. Either the page gets built or the claim gets a qualifier, and the operator should choose which.

areaSummaries.summary: The roadmap is, for these two issues, empty. Every item in §2 and §3 is marked done except §2.8 (concept-map curation, operator work), §2.9 (report readability, written as maintenance), the Phase-6 one-machine gate (A5/A7/A8) and two commercial checks — and none of those four, built in full, would change a single judge's verdict or remove a single dead end the audit walked into. The audit's 28 findings and §8's sixteen decisions appear in the roadmap only as one paragraph of preamble (ROADMAP.md:55-63); §2, §3 and §4 gained no entry from any of them, and remaining-work.md was last touched 2026-09-04 (cb26dd5), a week before the pass ran, so its phase table has no row for any of this. Both documents also carry stale "next" pointers — §2 still says "§2.1 is next" (:120) and §3 still says "§3.1 is the one an operator is currently blocked by" (:391), both closed. The consequence for the plan being written: almost everything it proposes is a *new* item, not a re-ordering, so it cannot jump a queue that has nothing left in it — but it must be written into §2 and §3 with section numbers, because the repository's rule is that the roadmap is the authority on scope and an item that is not in it does not exist. The three deepest gaps are not in §8 either: no code anywhere writes `reports.rating`, the segment facts the platform already stores are filtered out of the evidence pack that needs them, and the Markdown the judges actually read drops every exhibit.
openQuestions: Why market capitalisation was withheld on AZN, AZN #2 and MTB when the feed worked on MSFT. The audit records the absence (§3.4) and its consequence (azn2/report.md:402) but never names the cause. It is settleable at no spend from the committed run exports in docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/ and the run store, by reading acquire_prices' step output for those three jobs.

Whether the operator's own universe is UK-listed. F-04 and §8.14 put a Companies House acquisition path to the operator, and the audit's fix narrowed the product documents to 'a filer with the SEC, which means any US listing and a UK plc with a 20-F'. If the operator mostly researches LSE-listed companies, the UK adapter is decisive for ISSUE 1 and belongs near the front; if not, it is a scope expansion that serves neither issue directly. Nothing in the repository settles which, and only the operator can.

Whether the judges should be re-run against the PDF rather than the exported Markdown. All eighteen judge reads used report.md (judges/reads.json), which drops every exhibit. How much of the practical verdict is the document and how much is the export is not separable from the present record; re-reading one existing PDF with the same rubric would separate them before any code is written.

Whether raising a section's evidence tier to T5 is compatible with ADR 0092's claim that granting web_search moved no trust boundary. The ADR's argument rests on search results reaching the model as an untrusted listing that is never citable; §8.12 proposes making some of them citable. The ADR itself does not anticipate that, so the new record has to say whether it amends 0092 or sits beside it.

What 're-measure a finished run' means for the audit trail. §8.10 asks it as one question about what re-runs after a late change, and F-22's residual is the concrete case: a £6.80 run that cannot be recovered. Whether a re-evaluation appends to the same job (ADR 0090's posture) or creates a new audit record is not settled anywhere, and the recovery-without-a-terminal item depends on the answer.

areaSummaries.summary: The September pass measured both issues well and left behind only half an instrument. The technical half is reproducible: `audit/driver/` drives runs through the platform's own services, `audit/scoring/` scores them from the record, and `audit/ledger.py` holds a £100 ceiling across both sides. The practical half — the eighteen judged reads and nine blind comparisons that produced the verdict "all six comparisons chose the console" — exists in the repository only as its output, `docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/judges/reads.json`; no code runs it, so a repeat would be a different instrument wearing the same name. ISSUE 1 has no instrument at all: "gate stops, dead ends, terminal escapes, values typed" were counted by hand from `driver.jsonl` and screenshots, the browser journey test clears the conditional gates from the test process rather than by clicking, and the audit's "gate waits" are the driver's polling intervals, not an operator's minutes. The cheapest credible re-measurement of ISSUE 2 is two subjects, three platform runs, zero new baselines and £31.50 — inside the £36.68 the audit left unspent — because the three September console notes can be reused and because the contingent freshness control need only be bought if the platform wins. Two audit scorers deserve promotion to permanent run-time metrics at zero model spend, but the numeral matcher must go in advisory with a mutation corpus, because it was calibrated to zero on the very reports it would be gating and its recall has never been measured.
openQuestions: What a re-measurement still would not establish, stated plainly: anything about Windows (§9, and §4.10 of the roadmap records that two of the three defects the manual sheet has found were invisible to CI by construction); a domestic UK filer live (F-04 is proved only offline, on the fake scene); the console itself rather than the same brief through the API with the same model, effort and search tool (§9); the matcher's recall, unless the mutation corpus is built (§9); whether the valuation a run produces is right rather than traceable (§9); anything about a bank until §8's decision 2 is taken (§9); and whether a human reader agrees with three model judges, which §4.4 exists to answer and no harness can.

Are the three lenses three judges or one opinion sampled three times? Across 9 comparisons and 6 dimensions the vote was 51 console, 3 equal, 0 platform, and on 'would you act on it' the three lenses agreed 9 times out of 9. That unanimity is either a very strong signal about the documents or an artefact of three prompts to one model sharing a prior, and nothing in reads.json distinguishes them. What would settle it: include one discriminating pair in the round where the lenses should disagree — for example the platform's MSFT report against the platform's own AZN report — and check that they do. Hypothesis, not established.

Does the platform's document improve because it is better, or because the September console note has gone stale? Settled only by the contingent freshness baseline in item 2, and only if the platform wins first.

Is 4 of 6 the right bar for ISSUE 2, or is 'at least split' the honest first milestone? This is the operator's call and it has to be made before the round, not after. My recommendation is 4 of 6 on 'better answers the brief' with the other five dimensions reported but not gated, because a platform that answers the brief better and still loses on argument is a different problem from one that loses everywhere.

How many live runs is reliability worth? Three of six reached an approved rendered report in September. Three of three in the re-measurement window is a weak proof of a reliability fix — the binomial arithmetic is unkind at n=3 — but six runs costs £48 and buys little the dead-end inventory does not. My recommendation is three runs plus a green dead-end inventory, and to say in the protocol that the reliability claim rests on the inventory rather than on the run count.
Whether the numeral matcher, once promoted, should ever become blocking. That needs the recall number the mutation corpus would produce, and it cannot be decided before it exists.

Nothing in the committed record says how the September judges were invoked — model, effort, context, whether each read was a fresh agent. reads.json holds the answers but not the configuration. If the re-measurement's judges differ in any of those, the two rounds are not comparable, and the only mitigation available now is to pin the new round's configuration explicitly in audit/judging/ and note that the September configuration is unrecorded.

items.title: The report disagrees with itself, and publishes unresolved accusations against its own headline numbers
items.problem: Every judge who read a platform report found it saying two incompatible things about a load-bearing figure, and found it shipping red-team entries at severity 5/5 asserting that its own margins, coverage and leverage are wrong — marked "Escalated for human decision at approval" and never decided. All three msft1 judges nominated the Executive Summary as the weakest paragraph for exactly this reason; all three azn2 judges nominated the disagreements log or the arithmetic it contaminates as the first thing to check. msft1 reader: "a reader cannot tell which half of the document to believe." msft1 operator (decisive field): "A reader with money at stake is told, by the document itself, not to trust its headline numbers." azn2 reader: "I cannot trust a single headline number in A on A's own account." Concrete instances, all inside one document: msft1's Executive Summary says "No discounted cash flow, cost of equity, weighted average cost of capital, terminal value, value per share or peer multiple sits on this record" thirty lines below an At-a-glance table printing WACC 9.3% and Value per share $485.29, and above a full DCF section; msft1's Key Risks says "no prior-period comparatives sit here to test durability" while footnotes [^42]–[^56] carry five years of gross, operating and net margin; msft1's Key Risks says operating cash flow "is not among the figures available here" while six sections cite $182.9bn; azn2's header says "Non-binding view: no view reached" while its Investment Thesis says "We therefore hold a constructive but low-confidence view"; azn2's Balance Sheet says "Interest cover is not established by the figures available" while Earnings Quality, Growth Outlook and Scenarios all quote 8.11x; azn2's Cost of Capital table says beta 0.4 and capex intensity 0.033377 while Prior Research Comparison says "Confirmed at 0.3" and "Confirmed at 0.05". The self-accusation compounds it: azn2 sceptic traced the challenge footnotes and found them to be FY2021/FY2022 calculations set against FY2025 claims — "That took footnote forensics, not minutes, and no reader should have to do it."
items.rootCause: Two independent causes. (1) No step's subject is the assembled document. The 18 sections fan out concurrently and, by design, "each depends on the evidence pack and on nothing another section produces" — src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3336-3338; the revise step is also per-section ("the sections the material challenges attack are redrafted once", :1808-1820), so nothing ever reads the whole draft for agreement. The eleven validator metrics measure within-section and per-calculation properties — numerical_consistency is calculation-replay divergence (src/aer/eval/metrics.py:406-418), presentation_integrity counts UUIDs, gap sentences and process language (src/aer/eval/runtime.py:297-308) — so azn2 scored all eleven green while saying three different things about interest cover. There is no cross-section consistency metric. (2) An unsettled challenge is rendered verbatim into the published report: src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:325 maps resolution "escalated" to the literal string "Escalated for human decision at approval.", and ADR 0095's challenge_brief writes an advisory brief for the gate-3 screen but nothing writes the operator's settlement back into the document, so the approved artefact carries the accusation with no answer. The period-mismatch that generated the false accusations is fixed in code (src/aer/services/red_team.py:330-348 now selects one row per calculation name at its newest period, with the period stated, and the comment records this exact audit incident) — but azn2, run after that fix, still shipped eight escalated entries, so the fix removed one source of spurious challenges and not the shipping of unresolved ones.

items.recommendation: Do both halves. (1) Add a reconciliation step whose subject is the frozen assembled draft — ADR 0087's frozen test applies unchanged — that does two things a section writer structurally cannot: a deterministic pass that indexes every figure printed anywhere in the document by name and period and refuses the run when the same named figure appears with two values or when a section asserts a figure is unavailable that another section prints; and a model pass (a new role, so ADR 0035 requires a record) that rewrites only the offending sentences, proposing no figure of its own. The deterministic half is the load-bearing one and should ship first: it turns every instance above into a gate stop rather than a published contradiction. (2) Make an escalated challenge unpublishable: gate 2 already forces the operator to settle each one (ADR 0095 briefs them); write the settlement back into the disagreement row and render the decision — 'Kept: …' / 'Accepted: …' with the operator's rationale — so no approved report can contain the word 'escalated'. This is an amendment to ADR 0095's scope, not a reversal: it still briefs rather than decides, it just refuses to ship undecided.

items.title: The run fetches a price series and the report never states a price, so every per-share figure is unanchored
items.problem: Eight of nine comparisons name this in the decisive field. msft1 operator: "A's header says 'Non-binding view: no view reached' and A never states a share price or market capitalisation anywhere, so its value-per-share figures cannot be compared to anything." azn2 reader: "A prints no share price at all — I grepped; there is none — so its outputs of $169.80 and $333.48 cannot be compared to anything." The azn2 operator judge's first_thing_to_check is entirely this: "One NYSE ADR is half an ordinary share, so $169.80 is either roughly fair value against the London line (~£130 ≈ $175) or 100% upside against the ~$85 ADR. Nothing else in the note is decision-relevant until that is settled." The knock-on is worse than the omission: because no market capitalisation reaches the WACC, the DCF is discounted at book-value weights, and the report's own Recorded Caveats say so — "the equity weight is understated, the debt weight overstated, and the resulting WACC too low. Every valuation discounted at it is correspondingly too high." Two judges praised that caveat as the strongest paragraph in the document and then declined to use the valuation it discredits. The price series is in the Sources table on both runs and appears in no figure.
items.rootCause: The acquired price is computed into a market capitalisation only inside the comps pipeline: src/aer/services/price_acquisition.py:234 and :358 compute it, and src/aer/services/comps_run.py:391-410 is the only consumer. When the comps table is empty — which is every run to date, see the peers item — the price-derived figures leave no trace in the document. The front page's curated headline set has no price and no market-capitalisation row at all (src/aer/render/glance.py:98-110). The DCF takes book weights independently and stamps its own excuse: src/aer/sections/valuation_method.py:247 appends "(book values — this run holds no market prices)" whenever basis == 'book'. And the licence position is not the blocker people assume: ADR 0030 route 2, as the operator determined on 2026-08-09, permits derived figures — a market capitalisation, a multiple, a beta (src/aer/services/price_acquisition.py:19-24; src/aer/fetch/policy.py:192 sets derived_figures_publishable True for EODHD). What ADR 0030 forbids is the series and charts of it. A market capitalisation, a P/E and an upside percentage are already publishable; a printed raw closing price is the one genuinely open licence question.

items.title: A rating is never recorded, so the header announces "no view reached" over a thesis that states one
items.problem: Eight of nine comparisons name the absent view in the decisive field. msft1 operator, on what the console has that the platform lacks, opens with one word: "A decision." msft1 sceptic: "for a note asked for a 12-month view, that is a non-delivery." The audit's §4.1 table records an investment view stated in 1 of 6 platform reads against 6 of 6 console reads. But the record contains a sharper finding than 'the tool states no view': on azn2 the judges recorded view_stated true 3/3 and argued true 3/3 — because the Investment Thesis does state and argue a view — while the header six lines from the top still says "Non-binding view: no view reached". The document's first substantive line contradicts its thesis, and all three judges still said no. So this item is necessary and, on its own, provably not sufficient: fixing the header without fixing contradiction, price and missing figures changes nothing, which is exactly what the azn2 re-run measured.
items.rootCause: `reports.rating` is nullable so that a run unable to reach a view can say so (src/aer/db/models/report.py:12-16,73) — but nothing ever writes it. src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3765 assigns `report.rating = None` unconditionally at publication, on every path. The renderer then prints `header.rating or 'no view reached'` (src/aer/render/markdown.py:162). No agent role may supply one either: the section writer's envelope keeps "ratings and valuation ranges unrepresentable" by `extra="forbid"` (src/aer/agents/section_writer.py:16). There is no gate field, no role, and no deterministic derivation. The sentence is a constant, not a finding — and the thesis section is free to argue a view in prose that the header then denies.

items.recommendation: Give the run a place to put a view, and make the header incapable of disagreeing with the thesis. Whether the tool may state a rating at all, and in what vocabulary, is the operator's decision: the framing constraint is that it stays a non-binding personal view on a personal research tool, which the existing disclaimer already carries on every surface. If the answer is no, then the honest fix is to delete the header line rather than print a denial, and to have the thesis section own the view in prose — but the record says a document with no conclusion will keep losing.

items.title: The operator's focus questions reach the planner and nothing else, and no gate asks whether they were answered
items.problem: Across 27 focus-question readings of platform documents the judges recorded 1 yes, 17 partly and 9 no; across the same 27 for the console, 6 yes, 21 partly and 0 no. Not one platform run answered any question 'yes' on all three lenses. The judges' descriptions are consistent: the report identifies the right mechanism and then declines to size it. msft1 operator on Q1: "Direction argued, magnitude absent." msft1 sceptic on Q2: the note "declines both halves". azn2 operator on Q1: "The note states four separate times that it cannot be answered." Meanwhile the console note explicitly labels its sections against the brief — "The patent-cliff question (part 2 of 3 posed in the brief)" — and answers each with an arithmetic it shows. The judges noticed the difference in kind: the platform report reads as a survey of the company's accounts that happens to have been commissioned by a brief; the console note reads as a reply to a question.
items.rootCause: `ResearchRequest.focus_questions` (src/aer/db/models/request.py:100) is consumed in exactly two places: the planner's user turn (src/aer/agents/planner.py:272-275) and the plan critic's (src/aer/agents/plan_critic.py:158-160). It reaches no section writer, no researcher, no red team, no validator. The section writer sees only the planner's derived per-section `focus` line (src/aer/agents/section_writer.py, SectionWriterInput.focus; assembled at vertical_slice_v1.py:3344-3348), so the operator's own wording survives only insofar as the planner chose to paraphrase it into a section brief. And nothing anywhere measures coverage: the eleven metrics are about citations, figures, replay and presentation; none asks whether the document answers the questions it was commissioned to answer.

items.title: The bear case has no number because no run has ever created a scenario
items.problem: "A bear case with a number attached" is absent on all three msft1 reads and, on azn2, present only as its own inputs. msft1's Scenarios section says outright: "None of these swings can be sized without recorded scenario outputs, and we do not supply figures we cannot source", and its bear case concludes "the direction is assertable and the magnitude is not". The rendered Scenarios table degenerates to six rows labelled "Base anchor — gross margin, FY2026" and so on — FY2026 actuals, nine times over on azn2, which the azn2 operator judge caught: "A's 'Scenarios' table moves nothing — it lists FY2025 actuals nine times." The console, by contrast, printed bear/base/bull at $186/$341/$488 with 25/50/25 probabilities on msft1 and $70.72/$126.98/$203.48 on azn, every input changed explicitly. Three judges named the probability-weighted scenario set among the things the console has that the platform lacks. The 25-cell WACC-by-terminal-growth heatmap the platform does record is, as two judges observed, not a bear case at all — on azn2 its lowest cell ($227.13) sits above the headline $169.80, "so the published 'range' has no downside in it at all".
items.rootCause: The scenario machinery is complete and unwired. `aer.services.scenarios.create_scenario` (src/aer/services/scenarios.py:70) and `set_override` (:111) have no caller anywhere in `src/` — a repository-wide grep finds them only in tests (tests/test_valuation_service.py, tests/test_assumptions.py, tests/test_residual_income_run.py). The DB models (Scenario, ScenarioOverride), the resolver that treats a scenario as a diff on the confirmed assumptions, the calculation path and the `scenario_bridge` chart builder (src/aer/services/exhibits.py) all exist; no workflow step creates one. So `scenarios_for_request` returns nothing, and the section falls back to base anchors. The only recorded variation on any run is the sensitivity grid, which varies the discount rate and terminal growth — financial parameters, not operating assumptions — so it can never express 'what if the business does worse'.

items.title: Every peer is excluded on every run, and the report words it as a judgement about the peers
items.problem: No run has ever produced a peer multiple — 5 of 5, per the audit's completeness measure — and the sentence the reader meets is: "A comparable-company analysis was attempted as at 11 September 2026, but every one of the eight proposed peers was excluded, because this research holds no filings and no price series for it, and a peer multiple needs both." The eight are not even named. msft1's Industry & Competitive Positioning names no company at all; azn2's describes rivals as "a small set of research-intensive multinationals". The azn2 sceptic noted the consequence for the valuation: with no comps "the DCF has no cross-check" — a criticism he also made of the console, which is the one place the two documents fail alike.

items.title: A 20-F filer gets no interim results at all, and the five newest current reports are spent on administrative filings
items.problem: AZN's report, dated 12 September 2026, is built on a financial record that stops at 31 December 2025 and compares it against 30 June 2025 — nine months stale at its own as-of date, and it says so: "no FY2026 interim results are available, so this picture may be stale as of September 2026." All three azn comparisons and two of three azn2 comparisons name staleness in the decisive field. The console had H1 2026 revenue $30,672m, Core EPS $5.21, OCF down to $6,224m, net debt $26,912m, FY2026 guidance reconfirmed 27 July 2026, and the 9 July CARDIO-TTRansform failure with its 9–10% share reaction. azn sceptic: "A note dated 11 September 2026 that never sees H1 2026 cannot say whether a balance sheet supports anything 'through the horizon'." Separately, 'management guidance or outlook' is absent in 6 of 6 msft1 and azn2 reads, and azn2's Catalysts section fails its own policy with "its claims cite 0" sources — no dated event inside the twelve-month horizon, which is the horizon the brief asks about.
items.rootCause: Three compounding narrowings. (1) `QUARTERLY_FORMS` is `{10-Q, 10-Q/A}` only (src/aer/sources/sec/submissions.py:52). A foreign private issuer files no 10-Q — its interims arrive as 6-K — so a 20-F filer structurally receives zero interim financial statements. (2) 6-K is in `CURRENT_FORMS` (src/aer/services/filings.py:65) but only the five newest are taken (`MAX_CURRENT_REPORTS = 5`, :69), and AZN's newest 6-Ks are administrative — azn2's Business Overview names exactly "a bond offering, admission of securities to trading, total voting rights" — so the July interim-results 6-K never made the window; azn2's Sources table holds only two 6-Ks, both press releases of 8 September 2026. (3) The substance of a results 6-K is in its EX-99 exhibit, which is not fetched at all (see the exhibits item), so even a selected one would yield a cover page. On top of that, news and consensus can never reach a section: every built-in section's evidence policy sets `max_tier: T4_LICENSED_MARKET` (migrations/versions/0023_the_eighteen_section_spine.py:43-48), so T5_SECONDARY documents a run admits are cited nowhere — the audit's F-21 and §8 item 12.
