items.recommendation: This is §8 item 8 and remains the operator's to decide, but the audit's framing understates it: the definition is not untested, it is live and worth roughly 5-7% of the appraisal on M&T. The minimum honest answer is to state both conventions on the rows they affect — 'book value is total equity including preferred' and 'per share on the FY2025 diluted weighted average of 158,791,000' — which is a change to `_treatment_rows` and `_shares_input` in src/aer/sections/valuation_method.py:315-341 and costs nothing but words. The better answer is to map a preferred-equity concept, subtract it from the opening book, and prefer a point-in-time share count over a weighted average for a balance-sheet-dated value. That is a modelling change and needs the ADR.

options.name: State the conventions
options.change: Add the basis to the 'Premium to book value' and 'Shares outstanding' rows and to the recorded caveats.
options.risk: The figures stay wrong; the reader is told which way.

options.name: Common-equity basis
options.change: Map a preferred-equity concept, subtract preferred (and non-controlling interests) from `opening_book_value`, and take the share count from the balance-sheet date rather than the year's average.
options.cost: A few sessions: a new concept with its tags, a change to `_inputs_from`, a change to `share_count`'s preference for a point-in-time valuation, and the caveats.
options.risk: Changes every bank and insurer appraisal the platform has produced. Needs the ADR and a stated migration position on prior reports.

items.adrSubject: A bank's opening book value is common equity, and a per-share appraisal divides by the count in issue at the valuation date rather than the period's weighted average.
items.tests: tests/test_residual_income_run.py — a filer reporting preferred equity produces an opening book value net of it, and a per-share figure on the point-in-time count; a filer reporting neither is unchanged. A property test that value per share × shares reconciles to the equity value under both bases.
items.acceptance: M&T's appraisal recomputed on common equity and the July 2026 count, with both bases named on the rows, and a stated book value per share beside the appraised value so a reader can see the premium for themselves.
items.challengeNote: Two additions. (1) There is better evidence than the EPS reconciliation the item infers preferred from: report.md:396 states outright that common equity was $27.946 billion at 30 June 2026 against the $29,177m at 31 December 2025 used as the opening book — a $1.23bn (4.2%) gap the document itself prints, no inference needed. (2) The 'subtract non-controlling interests' half is underdetermined as written: `StockholdersEquityIncludingPortionAttributableToNoncontrollingInterest` also maps to `equity` (src/aer/core/concepts.py:280), so the `equity` fact may already be inclusive or exclusive of NCI depending on which tag the filer used, and the ADR must say which tag wins before any subtraction is safe. That is extra work the 'a few sessions' estimate does not carry, though it stays within range.
items.invariantRisk: ADR 0070 (a bank is valued on the spread over its book value) records what the opening book is; redefining it as common equity amends that decision. The item flags adrNeeded correctly, and the ADR must also state a migration position for reports already produced on the old basis.

items.title: The residual-income answer is illegible to a private investor: no price, no book value per share, and the sensitivity rendered somewhere else
items.problem: The method is well explained — better, I think, than a console note would manage, because it is assembled from the ledger rather than written. The answer is not usable. A reader is given '$184.47' and '$186.53' per share with no share price anywhere in the document, no book value per share to compare them against, and no way to see that the two figures differ by 1.1% because the assumed return on equity (9.4%) sits seven basis points above the cost of equity (9.33%). The commentary calls the gap between them 'the price of franchise durability'. It is $2.06. And the only two surfaces that would show the sensitivity — the football field and the heatmap — say '*Rendered in the HTML and PDF editions of this report.*' and leave twenty-five bare footnote markers in the Markdown the reader was handed.
items.rootCause: Four separate causes with one effect. (1) No price reaches the report: the run held a T4 licensed market document dated one day before the as-of date and the draft nonetheless states that price and tangible book are unrecorded — the run's own adversary caught this. (2) Book value per share is never computed or shown, although `premium_to_book` and `opening_book_value` are both recorded, so the reader cannot tell that $184.47 is $0.72 above book ($29,177m ÷ 158,791,000 = $183.75). (3) `_treatment_rows` (src/aer/sections/valuation_method.py:315-341) presents the two treatments as a table of point estimates with no spread and no statement of how thin the excess return is. (4) The exhibits are placeholders in Markdown by design.
evidence: docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/report.md:347-406 — the whole valuation section
report.md:370-378 — the two terminal methods, $184.47 / $186.53, premiums $115m and $442m, shares 158,791,000
report.md:392 — 'The distance between them… is the price of franchise durability'
report.md:62 and :400 — 'No price or tangible book value is recorded'; 'this appraisal is internally consistent but unbenchmarked'
report.md:535 — the run's own red team: 'The source index contains a T4 licensed market document dated 2026-09-11, one day before the as-of date'
report.md:402-406, 434-438 — football field and heatmap as placeholders with 2 and 25 footnote markers
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/scorecard.md:9 — 'headline missing: market_capitalisation, enterprise_value, ev_ebitda, pe'
audit §4 — six of six judges would not act on the platform's report, the reasons including 'the figures a research note is read for are withheld'
items.recommendation: Three changes, in this order, and none of them is more prose. First, put book value per share on the same table as the appraised value — it is a division of two figures the run already records, it is a traced calculation, and it converts '$184.47' from a number into a claim ('worth 0.4% more than its book'). Second, settle whether a price may appear (audit §8 item 1 and ADR 0030/0034's territory) — without one, no valuation section in this platform answers an investor's question, and that is the single largest gap against the console for every sector, not only banks. Third, render the football field and the heatmap in the Markdown edition too, even coarsely, or say in words what the grid's corners are: a sensitivity nobody can see is a sensitivity nobody has. Also state, from the recorded inputs rather than from the writer, that the spread between the assumed return and the cost of equity is 7bp and that the appraisal is correspondingly unstable — the commentary gestures at this and the figures do not.
items.tests: tests/test_residual_income_run.py — a book-value-per-share calculation is recorded for every residual-income run and appears in the section block. A render test asserting the Markdown edition of a football field carries the band values as text, not only a placeholder line.
items.acceptance: A private investor reading M&T's valuation section can answer, without leaving the page: what is it worth per share, what is its book value per share, what does it trade at, and how much does the answer move if the sustainable return on equity is 50bp lower.
items.challengeNote: Split the item. Change 1 (book value per share on the same table) and change 3 (render the football field and heatmap bands as text in Markdown) need no ADR and are measurable — publish them as their own item and ship them. Change 2 (settle whether a price may appear) is a different kind of thing entirely and must carry adrNeeded:true; it is also the one the audit's judges actually refused on, so it should not be buried as a middle bullet. Separately, change 1 depends on the item above, not just on the revenue fix: a book value per share computed from total equity at Dec-2025 over the FY2025 diluted average is the same two conventions the item above calls wrong, so shipping it first publishes a traced figure on a basis the next change will move. Add residual-income-book-and-share-count to dependsOn, or state both conventions on the row as that item's cheap option recommends.
items.invariantRisk: ADR 0034 (a withheld figure is a type with no field for it) and ADR 0030 route 2. A share price or market capitalisation on a report surface is precisely what `for_audience(SHAREABLE)` is built to make structurally impossible — the shareable type has no field for it. Putting a price into the valuation section requires a new ADR superseding or amending 0034, not a rendering change; the item says 'ADR 0030/0034's territory' in prose while recording adrNeeded:false.

items.title: A bank's residual-income appraisal is headed 'Valuation — Discounted Cash Flow'
items.problem: ADR 0029's acceptance criterion is that a bank ticker cannot produce a discounted cash flow by any route. M&T's did not. The section its reader lands on is nonetheless headed 'Valuation — Discounted Cash Flow'. A reader scanning headings — which is how a research note is read — is told the opposite of what the platform did, and the correction is four paragraphs down.
items.rootCause: The heading is the section definition's contract title, seeded by migration and stored on the row: `"title": "Valuation \N{EM DASH} Discounted Cash Flow"` (migrations/versions/0044_the_valuation_method_is_rendered_not_written.py:59, first seeded at migrations/versions/0023_the_eighteen_section_spine.py:288 and :451 under the key `valuation_dcf`). `aer.sections.valuation_method` branches on the model for the body — the method note, the driver rows, the treatment rows (src/aer/sections/valuation_method.py:117-118, 142-152, 181-182) — but the title is not the renderer's to change.
evidence: docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/report.md:347
migrations/versions/0044_the_valuation_method_is_rendered_not_written.py:59
migrations/versions/0023_the_eighteen_section_spine.py:288,451
src/aer/sections/valuation_method.py:100-158,181-182
docs/adr/0029-the-sector-block-is-a-type-not-a-check.md; docs/adr/0070-a-bank-is-valued-on-the-spread-over-its-book-value.md
items.recommendation: Render the heading from the model the value step recorded, the way the body already is: 'Valuation — Residual Income' when `produced['model'] == 'residual_income'`, 'Valuation — Discounted Cash Flow' otherwise, and a neutral 'Valuation' when no model ran. The section *key* stays `valuation_dcf` — it is an identifier, and renaming it would churn every stored row for a display string. This is a render-time title override, not a new section version, so it needs no migration and no ADR; it is the smallest change on this list with a visible effect on a reader.
items.tests: A render test: a job whose value step recorded `residual_income` produces a document whose valuation heading contains 'Residual Income' and does not contain 'Discounted Cash Flow'; a standard job is unchanged. `presentation_integrity` must still pass on both.
items.acceptance: M&T's document, re-assembled from its own record, heads its valuation 'Valuation — Residual Income'.
items.challengeNote: One thing to check before committing to 'no migration': the title also appears inside the stored JSON contract at migration 0044:59 (`_CONTRACT['title']`). If section content or `presentation_integrity` is validated against that contract's title, a render-time override will either fail validation or force the contract to change after all. Verify how the contract title is consumed before promising an hour.

items.title: None of the five metrics the platform itself requires for a bank is computed anywhere
items.problem: `SECTOR_PROFILES['banks']` declares five metrics 'without which a report on that sector is not worth reading': net interest margin, CET1 ratio, cost-income ratio, loan-loss provisions and tangible book value per share. All five are absent from every bank run, and `metric_disclosure` would say so — except the disclosure never reaches the document at all (see `gate-document-is-not-the-report`). The result is a bank note that carries none of the five figures a bank is read for and does not admit it.
items.rootCause: The five strings appear in `src/` only as the profile's `required_metrics` (src/aer/core/sectors.py:159-165); `tangible_book_value_per_share` appears once more as a comps denominator (src/aer/calc/comps.py:507), in a table that is empty on every run. No ratio definition, no calc function and no concept produces any of them. `metric_disclosure` (src/aer/services/sectors.py:330-346) correctly reports all five missing, and `sector_note_for` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3609-3633) correctly builds the paragraph — which is then dropped on the floor by the review-page assembly.
evidence: src/aer/core/sectors.py:159-165 and the docstring at :114-116
grep across src/: the five names occur only at src/aer/core/sectors.py:160-164 and src/aer/calc/comps.py:507
src/aer/services/sectors.py:280-346
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/report.md — no metric-disclosure paragraph anywhere; the model instead writes around the gap at :30, :98 and :127
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/run-export.json — 643 calculations, none named for any of the five
items.recommendation: Two of the five are reachable from concepts already mapped and should be built with the revenue fix, because they are what turns a bank's report from thin into useful. `tangible_book_value_per_share` = (equity − goodwill − intangible_assets) ÷ shares: every input is mapped and M&T's run holds all of them (equity $29,177m, goodwill $8,465m, intangibles $48m). `loan_loss_provisions` has its concept mapped (`provision_for_credit_losses`, src/aer/core/concepts.py:212) and needs only a ratio row and the CECL-era tag, which M&T's own unplaced list would name. The other three need inputs the concept map does not carry — non-interest expense for the cost-income ratio, average earning assets for the net interest margin, and CET1, which most filers do not tag in us-gaap at all — so they should stay declared-and-missing and be honestly disclosed. Getting the disclosure into the document (the other item) is worth more than any one of them.
items.tests: tests/test_ratios.py — tangible book value per share computed from equity, goodwill, intangibles and shares, absent with a stated reason when any input is missing, and never coercing an absent intangible to zero. tests/test_sectors_service.py — `metric_disclosure` for a bank run that computed two of five names exactly those two as present and three as missing.
items.acceptance: M&T's report carries a tangible book value per share (roughly $132 on $20.66bn of tangible common equity over 156m shares, to be confirmed from the run's own rows) beside its $184 appraisal, and a paragraph naming the three metrics it still does not carry.
items.challengeNote: `metric_disclosure` matches `required_metrics` against `Calculation.name` strings (src/aer/services/sectors.py:341-343, fed by the calculation names collected at vertical_slice_v1.py:3624-3627). So a new ratio only satisfies the disclosure if the persisted calculation name is exactly `tangible_book_value_per_share` — a ratio *key* is not automatically the traced calculation's name, and nobody checked which string `compute_ratios` persists. Verify that before writing the test, or the test will assert a disclosure that never flips to present. Also amend the dependsOn rationale: the disclosure is absent from mtb's document because the run never reached the render step at all, not because the review page dropped it (see the verdict on gate-document-is-not-the-report).

items.title: The bank profile refuses one meaningless ratio and computes seven others
items.problem: `not_meaningful_ratios` for banks carries a single entry, debt-to-equity. The M&T run nonetheless computed and made available to the drafter: asset turnover (the figure that should have tripped the plausibility floor), free cash flow, capital expenditure to depreciation, a depreciation rate, an interest-capitalisation gap, cash conversion and an accruals ratio. Several are not merely uninformative for a depository but actively misleading — the run's own adversary observed that 'a cash conversion far above one at a bank usually reflects loan-held-for-sale and trading flows rather than earnings quality'. Every one of them is a figure the writer may cite and a reader may act on.
items.rootCause: `SectorProfile.not_meaningful_ratios` (src/aer/core/sectors.py:132-135) is the right mechanism and is barely populated: the banks profile declares one pair (src/aer/core/sectors.py:172-180). `compute_ratios` honours it properly (src/aer/calc/ratios.py:848-896), turning a listed key into an absent ratio carrying the sector's own reason — so the cost of adding entries is a tuple, not code. The quality and cash-use suites (`aer.calc.quality`, `aer.calc.cash_uses`) have no equivalent mechanism at all, so nothing can suppress cash conversion or the accruals ratio for a sector that does not mean them.
evidence: src/aer/core/sectors.py:132-135,171-180
src/aer/calc/ratios.py:848-896

docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/run-export.json — calculation names: asset_turnover ×5, free_cash_flow ×3, capex_to_depreciation ×2, depreciation_rate ×4, interest_capitalisation_gap ×3, cash_conversion ×5, accruals_ratio ×5
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/mtb/report.md:539 — the run's red team on cash conversion at a bank
src/aer/core/sectors.py:181-183 — the profile's own warning that free cash flow to the firm is not meaningful here
items.recommendation: Populate the banks profile with the ratios that genuinely compute and do not mean anything here — asset turnover, free cash flow, days sales outstanding and the cash conversion cycle — each with the sentence a reader should be given, in the style of the existing debt-to-equity entry. Do not list ratios that are already absent for want of an undefined input (gross margin, operating margin, EBITDA margin, interest cover, ROIC, net debt to EBITDA all fall out of `undefined_concepts` at src/aer/core/sectors.py:171): the module's own comment says listing them twice says the same thing in two voices. Extend the same `not_meaningful` mechanism to `assess_quality` and `assess_cash_uses` so cash conversion and the accruals ratio can be refused with a reason for a depository — that part is a small design change, not a data edit. Note the interaction: under the withhold option, asset turnover and the margins become absent for want of revenue and would carry the wrong reason ('no fact for this concept') unless they are listed here.
items.tests: tests/test_ratios.py — a bank profile refuses asset turnover and free cash flow with the profile's own sentence attached, and an unclassified company still computes both. tests/test_sectors_service.py — every key in a profile's `not_meaningful_ratios` is a real ratio key and none of them is also in `undefined_concepts`, so the two mechanisms cannot disagree.
items.acceptance: M&T's report shows no asset turnover, free cash flow, days sales outstanding or cash conversion cycle, and where a reader would have looked for one there is a sentence saying why a bank does not have it.
items.challengeNote: Drop days sales outstanding and the cash conversion cycle from the proposed banks list. Both are real ratio keys (src/aer/calc/ratios.py:796, :826) and neither computed on the M&T run — no calculation row of either name exists among the 643 — because a bank reports no receivables or inventory line, so they are already absent for want of their inputs. src/aer/core/sectors.py:128-131 says explicitly that such a ratio must not be listed, since doing so 'would say the same thing in two voices'. The defensible additions are the ones that genuinely computed: asset_turnover and free_cash_flow, plus capex_to_depreciation, depreciation_rate and interest_capitalisation_gap if the operator wants them refused too. The effort is also understated once the second half is counted: extending the `not_meaningful` mechanism to two pure modules, threading it through `analyse_company`, and keeping both under mypy --strict is more than the 'a session' the data edit takes — call it two, which is inside tolerance but should be stated as two pieces of work rather than one. The acceptance criterion inherits the same error and should name only the ratios that would otherwise have been computed.

items.title: The form offers LSE, takes the money, then dies at acquire
items.problem: An operator picks LSE in the exchange select, fills in the brief, waits for the planner, reads the critique, approves a costed plan at gate 1 — and the run then fails at `acquire` with a ticker-resolution error. About £0.55 of model spend and one human decision are gone before the platform says the thing it knew before the operator typed anything: it cannot research a domestic UK listing.
items.rootCause: `_EXCHANGE_CHOICES = sorted(SUPPORTED_EXCHANGES)` (`src/aer/web/routes.py:79`) and `SUPPORTED_EXCHANGES` contains "LSE" (`src/aer/core/universe.py:70`). `check_universe` (`src/aer/core/universe.py:172-215`) tests venue, OTC status, fund naming and micro-cap, and has no rule for "this venue has no acquisition path", so `services/requests.py:216` admits the request. The first code that can tell is `_acquire`, which calls `client.resolve_entity` on the `sec_client` only (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:2228`). The steps before it — `plan` and `critique_plan` — both spend (`vertical_slice_v1.py:401,406-410`).
evidence: docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:367 — use case 3, 'A domestic UK filer (LSE): no'
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:470-492 — F-04
src/aer/web/routes.py:79
src/aer/core/universe.py:70
src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:2228 (audit cites 2226; the file has since shifted two lines, cf. F-03)
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/azn2/steps.json — plan £0.1569 and critique_plan £0.3906 both complete before `acquire`
src/aer/services/requests.py:205-233
items.recommendation: Separate *researchable* venues from *supported* venues and refuse at request creation with a message that names the route that does work. Do not simply drop LSE from `SUPPORTED_EXCHANGES`: `services/watchlist.py:206` shares `check_universe`, and `services/listings.py:58` plus `calc/prices.py:120` make an LSE holding fully dealable and priceable today — removing the venue would stop an operator watching or holding a London line they legitimately own. A new `RESEARCHABLE_EXCHANGES` (or a `research_supported` flag on the exclusion rule) checked only from `services/requests.py` keeps the book's venue list intact while the research surface stops promising what it cannot do.
items.tests: A request-creation test that asserts an LSE payload is refused with an `unsupported_for_research` rule and a message naming the US-listing route; a watchlist test that asserts the same LSE symbol is still followable, so the two lists cannot silently re-merge. `audit/smoke.py:120-148` currently asserts `uk_refusal_status == "FAILED"` — it must move to asserting a clean refusal at creation, or the harness will fail on the fix.
items.acceptance: Submitting the audit's own Tesco brief (`audit/subjects.py:282-294`) through the web form produces a field-level refusal on the exchange with zero model spend and no job row, instead of a FAILED run costing £0.55.

options.name: Refuse at creation
options.change: Add a research-scope rule to `check_universe`'s caller in `services/requests.py`, keep `SUPPORTED_EXCHANGES` as the venue list.
options.risk: An operator who *could* have used the US line is refused without being told so — mitigated by the message in the next item.

options.name: Pre-flight resolution before gate 1
options.change: Resolve the ticker against EDGAR's table at request creation, as ADR 0093 already does for a never-seen listing in the portfolio's third door, and refuse or confirm there.
options.cost: A session; one free SEC fetch per request.
options.risk: Puts a network call in a validation path that is pure by design; needs the ADR 0093 precedent argued explicitly.

options.name: Warn only
options.change: Leave the form as it is and add an inline note that LSE cannot be researched yet.
options.risk: A note does not stop a run. The dead end and the £0.55 survive.

items.challengeNote: The `dependsOn` is backwards and should be dropped. If an LSE request is refused at creation, the resolution message this item depends on never fires for an LSE request at all — `resolve_ticker` is only reached from `_acquire`, and `_acquire` only runs on a request that was admitted. Item 2 becomes reachable only for non-LSE venue mismatches (a NASDAQ symbol typed as NYSE) and for the audit harness, which bypasses the web form. Ship item 1 first, unblocked.
items.invariantRisk: None for the recommended option. Option 2 ("pre-flight resolution before gate 1") would: `check_universe` lives in `src/aer/core/universe.py`, which CLAUDE.md requires to be mypy --strict, pure and free of I/O. The item says the call would sit in `services/requests.py`, which keeps core clean — but that must be stated as a constraint on the option, not left implicit, or the obvious implementation puts a fetch inside the core module.

items.title: The refusal tells an operator that their own company is 'a different company'
items.problem: F-04's message fix is correct for Tesco and wrong for exactly the UK case that works. Ask for AstraZeneca, AZN, LSE and the platform answers: 'AZN is in the SEC's ticker file, but on NYSE rather than LSE, where it belongs to ASTRAZENECA PLC. That is a different company from the one this request names…'. It is the same company, the 20-F route is open, and the operator is told to go away.
items.rootCause: `resolve_ticker` builds the message from the matched records alone and never sees the requested company name, so it cannot tell 'the symbol belongs to somebody else' from 'the symbol belongs to you, on another venue' (`src/aer/sources/sec/tickers.py:246-270`). `resolve_entity` is called with the ticker and exchange and nothing else (`src/aer/sources/sec/client.py:214`, `vertical_slice_v1.py:2228`), although `ResearchRequest` holds `company_name` — it is what `check_universe` already reads at creation.
evidence: src/aer/sources/sec/tickers.py:241-270 — the narrowed-to-empty branch and its message
tests/test_sec_tickers.py:149-160 — asserts 'a different company' unconditionally
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:485-492 — F-04's message fix
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:368 — use case 4, 'A UK plc through its 20-F: yes, with the peer gap'
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/azn2/run-export.json — the AZN run was commissioned on NYSE, 12 source documents, 43/43 citations verified
items.recommendation: Pass the requested company name into resolution and branch the message on whether the matched filer is the same business. When it is, say so plainly and name the route: 'AstraZeneca PLC files with the SEC as a foreign private issuer. Its filings are reachable on NYSE — commission this request there.' When it is not, keep the Tesco wording exactly as it is. This is the cheapest honest interim in this whole area and it turns a dead end into a working instruction. It must ship together with a statement of the per-share basis (audit F-28, §8 item 3): telling a UK operator to use the depositary line while the valuation divides by the ordinary share count is how 'roughly fair value' and '100 % upside' become the same number.
items.tests: A resolution test with a UK-plc record listed on NYSE and a requested name that matches, asserting the message names the venue as a route rather than the filer as a stranger; the existing TSCO test kept unchanged, so the two cases cannot collapse into one message again.
items.acceptance: Driving 'AstraZeneca PLC, AZN, LSE' offline through the real ticker table produces a refusal whose text, read cold, tells the operator to re-commission on NYSE — and driving 'Tesco PLC, TSCO, LSE' still names Tractor Supply Company as a different business.

options.name: Name-matched branch
options.change: Compare the requested name with the matched filer's and emit one of two messages.
options.risk: Name matching is fuzzy ('ASTRAZENECA PLC' vs 'AstraZeneca plc'); a normalised comparison with a conservative fallback to the existing wording keeps the failure safe.

options.name: Always list the venues and let the operator judge
options.change: Drop the 'different company' claim entirely and list the filer names and venues without asserting identity.

items.challengeNote: Impact is moderate, not large. Restate the problem as "the refusal hedges instead of naming the route", quoting the full sentence. Note also that `resolve_entity` is on the `@runtime_checkable` SourceAdapter Protocol (src/aer/sources/base.py:69,83), so adding a company_name argument changes the protocol and both adapters, not just tickers.py — closer to half a session than an hour, though only two call sites exist (peer_discovery.py:185, vertical_slice_v1.py:2228).

items.title: Nobody has established what Companies House actually hands back for a listed plc's accounts
items.problem: The whole UK path rests on an untested premise: that the accounts a FTSE-listed plc files at Companies House arrive as inline XBRL this platform can extract facts from. If they arrive as a PDF print of the annual report, the path yields prose and no facts, and every design below it changes shape. The repository asserts the premise in documentation and nowhere tests it against the live register.
items.rootCause: `docs/data-sources/companies-house.md` states 'A UK company's accounts are usually inline XBRL', and the four fixtures in `tests/fixtures/uk/` are hand-constructed JSON envelopes — none is a real document body. Separately, `CompaniesHouseClient.fetch_document` sends no `Accept` header (`src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:380-388`); `SafeFetcher` sends only `User-Agent` and `Accept-Encoding` plus `policy.extra_headers` (`src/aer/fetch/client.py:455-458`), and the Companies House policy's `extra_headers` is empty (`src/aer/fetch/policy.py:137-145`). The document API selects a representation by `Accept`, so which representation this code would receive is undetermined. (Hypothesis, not established here: that the endpoint requires the header at all, and that large plcs file iXBRL rather than PDF.)
evidence: src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:380-388
src/aer/fetch/client.py:455-458
src/aer/fetch/policy.py:137-145 — FetchPolicy for COMPANIES_HOUSE, extra_headers defaulted empty
docs/data-sources/companies-house.md — 'usually inline XBRL', unsourced
tests/fixtures/uk/ — four constructed JSON files, no document body
docs/plan/ROADMAP.md:826-836 — the rate limit was verified against primary documentation; the document format never was
items.recommendation: Spend one session and £0 of model budget on a probe before anything is designed: with a free Companies House key, fetch the filing history and the newest accounts document for three real subjects of different shapes (a large retailer, a bank, a mid-cap), record the content types offered and returned, and run `extract_ixbrl` over whatever arrives. Write the answer into `docs/data-sources/companies-house.md` with the date it was read. If the answer is 'PDF', the UK path becomes a prose-and-issuer-site path rather than a facts path, and items `uk-facts-need-an-ixbrl-path` and `uk-citations-need-a-presentation-locator` are rewritten rather than built. This is the one piece of work that cannot be skipped and cannot be guessed.
items.tests: A replayed `respx` test over the real bytes the probe captured (one iXBRL body, one PDF body), asserting the client sends the `Accept` the register expects and that `sniff` classifies each correctly.
items.acceptance: The data-source note states, with a read-at date, what a listed plc's accounts arrive as, and a stored fixture of a real body exists for the suite to replay.

options.name: Probe first
options.change: Read the register before designing.
options.cost: A session, no model spend, a free key.
options.risk: None beyond the operator needing to register a key.

options.name: Design for both
options.change: Build the path so a PDF degrades to prose-only evidence and iXBRL adds facts.
options.cost: Widens the adapter work by roughly a session.
options.risk: Building two paths for a question one fetch would settle.

items.challengeNote: Two additions. (a) The probe must run through `SafeFetcher`/`CompaniesHouseClient`, not curl: CLAUDE.md states only `aer.fetch` may make outbound requests, and the captured bytes must land as a respx fixture because tests run with no network. Say so, or the probe as written is itself a convention breach. (b) The probe should also record what the fetch layer does with each representation: `SafeFetcher` only enforces media type when a caller passes `expected_media_types` (fetch/client.py:344-345), and `fetch_document` passes none, so a PDF, an iXBRL body and an HTML error page are all accepted identically today. That is part of the answer the probe exists to produce.

items.title: Two finished UK adapters that no runtime object can reach
items.problem: The Companies House client is 467 lines of careful, tested code — ambiguity refused rather than resolved, company numbers validated before they enter a URL path, documents read back from the store by hash. It is constructed exactly once in the repository, inside its own test file. `aer.sources.issuer`, which ADR 0022 names as the other half of the UK path, is likewise imported only by a test. Neither can be called from a run, and no error message anywhere tells the operator that the capability the documentation once advertised exists but is not plugged in.
items.rootCause: `ServiceBundle` declares `sec_client` and no Companies House client (`src/aer/runtime.py:47-79`); `build_services` constructs `SecEdgarClient` and nothing UK (`runtime.py:114-122`); `for_execution` — the one list both the worker and `aer step` spread into the executor — has no slot for one (`runtime.py:73-79`). Only the credential is wired (`runtime.py:197-199`). `CompaniesHouseClient` appears in `src/` solely in its own module; `aer.sources.issuer` is imported only at `tests/test_discovery.py:35`.

tests/test_companies_house.py:80 — the only construction

docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:475-476 — 'exists, is credential-wired in runtime.py, and is called by no step'
docs/adr/0022-the-fca-nsm-is-not-fetched-automatically.md — 'The UK path relies on Companies House and the issuer's own site'
items.recommendation: Treat this as the umbrella item and write the ADR before any of the code. The decision it records is not 'add an adapter' — it is what a UK run's evidence base *is*, now that ADR 0022 removed the NSM: annual statutory accounts from Companies House at Tier 1, the issuer's own annual report and RNS archive at Tier 2, no interim statements, and a point-in-time anchor that is the register's acceptance date rather than the announcement date. Each of those is a statement about invariants 1 and 4 that a reader of a UK report has to be told, so it belongs in an ADR and then in the report's own coverage notice. Wire the clients into `ServiceBundle` and `for_execution` together, since the price feed went missing for exactly the reason of being built in one place and not forwarded in the other.
items.adrSubject: A UK run's evidence is Companies House accounts plus the issuer's own site, anchored on the register's acceptance date, with no interim statements and no NSM.
items.tests: A runtime test asserting `for_execution()` carries every client a step names, so a client built in `build_services` and not forwarded fails the suite rather than a live run; an adapter-conformance test mirroring `tests/test_sec_client.py:79`.

items.challengeNote: Two things the framing gets wrong. (a) `aer.sources.issuer` is not a client and cannot be "wired into ServiceBundle": it is a 306-line module of pure functions — `discover_documents(...)` at src/aer/sources/issuer.py:167 is a synchronous function, with PROVIDER and SOURCE_TIER as module constants (:56-57). There is no object to forward, so the "wire the clients into ServiceBundle and for_execution together" instruction applies to Companies House alone, and the issuer half is a different kind of change. (b) The acceptance criterion is not runnable in the default suite — it needs a live key and a network. Split it: a respx-replayed acceptance over the probe's fixture that the suite can run, plus the live run as a separate operator-gated check.

items.title: A company number written into a column that must be ten characters
items.problem: Wiring Companies House into `acquire` without touching anything else does not produce a UK report; it produces a database integrity error. The resolved identifier goes straight into `Company.cik`, which a check constraint pins at ten characters. A company number is eight ('00445790', 'SC123456'). The run would die with a constraint violation, several layers below anything that could explain it.
items.rootCause: `upsert_company` looks the company up by `Company.cik == entity.identifier` and writes `cik=entity.identifier` on creation and `company.cik = company.cik or entity.identifier` on refresh (`src/aer/services/facts.py:117,126,143`), with no knowledge of which registry issued the identifier. `Company.cik` is `String(10)` with `CheckConstraint("cik IS NULL OR char_length(cik) = 10")` (`src/aer/db/models/company.py:48,97`). `Company.company_number` exists and its own comment says 'Reserved for the UK adapter; nothing populates it yet' (`company.py:53`). The type-level cause is that `ResolvedEntity` carries `identifier` and no registry (`src/aer/sources/base.py:45`), while its docstring already says the field means two different things.

src/aer/db/models/company.py:48,53,91,97
src/aer/sources/base.py:39-49

src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:70,89-115 — eight characters, validated
items.recommendation: Give `ResolvedEntity` a registry discriminator and make `upsert_company` dispatch on it, writing `cik` or `company_number` accordingly and matching on the right column. Do it before the adapter is wired, not after: it is half a session, and it is the difference between a UK run failing with a sentence and failing with a Postgres error. Add the `SourceAdapter` conformance assertion for `CompaniesHouseClient` in the same change — it currently lacks `fetch_facts` (`sources/base.py:106`) and so does not satisfy the protocol, and nothing says so because only the SEC client is checked (`tests/test_sec_client.py:79`).
items.adrSubject: A resolved entity names the registry that issued its identifier, and a company row stores it in that registry's column.
items.tests: A `upsert_company` test with a Companies House `ResolvedEntity` asserting `company_number` is set and `cik` stays NULL, and that a second call matches the existing row rather than creating a duplicate; an `isinstance(client, SourceAdapter)` assertion for the UK client.

items.challengeNote: "The run would die with a constraint violation" understates it: there are two failure modes and the quieter one is worse. The lookup at facts.py:117 first silently misses; the fallback at :118-121 then matches on `Company.ticker == ticker, Company.exchange == exchange`, so a UK company sharing a TICKER+EXCHANGE row with an existing listing would be attached to that company rather than raising at all, and only a genuinely new insert reaches the check constraint. State both. Also add: `company_number` is `String(16)` with no length or format constraint (company.py:53) while `cik` has two — if the discriminator lands, the same migration should add the matching constraint, or a checked column is being replaced by an unchecked one.

items.title: The extract step can only read EDGAR's aggregate, and Companies House has no aggregate
items.problem: Every figure in a report comes from facts the `extract` step writes, and that step reads exactly one artefact and parses it as EDGAR's companyfacts JSON. Companies House publishes no such aggregate — it publishes documents. Without a second way to produce facts, a wired-up UK acquisition would hash a set of accounts and then have nothing to calculate from: no statements, no ratios, no valuation, no At-a-glance table.
items.rootCause: `_extract` reads `acquired["artefact_sha256"]` and calls `parse_company_facts(payload)` unconditionally (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:2793-2794`). `acquire_filings` is equally SEC-shaped: it calls `client.fetch_submissions` and selects on `ANNUAL_FORMS` / `QUARTERLY_FORMS` / `CURRENT_FORMS` (`src/aer/services/filings.py:227-263, 48, 65`). No Companies House method produces facts at all — the client has no `fetch_facts`.

src/aer/services/filings.py:48,65,227-263
src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:347-454 — profile, history, search, document, resolve, discover; no facts
src/aer/services/segments.py:151,158,182-201 — iXBRL facts already become `RawFact`s in production
src/aer/sources/sec/pit.py:1-30 — `select_point_in_time` is generic over `RawFact`
items.recommendation: Do not write a new extractor. The machinery exists and is exercised on every US run: the segment sweep already loads an inline XBRL document offline through arelle, filters by entity, maps tags through the concept vocabulary and builds `RawFact`s with a filed date supplied by the caller (`services/segments.py:151-201`). Mirror `sources/sec/companyfacts.parse_company_facts` with an `aer.sources.uk.accounts` parser that does the same over the *undimensioned* facts of the last several years of accounts, taking `filed_date` from the Companies House filing history entry each document came from. `select_point_in_time` then needs no change at all — it groups by concept, unit, period end and fiscal period and prefers the latest filed date, which is exactly right when each year's accounts restate the prior year's comparatives. The IFRS alias table is already there and was corrected against a real 20-F during the audit (`core/concepts.py:395-508`), and the taxonomy-extension gate already exists and is declared unconditionally (`vertical_slice_v1.py:463-467`).
items.tests: A parser test over the fixture the probe captures, asserting the same fact set is produced twice from the same bytes; a property test that every input fact lands in `chosen` or `rejected` after `select_point_in_time`, as the SEC path already asserts; and a test that an accounts document tagged only with filer extensions raises the unmapped-concepts gate rather than producing an empty statement.
items.acceptance: A UK subject reaches `calculate` with a three-year income statement, balance sheet and cash flow assembled from Companies House artefacts, every line traceable to a hashed document, and the unmapped tags shown at the gate with the numbers behind them.

items.challengeNote: Three gaps the recommendation must close before it is buildable. (a) The segment sweep's entity guard does not transfer: `_entity_matches(fact, cik=company.cik)` returns True whenever cik is falsy (services/segments.py:229-239), so on a Companies-House-resolved company with a NULL cik the guard that stops a subsidiary's tagged facts becoming the subject's silently disengages. The UK parser needs its own guard on company number or LEI. (b) `select_point_in_time` lives in `aer.sources.sec.pit`; a `sources/uk` parser reusing it makes the UK package depend on the SEC package. Move it to a neutral module or record the exception in the ADR. (c) `_extract` also calls `extract_bytes(payload, extractor="json")` at vertical_slice_v1.py:2814 to produce the text `record_excerpts` writes against; an accounts document is not JSON and the item never names what replaces that extractor.

items.title: A UK fact would have no excerpt, so no claim could cite it
items.problem: A figure that cannot be located in the archived bytes gets no extraction row, and a numeric claim naming it carries no citation for the verifier to confirm. On the US path the locator looks for the value as JSON spells it. In an annual report the same figure is printed as '58,739' in a table headed '$m', while the fact's value is 58739000000. Nothing would be found, and a UK report's numbers would be traceable to a document without a single verifiable excerpt in it.
items.rootCause: `_extract` locates each fact with `extracted.locate(f'"val":{fact.value}') or extracted.locate(str(fact.value))` (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:2816-2821`) — both forms of the raw decimal, neither of them how a report prints a figure. The iXBRL extractor already applies the document's own `scale`, so the parsed value is in pounds and the printed value is in millions with separators (`src/aer/extract/ixbrl.py:19-22`; `docs/data-sources/uk-ixbrl.md`, 'The document's scale is already applied by arelle').

items.recommendation: Locate a UK fact by the text the document itself displays. An inline XBRL fact carries its own presented string in the markup, so the locator can look for that rather than reconstructing it — which is more robust than formatting the decimal and guessing the separator and scale. This is worth doing well rather than minimally, because it is the one place the UK path is *better* than the US path for issue 2: a citation would point at the sentence or table cell in the company's own annual report instead of at a row in a generated JSON aggregate, which is precisely what a sceptical reader asked to check the work wants to follow.
items.tests: An extraction test asserting that a fact tagged with scale=6 and displayed as '58,739' is located in the extracted text and that the recorded excerpt contains the displayed form; a verifier test re-reading that excerpt by hash and confirming it.

Replace the acceptance with something countable: a run-level assertion that the count of fact extractions is at least N% of persisted facts, with N fixed from a measured US run, plus the citation-verifier test the item already proposes (which is the measurable half and should carry the criterion).

That should be said in the item, not only in the option's risk field.

items.title: Companies House classifies under a different SIC scheme, so a UK bank would take the standard model
items.problem: F-23 — a bank that met no sector gate and was asked for its EBIT margin — was the audit's second blocking finding. It would come straight back on the UK path. The sector profiles match on US SEC SIC prefixes; Companies House publishes UK SIC 2007 codes, which share no prefix with them. A UK bank's code would match nothing, the classification would be empty, no sector gate would be raised, and ADR 0029's block on discounting a bank's cash flows would never engage.
items.rootCause: `SECTOR_PROFILES` carry US SIC prefixes — '602' and '6021' for banks, '2836' and '8731' for biotechnology, '1311' for oil and gas (`src/aer/core/sectors.py:151,194,234,249,263,278,292,304`) — and `suggested_profiles` matches by `str.startswith` (`sectors.py:593-603`). UK SIC 2007 codes are five digits on an entirely different numbering (a UK bank is in the 641xx range), so nothing matches. Worse, the question does not even arise yet: `parse_company_profile` does not read the register's `sic_codes` field at all (`src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:198-230`), while `_classify`'s docstring asserts that '`Company.sic` is populated by the adapters that parse it, which means Companies House and the SEC submissions index' (`vertical_slice_v1.py:2322-2323`) — a claim that is true of one adapter and false of the other.

Record which scheme a stored code belongs to, so `suggested_profiles` never matches a UK code against a US prefix by coincidence. This is a data change, not an architectural one, and it needs no ADR — but it must land in the same change as the adapter wiring, because the permissive state here is reached silently and the audit already paid once to learn that.
items.tests: A classification test with a Companies House profile carrying a UK banking SIC code, asserting the bank profile is suggested and the sector gate is raised — the regression test F-23 would have needed; plus a test asserting a UK code never matches a US prefix.
items.acceptance: A UK bank driven through `classify` proposes the bank profile, meets the sector gate, and is refused a discounted cash flow by type, exactly as M&T is after F-23's fix.

items.challengeNote: The failure mode is worse than stated, which strengthens the recommendation. It is not only that a UK code matches nothing: because matching is bare `startswith` over three- and four-character prefixes, a UK SIC 2007 code can match the *wrong* US profile by coincidence — UK 63110 (data processing and hosting) starts with "631", which is the insurance-carrier prefix at sectors.py:194. So the permissive state is reachable and so is a confidently wrong specialist proposal. Recording the scheme alongside the code is therefore not a tidiness measure; it is what prevents a silent miscategorisation, and the item should lead with that rather than with "nothing matches".

items.title: The register's acceptance date is months after the market knew
items.problem: A UK point-in-time run would be honest and badly stale. A plc announces its results by RNS in, say, February and files the statutory accounts at Companies House in, say, June; the platform's UK clock starts in June. A run as at March would find nothing for the year just reported. And Companies House holds no interim statements at all, so the half-year a US run gets from a 10-Q or a 6-K simply does not exist on this path. A reader comparing a UK note with a US one would be reading two different recencies under the same heading.
items.rootCause: `FilingHistory.filed_on_or_before` filters on the register's `date` field, which is the acceptance date (`src/aer/sources/uk/companies_house.py:181-187`), and `discover_documents` applies it at acquisition (`companies_house.py:440-454`) — correct under invariant 4, and anchored to the wrong event for a listed company. `ACCOUNTS_CATEGORIES` is `frozenset({"accounts"})` (`companies_house.py:66`), and the register has no category for a half-year statement. The venue that does index RNS is the FCA's National Storage Mechanism, refused structurally by ADR 0022.

items.recommendation: Decide this explicitly and tell the reader. The honest position is that a UK run's Tier 1 evidence is annual and lags the announcement, and that the gap is filled — if at all — by the issuer's own site at Tier 2 with dates scored rather than trusted (`aer/extract/dates.py`, which ADR 0022 already names as the replacement point-in-time mechanism). This belongs in the same ADR as `uk-adapter-unwired` and then in the report's coverage notice, because it is exactly the kind of difference that makes a judge distrust a document when they discover it themselves and trust it when the document says it first. Do not paper over it by dating a filing by the period it covers; that would break invariant 4 for a presentational gain.
items.adrSubject: A UK run is anchored on the register's acceptance date, holds no interim statements, and says so on the document.

options.change: Wire `aer.sources.issuer` with an operator-supplied domain; dates scored by `extract/dates.py`.

items.challengeNote: One link in the chain is asserted, not established, and should be marked as a hypothesis in the text. `_one_filing` sets `filed_on = _parse_date(raw.get("date"))` (companies_house.py:285) — the register's `date` field. Nothing in the repository establishes that that field is the *acceptance* date rather than the received or made-available date, and the item's whole staleness argument turns on it. It is the same unknown as the item's own openQuestion 4 and should be folded into the item 3 probe, which is already fetching a real filing history.

items.title: A Companies-House-resolved company has no CIK, so peers and full-text leads both go quiet
items.problem: The peer gap is the audit's first §8 decision and the single most-cited reason judges preferred the console. On the UK path it is strictly worse: every peer a model proposes is resolved against EDGAR's index, so a UK peer set — the only peer set that makes sense for a UK retailer or bank — is refused wholesale. And the research workers' full-text search keys on the subject's CIK, which a UK-resolved company does not have, so the leads that feed 'recent developments' return nothing.
items.rootCause: `peer_discovery` resolves each proposed ticker with `client.resolve_entity` against the SEC client and looks the result up by `Company.cik` (`src/aer/services/peer_discovery.py:185,196,239`). `services/research.py:243` selects `Company.cik` and passes it to `sec_client.search_full_text` (`research.py:257`); with a NULL CIK the search is skipped. `_peers`' own docstring states the rule: 'Every ticker the model returns is resolved against EDGAR's own index' (`vertical_slice_v1.py:2391-2392`).

items.recommendation: Scope this out of a first UK path deliberately and say so, rather than letting it fail quietly. A UK run should record its proposed peers as refused-with-a-reason ('this platform resolves peers against EDGAR; a UK-listed peer cannot be confirmed') so the report can say the table is structurally empty rather than implying the peers were judged and excluded — which is the wording the audit already flags as misleading on the US path. Resolving UK peers properly means Companies House name-resolution per peer, which the adapter refuses on ambiguity by design and which would put a dozen candidate confirmations in front of the operator. That is a second project, not part of this one.
items.tests: A peer-discovery test with a UK subject asserting every proposed peer lands in `refused` with a reason naming the registry, and none is silently dropped; a research-worker test asserting the absent full-text capability is reported rather than passed over.
items.acceptance: A UK report's comparables section states that no peer multiple could be computed and why, in a sentence a reader can act on, and no section implies a judgement about the peers themselves.

options.name: Refuse with a reason
options.change: Record UK peers as unresolvable and say so in the report.
options.risk: The UK report has no relative valuation at all — honest, and one of the two things judges most wanted.

options.name: Resolve UK peers through Companies House
options.change: Name-search each peer, confirm at a gate.
options.cost: A few sessions plus operator time per run.
options.risk: The adapter refuses ambiguity by design, so the operator confirms up to eight companies per run.

items.challengeNote: Replace the full-text half of the problem and the test. The defect there is that the refusal text is false for a UK subject: a Companies-House-resolved company *has* been resolved against a registry, and telling a worker otherwise misdescribes the run's own state. The fix is one message branching on which registry resolved the company — an hour, not part of a session's work — and the test should assert the UK wording, not the existence of a refusal. The peer half stands as written.

items.title: The missing gilt yield does not stop a UK run, and saying it does would be wrong
items.problem: The obvious objection to a UK path is that there is no GBP risk-free rate, so a sterling valuation cannot be discounted. On this workflow that is not true, and believing it would misdirect effort onto a licence problem that is not on the critical path.
items.rootCause: `RISK_FREE_SERIES` has no GBP entry and refuses rather than substituting, because the Bank of England's own robots.txt disallows the CSV handler its documentation describes (`src/aer/sources/macro/series.py:382-410`, ADR 0026). But `_propose_assumptions` states plainly that 'this workflow acquires neither a macro series nor a price history', so the risk-free rate, the beta and the equity risk premium are named as outstanding and confirmed by the operator at the assumptions gate on *every* run, US or UK (`src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1335-1344`; `src/aer/services/assumption_gate.py:85,718-723`). AZN #2's 5.83 % WACC was built that way. The FX half is also already solved: the ECB adapter supplies a GBP/USD cross-rate as a recorded calculation (ADR 0045, `src/aer/sources/macro/ecb.py`), and pence-to-pounds is definitional arithmetic in `calc/prices.py:115-120`.

src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1335-1344
src/aer/services/assumption_gate.py:85,718-723
docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md:368 — AZN #2, 5.83 % WACC from confirmed assumptions
docs/adr/0045-the-euro-is-the-pivot-because-the-bank-of-england-is-closed.md
src/aer/calc/prices.py:115-120
src/aer/sources/eodhd/proxies.py:91-95 — LSE is already a mapped venue
items.recommendation: Do not put a GBP risk-free adapter on the UK critical path. State in the ADR that the rate is operator-confirmed on every run and that this is unchanged by jurisdiction, and correct `docs/product/what-it-is.md:152-157`, which currently lists the missing UK risk-free rate among the things holding coverage back — true of automation, misleading about capability. Separately, and later, a licence determination on the UK Debt Management Office's published gilt yields would be the natural companion to ADR 0026 and ADR 0045: a verification against a primary source, done before any code, exactly as the Companies House rate limit and the Langfuse licence were.
items.tests: None for the correction itself. If a GBP series is later added, the existing pattern applies: a series-allowlist test asserting the identifier is refused until a row with an originator and a licence sentence exists.
items.acceptance: A UK run reaches an approved valuation with an operator-confirmed sterling risk-free rate, and the product documentation no longer implies a UK valuation is impossible without a gilt feed.

options.name: Leave it operator-confirmed
options.change: Documentation only.
options.risk: None. It is what already happens on every run.

options.change: Licence and robots determination, then a macro series row and an adapter.

Also point the reader at ADR 0045 ("the-euro-is-the-pivot-because-the-bank-of-england-is-closed") alongside ADR 0026, since 0026 is titled for FX arithmetic and 0045 is the one named for the closed Bank.
