items.recommendation: Build the offsets in one pass instead of N scans — a single sweep over the extracted text producing a map from the value token to its offset, consulted per fact — and assert the resulting excerpts are byte-identical to today's. This is pure deterministic code in the layer the architecture says owns facts; it touches no invariant, changes no output, and should take a bank's extract from 3.6 minutes to seconds. Combined with the previous item (extract off the plan's critical path) it removes the step from the operator's experience entirely. I have not profiled this — the linear-in-facts scaling across three filers is strong circumstantial evidence, not a measurement, and the first half-hour of the work should be a profile that confirms or refutes it before any code changes.

options.risk: Memory on a large aggregate. Bounded and measurable.

options.risk: Invariant 2 says code confirms a citation by re-reading the artefact by hash; deferring means a citation could name a fact whose excerpt was never found. Needs care and probably an ADR.

Keep the profile as the first half-hour — the item already says so — but make it a gate on the item rather than a footnote, and treat the acceptance ('extract under 30s on M&T') as conditional on the profile, since it is unreachable if persistence dominates. Also `whichIssue` should be 'both': extract sits on the path to the operator's second decision, not only on quality.

items.title: A refreshed subject is stopped four times to re-approve answers identical to last time's
items.problem: Use case 2 is "refreshing a company already researched", and a refresh pays the same six stops as a first run. The audit's own records show that four of them ask a question whose answer has not changed: MSFT's second run was shown the identical 496 unmapped tags the first run had already approved, the same eight peers, the same five themes and the same classification. The unmapped-concepts page on that run carried 105 items; on the bank it was 304 items across 13,592 words.
items.rootCause: An approval is recorded against a job and a payload hash (src/aer/services/approvals.py:97-133) and nothing carries a decision forward between runs. `unmapped_gate_required` fires on any unmapped tag at all (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1244-1257), the gate page writes no mapping and records no disposition per tag (src/aer/web/pages.py:723-780), so the same filing produces the same stop every time. The payloads are not byte-identical — peers and themes come back in a different order — so a naive hash comparison would never match; a standing decision would have to compare canonicalised sets.

audit §4.3 use case 2
items.recommendation: Give the four repeatable gates a standing decision per company: an approval the operator explicitly elects to carry forward, recorded as its own event with what it covers (the canonicalised tag set, the peer set, the theme set, the sector key), which pre-clears a later run whose set is identical and stops the run the moment it differs by one element. That is what turns a refresh into two decisions — the plan and the final review — which is what a refresh ought to cost. It needs an ADR: the approvals model has no concept of a decision outliving the job that made it, and audit §8 item 5 (F-16) already records that the same model has no superseding decision either. Do not weaken the gate itself: a set that has grown by one tag must stop, and the page must say which tag is new.

options.name: Standing decision per company, opt-in
options.change: A new event kind and a set comparison at each of the four conditional gates.
options.cost: A few sessions plus an ADR.
options.risk: An operator who approved 496 tags once has approved them forever. Mitigated by requiring an explicit election and by stopping on any difference.

options.name: Show the diff rather than skipping the gate
options.change: Keep all four stops but render only what changed since the last approved run of the same filer.
options.cost: A session or two per gate.
options.risk: Cheaper, no ADR, keeps six decisions but makes four of them near-instant. The bank's 13,592-word page becomes a short one.

options.name: Leave it
options.change: Nothing.
options.risk: Use case 2 stays as expensive in attention as use case 1, which is the opposite of what a refresh should be.

items.adrSubject: A gate decision may be carried forward for one company while the thing it decided is unchanged, and stops the run the moment it is not
items.tests: A test that a second job on the same company with an identical unmapped tag set does not raise UNMAPPED_CONCEPTS when a standing decision exists, and does raise it when the set differs by one element, naming that element. Equivalents for peers, themes and the sector key, each comparing canonicalised sets rather than payload hashes.
items.acceptance: A refresh run of MSFT stops twice — plan and final review — where the audit's msft2 stopped six times, and a run whose filing has added a single extension tag stops at the financials gate showing that one tag.
items.challengeNote: Restate the benefit: on the audit's own records a standing decision would have turned MSFT's six stops into two or three, and AZN's into four or five. Say explicitly that peers and themes are non-deterministic model output, so canonical-set comparison will re-open those gates often enough that the saving is mostly the unmapped-concepts gate — which is also the longest page, so the item survives, at a smaller size. The 'show the diff' option is then the better-value one and deserves to be the recommendation.
items.invariantRisk: CLAUDE.md's framing is 'one institutional-style research report at a time, under explicit human approval'; a pre-cleared gate must still write an approval row to satisfy `_refuse_if_out_of_order`, so the new ADR must say what actor and what evidence that row carries. The item is right that an ADR is needed and right that it must stop on any difference.

items.title: The operator's attention, not the machine's minutes, is what makes a run take an afternoon
items.problem: A run asks for six decisions (seven on a bank). Five of them arrive inside the first eight minutes and are then followed by twenty-two minutes of silence. The pages those decisions are taken on total 26,392 words (AZN), 31,014 (MSFT) and 34,540 (M&T) — roughly two hours of reading if read in full — and the report itself is another 12.5–15.3k words that the audit's judges took 35 to 55 minutes over. Against that, the run's 30–37 minutes of machine time is not the binding constraint.
items.rootCause: The gates are presented one at a time, in the order the linear chain reaches them, each as a full page. On the collapsed clock, gates 1 through 4 are decided at 5.11, 5.38, 5.49 and 5.86 minutes on AZN — four separate page loads inside forty-five seconds of machine work, each a context switch for the operator. Nothing composes them into one sitting because peers, themes and the extraction do not exist until gate 1 has been approved (see the plan-spine item). The financials gate is the worst of them because it renders every unmapped tag and every mapped concept: 2,503 words on AZN, 7,911 on MSFT, 13,592 on M&T.
evidence: docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/{msft2,azn2,mtb}/screens/*.json — per-page word counts: plan 2796/2814/2703; peers 647/651/698; themes 498/473/423; financials 7911/2503/13592; assumptions 1151/1229/931; review 18011/18722/15850; sector 343 (mtb)

items.recommendation: Once the plan-spine change lands, all four early payloads exist by minute six; compose them into one sitting — one page, four decisions, four hashes, `GATE_ORDER` still enforced — and leave the assumptions gate as a second, short sitting once the research wave returns. That gives three sittings: a set-up sitting at six minutes, an assumptions sitting at eight to eleven, and the review at the end. Separately, and independently worth doing, cut what the financials page asks the operator to read: it currently renders the whole extraction, and what a person can actually decide on is the tags that carry a figure the report would otherwise use. Do not batch by removing hashes: each decision must still record the hash of exactly what was shown, which is what makes a batched sitting safe.

options.change: A composed gate page posting four decisions; the workflow pauses once instead of four times.
options.risk: A batched page is longer. Mitigated by ranking each gate's contents and putting the rest behind disclosures.

options.name: Keep six stops, shrink the pages
options.change: Rank and truncate the financials gate; keep the sequence.
options.risk: Least disruption, biggest single reading saving (the bank's 13,592 words), but the four context switches remain.

options.change: Nothing.
options.risk: Use case 7 stays unsupported however fast the machine gets.

items.tests: A test that the composed set-up page renders four payloads and four hashes, that posting it records four approvals in `GATE_ORDER`, and that a payload which changed between render and post is refused per gate rather than wholesale. A test that the financials page's rendered word count for the M&T fixture falls below a stated ceiling while every unmapped tag remains reachable.

items.challengeNote: The item's own open question already concedes that no human gate time was ever measured, so 'roughly two hours of reading' is an inference from word counts. Say that in the item, not only in the open questions. And since the composed-sitting option depends on the plan-spine item, which I have weakened on the two-pending-gates problem, rank the independent half — cutting the financials page from 13,592 words — first; it needs neither dependency and carries the largest single saving.

items.title: The draft writes four sections at a time; the run's own research wave already runs five model calls at once
items.problem: `draft` is 6.6–11.4 minutes, 30–31% of the run, and the largest single step on two of three exported runs. It writes eighteen sections four at a time. List-scheduling the recorded per-call latencies shows it would take 299s instead of 545s at seven-wide on AZN, 216s instead of 398s on MSFT, and 326s instead of 681s on M&T.
items.rootCause: `DRAFT_FAN_OUT = 4` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:299), chosen deliberately: the comment above it (:293-298) says the bound is narrow because the budget guard reads committed spend, so every section in flight checks the cap against the same total and a wider wave widens the window in which the cap can be overshot. That is exactly what audit §8 item 6 (F-21) records as an open decision — sibling calls in the research wave and the draft fan-out cannot see each other's spend. The measured efficiency of the current bound is 3.53/3.64/3.15 against a bound of 4, so the mechanism is working; the bound is the constraint.

items.recommendation: This is the operator's call, and it is not free. Raising the bound to six or seven saves 2.3–4.8 minutes and widens the worst-case cap overshoot from four concurrent projections to seven. The clean order is to close F-21 first — publish cost before a step commits, so siblings can see each other's spend — and then raise the bound, at which point it costs nothing. If the bound is raised before that, raise it to six rather than seven and note that the platform would then run seven concurrent model calls at its peak where it runs five today (the research wave's seven nodes include two that make no model call). Do not raise `MAX_PARALLEL_NODES`: the engine refuses it by construction and calls it part of the cost model.

items.challengeNote: Fix the superlative — draft is the largest step on one of three exported runs. Widen the 7-wide projection to roughly 300–340s (azn2), 230–260s (msft2), 330–370s (mtb), i.e. 2.0–4.5 minutes saved rather than 2.3–4.8. The recommendation's ordering (close F-21 first, then raise) is sound and should stay.
items.invariantRisk: Invariant 6 — 'Cost is metered and capped in code. Caps that only warn are caps that do not work.' The bound's own comment records it as a cost-model decision made to keep the overshoot window narrow, so raising it weakens the cap's guarantee by construction. `adrNeeded: false` is defensible only for the 'close F-21 first' option; the 'raise to six now' option trades invariant 6's strength for three minutes and should say so in those words.

items.title: A short run is already implemented in data and was never exercised or measured
items.problem: The stated need is an answer under time pressure. The platform already has a depth control that drops nine of the eighteen sections and scales the drafting budgets to 0.6 — and all six audit runs were `standard`. Nobody knows what a quick run costs, how long it takes, or whether its document is worth reading, because none was ever made.
items.rootCause: `AnalysisMode.QUICK` exists (src/aer/core/enums.py:57), migration 0035 puts `{"analysis_mode": ["standard", "full"]}` on the nine deep-dive sections so a quick run resolves only the core spine, and `SectionPolicy.scaled` multiplies token and word budgets by 0.6 (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:89-93, :258-272). The applicability is evaluated in code by `resolve_sections` (src/aer/sections/registry.py:105-113). The audit's own harness fixed every subject at `standard` (each run-export's `subject.analysis_mode` reads "standard"), so the feature has no live evidence behind it at all.

items.recommendation: Spend one live run — about £4 at the scaled budgets — measuring a quick run on MSFT, and record it beside the audit's other runs so the depth control stops being a claim. On the recorded numbers a quick run should draft nine sections rather than eighteen at roughly 0.6 of the length: extrapolating the per-section latencies, `draft` falls to roughly 200–260s and `revise` has fewer sections to attack, which would put gate 2 at somewhere near sixteen to twenty minutes before any of the other fixes. That is the cheapest existing route to something near console parity on time, and the question it raises is the right one to put to the judges: is a nine-section note that keeps the summary, the thesis, the statements, the valuation and the risks better or worse than a console note, when the eighteen-section one lost six blind comparisons to it?

options.change: Flip the request form's default; full runs on request.
options.risk: Premature without the measurement. A quick run whose valuation section has too little evidence to cite would be worse, not faster.

items.tests: A test that a `quick` request resolves exactly nine section definitions and that each drafting policy's word and token budgets are 0.6 of the standard run's — the deep-dive keys asserted from the database rows, not named in the test, so the list stays data.

items.challengeNote: Two details. Nine sections remain, but one of the nine dropped (`prior_research_comparison`) is itself deterministic and one of the nine kept (`validation_disagreements`) is too, so a quick run drafts eight model-written sections, not nine — which changes the draft and revise extrapolations slightly. And depth is already a field on the request form (web/templates/requests/_form.html:123-124), so 'nobody has ever run one' is a statement about the audit, not about the product; only four of the six runs have an export to check.

items.title: The time the plan gate promises is over-stated by 12–30% and shown in raw seconds
items.problem: Gate 1 tells the operator "Estimated runtime — 2197 s". It is in developer units, and it is wrong: the estimate sums every step's own elapsed time, so the five research workers that run concurrently are counted five times over. The gap is exactly the phantom research time — 3.7 minutes on AZN's second run, 9.6 on MSFT's first — and it will get worse rather than better as concurrency improves, because making the draft twice as parallel does not move this number at all.
items.rootCause: `_projected_runtime_seconds` takes the median over past successful runs of `sum(finished_at - started_at)` per job (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:360-395). Its docstring justifies summing steps rather than measuring the wall clock — correctly, to exclude the operator's reading time — but summing overlapping steps is not the same as excluding idle time. The template prints the integer seconds directly (src/aer/web/templates/plans/review.html:191). The audit's own scorer makes the identical mistake, which is where §4.2's "31–42 minutes of step time" comes from (audit/scoring/platform_report.py:141-143, audit/report/generate.py:43).

Worth doing before any concurrency work lands, so the improvement is visible in the number the gate shows. The same correction applies to the audit's scorer, which is where the published 31–42 figure comes from; the true machine time on those runs is 26.5–36.8 minutes.

options.risk: Leaves a developer unit on a gate a private investor decides at — the F-25 family of defect the pass already fixed elsewhere.

items.title: Twenty-two minutes of silence and no way to be told when it ends
items.problem: Between the assumptions gate and gate 2 the run is silent for 22.4 minutes on AZN, 20.9 on MSFT and 25.5 on M&T. The only way to learn that gate 2 has opened is to have the browser tab open. There is no email, no webhook, no desktop notification, nothing outside the application. Under time pressure the operator either sits watching a page whose only movement is a step key, or walks away and comes back to a gate that has been waiting.
items.rootCause: The console updates itself through an event stream with a five-second meta-refresh fallback (src/aer/web/pages.py:149, templates/runs/console.html:39) and the shell paints a badge count (src/aer/web/routes.py:1277-1319), but both are in-application. A grep across `src/aer` finds no notification sink of any kind — no SMTP, no webhook, no OS notification. This is a real consequence of the silent tail rather than a separate defect: the shorter the silence, the less it matters.
evidence: Collapsed-clock gaps between the assumptions gate and gate_final: azn2 462.6s→1799.1s (22.3 min); msft2 595.2s→1850.0s (20.9 min); mtb 679.2s→2203.4s (25.4 min)

items.recommendation: Treat it as second-order: fix the silence first (concurrent revise, a first read, a wider fan-out) and it shrinks from 22 minutes to roughly 8. Then, if the operator still wants to leave the machine, a local-first tool's honest answer is a local one — a desktop notification or a small configurable command run when a run pauses — rather than mail. Anything that reaches outside the machine is a new egress path and only `aer.fetch` may make outbound requests, so a webhook would need that rule addressed explicitly.

options.name: Shrink the silence and leave notification alone
options.change: Nothing new; the other items do the work.
options.risk: An eight-minute wait is still a wait, but it is one a person can sit through.

options.change: A configurable command the worker runs when a job enters AWAITING_APPROVAL.
options.risk: A user-supplied command executed by the worker. Needs care and should be off by default.

options.change: Mail or a webhook.
options.risk: Crosses the egress rule ("Only aer.fetch may make outbound network requests") and puts the subject of a private research run into someone else's log. Would need an ADR and probably should be refused.

items.tests: A test that a job transitioning to AWAITING_APPROVAL invokes the configured sink exactly once per transition and not at all when none is configured, and that a failing sink never fails the run.
items.acceptance: A run left unattended reaches the operator's attention within a minute of pausing, by whatever means they configured, and a run with nothing configured behaves exactly as it does today.
items.challengeNote: `adrNeeded: false` is too comfortable for the 'local hook' option. Either scope it to something with no shell (a file written to a watched path, or an OS notification through a library) and keep no ADR, or keep the arbitrary command and draft one. The acceptance criterion ('reaches the operator's attention within a minute of pausing, by whatever means they configured') is not measurable in the suite as written — restate it as the test already given: one sink invocation per AWAITING_APPROVAL transition, none when unconfigured, and a failing sink never failing the run.
items.invariantRisk: CLAUDE.md: 'Only aer.fetch may make outbound network requests.' The item correctly refuses the outbound option on that basis. The local-hook option additionally touches ADR 0036/0071 on who may execute what.

items.title: The adversary compares figures across periods, which this repository already forbids in code
items.problem: On AZN #2 the red team escalated eight challenges, six of them asserting that the draft's headline figures contradict the run's own record: "the draft asserts gross margin 81.9% … the only recorded calculations carrying those names return gross margin 0.668 and 0.721 … No recorded calculation reproduces any draft figure." Every one of those comparisons is between a FY2025 figure and a FY2021 or FY2022 calculation of the same name. The report's own footnotes prove it — [^57] is interest cover "for FY2021" 0.8123, [^143] is interest cover "for FY2025" 8.1128 — and all three judges worked this out unaided, which means the platform could have.
items.rootCause: F-27's fix gave each calculation a period label and one row per figure at its newest period (src/aer/services/red_team.py:330-372), but nothing compares periods. The adversary is handed a list of names and values and asked to find contradictions, and matching by name across differing periods is left to a language model's judgement. The repository has already written down the opposite rule for facts: "same concept, same period, two different published values is arithmetic, and arithmetic belongs to code … Facts on different periods are deliberately not compared" (src/aer/services/consistency.py:1-21). That check runs one step before the red team (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1683) and was built after the red team found exactly this class of contradiction on a live AAPL report. It was never extended to calculations, and never applied to the adversary's own figure claims.

options.name: Adjudicate and publish the adjudication
options.change: After the challenges return, resolve every cited calculation_id in code, pair it with the calculation the attacked claim cites (claims.calculation_id already exists), and where the two share a `name` but differ in `period_end`, record a deterministic adjudication on the disagreement row: "this challenge compares FY2025 gross_margin 0.818978 with FY2021 gross_margin 0.667610; the periods differ, so the two are not in conflict." The challenge is still recorded and still published — ADR 0039's "never auto-resolved" is untouched — but the reader meets the code's finding beside it.
options.cost: A session. No model call; a join over calculations and claims plus one appendix block.
options.risk: A challenge that is half arithmetic and half judgement gets an adjudication that answers only half of it. Mitigated by adjudicating per cited id rather than per challenge.

options.name: Refuse the challenge outright when its premise is void
options.change: Extend `_unresolvable_evidence` (src/aer/services/red_team.py:404-424) from "does this id exist in the run" to "does this id support the comparison the challenge makes", and drop the challenge exactly as one citing a fabricated id is dropped.
options.risk: Collides head-on with ADR 0039 ("a challenge the system itself could dismiss would be worth nothing") and destroys the sceptic's record: the reader can no longer see that an adversary ran and what it tried. Also silently discards the judgement half of a mixed challenge.

options.name: Remove the figures from the adversary's remit altogether
options.change: Take calculations out of the evidence index; the red team attacks claims, sources and reasoning only, and the deterministic validators own every figure comparison.
options.cost: A session, plus a prompt rewrite.
options.risk: Loses the one thing the sceptic judge said the console has no analogue for — "B red-teams third-party sources in Section 18 but never its own computations". Throws away a real capability to fix a presentation failure.

items.recommendation: Adjudicate and publish the adjudication, combined with the materiality change in `void-premise-still-material`. It keeps ADR 0039 literally intact (nothing is dismissed, both positions published), it puts the deterministic answer where the reader meets the accusation, and it is the same move `consistency.py` already made for facts — the platform's own precedent for exactly this class of mistake, written after the red team found it on AAPL. Refusal is tempting and wrong: a sceptic who cannot see what the adversary tried has lost the thing the platform is better at.
items.adrSubject: Code adjudicates a challenge's arithmetic premise; it never adjudicates its argument — extending ADR 0039's evidence check from "the id exists" to "the comparison the id supports is between like periods".
items.tests: A red_team fixture where the run holds gross_margin FY2021 0.6676 and FY2025 0.8190, a claim citing the FY2025 row, and a challenge citing the FY2021 row and asserting a contradiction. Before: the disagreement row carries no adjudication and the appendix prints the accusation bare. After: the row carries a deterministic adjudication naming both periods and both values, and the rendered appendix prints it under the challenge. A second case where the challenge cites the same-period calculation and genuinely disagrees must produce no adjudication — the check must not be able to refute a true accusation.
items.acceptance: On the next live run of any subject, every published challenge that names a recorded calculation either carries a code-written period adjudication or is a same-period comparison. A reader can tell which from the document alone, without opening a footnote.
items.challengeNote: Re-state the root cause as a residual risk of today's code, not as the AZN #2 mechanism: with the F-27 index in place a challenge can still compare the newest recorded period against a claim about an earlier one, and nothing checks it. Before building the adjudicator, replay `_evidence_index` over AZN #2's stored calculations under current code and count how many of the five figure-citing challenges could still be constructed — the item's own open question, and it decides whether this is a session well spent or a session spent on a closed hole. Correct 'six of eight' to 'five of eight cite a calculation at all'.

items.title: The disagreement appendix is the only place in the report where a model writes figures with no code between it and the reader
items.problem: AZN #2's appendix publishes "the recorded interest_cover calculation is 0.812", "recorded net_debt is $24,452m", "recorded EBITDA is $7,586m/$9,237m", "the only recorded nopat is $4.95bn" — a dozen or more figures, unlabelled by period, written by the adversary into a free-text field and printed verbatim. None of them was checked against anything. The reader judge put it exactly: "for the rest (net debt $24,452m vs $23,911m, debt-to-equity 0.783 vs 0.61, EBITDA $7,586m/$9,237m vs $18,829m, NOPAT $4.95bn vs $11.3bn) no citation resolves the period at all. Those are exactly the figures focus question 3 turns on."
items.rootCause: `cited_figure_agreement` — the check built precisely so that "a writer can cite quick_ratio and then put a different number in the prose" cannot happen — joins `claims` to `calculations` on `claims.calculation_id` (src/aer/services/evaluations.py:569-596). A red-team challenge is not a claim: it is a `disagreements.detail` JSON blob (src/aer/services/red_team.py:471-486) with no calculation_id, so the join never sees it. `presentation_integrity` scans the rendered document, but it runs at the `validate` step, before the red team has written anything and before the appendix is refilled (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1689, 1737). Invariant 3 says no figure reaches a report unless it is a stored fact, a recorded calculation or an attestation; these figures are transcriptions of recorded calculations, and the transcription is unverified.

options.name: Structure the figures out of the prose
options.change: Give `RedTeamChallenge` a `figure_claims` list of (calculation_id, the value the challenge reads off it) and require every numeral in the statement to appear there; render the values from the stored rows at render time, never from the model's text. A value that does not match its row refuses the challenge the way a fabricated id already does.
options.cost: A session and a prompt version bump.
options.risk: Ungainly for a challenge that argues about a figure without quoting it; needs the numeral scan to tolerate ranges and words.

options.name: Run the numeral check over the appendix
options.change: Extend `cited_figure_agreement` (or add a sibling over `disagreements.detail`) to parse numerals out of challenge statements and check each against the cited calculations, and move `presentation_integrity` after `revise` so it scans the document that actually ships.
options.cost: A session, plus the step-order change in `metrics-describe-a-different-document`.
options.risk: Textual numeral hunting is exactly what `_cited_figures` was designed to avoid; false positives on severity scores ("5/5") and on years.

options.name: Publish no figures from the adversary at all
options.change: Render the challenge's argument and strip every numeral, replacing each with a footnote to the calculation it cites.
options.risk: Makes most challenges unreadable — "the recorded value differs from the claimed one" is not an argument a reader can weigh.

items.recommendation: Structure the figures out of the prose. It is the same move the platform made for claims (ADR 0109, a numeric claim stands on the figure it names) and for citations (ADR 0018, only code confirms one), and it makes `period-blind-figure-comparison`'s adjudication trivial because the pairing is already explicit. The textual option should be held in reserve for the residue.
items.adrSubject: A figure in a challenge is a reading of a recorded calculation, carried as the id and checked, not as a number in a sentence — the claims rule of ADR 0109 applied to the adversary.
items.tests: A challenge whose statement quotes 0.812 while its `figure_claims` entry says the cited calculation is 8.11: the challenge is rejected whole with a named reason and nothing reaches the appendix. A challenge whose quoted value matches its cited row is recorded and renders the value from the row.
items.acceptance: Every numeral printed in the disagreement appendix of the next live run resolves to a stored calculation or fact, and a replay can reproduce each one — the same guarantee the body already carries.
items.challengeNote: Keep the structured `figure_claims` list and render values from the stored rows, but drop the 'every numeral must appear' rule. Enforce instead what is structural and cheap: each entry's value must equal its cited calculation's `output_value` (refuse the challenge whole, as ADR 0039:29-31 already requires for a fabricated id), and the renderer prints the figure and period from the row. Leave stray numerals in the argument prose to the prompt rule that already exists ('You never produce a figure of your own', agents/red_team.py:173-174), or accept the residue explicitly rather than pretending a scan closes it.

items.title: F-27 fixed the calculation index and left the fact index at 40 rows of 4,171
items.problem: Three of AZN #2's eight challenges rest on "no such fact exists in the index": the severity-4 growth challenge asserts "There is no growth evidence in this run. The fact index contains no revenue, earnings or cash-flow series for any period" — printed in a report whose second table is a five-year revenue history, $37,417m to $58,739m, every cell footnoted to one source. The severity-5 balance-sheet challenge ends "No cash, EBIT or interest-expense facts exist in the index to reconcile the gap." The adversary's own coverage note says it plainly: "almost none of the draft's ~150 numeric claims can be traced to the evidence shown me."
items.rootCause: `EVIDENCE_ITEM_CAP: Final = 40` (src/aer/services/red_team.py:112) still bounds the fact index, and the query takes the first forty rows by `period_end DESC, concept` with no per-concept deduplication (src/aer/services/red_team.py:307-315). The run chose 4,171 facts. Forty of them is 0.96%. F-27's fix reasoned about calculations only — the comment at src/aer/services/red_team.py:113-118 explains why calculations were given their own larger cap, and the facts above were left alone — and prompt rule 4a says "Each recorded calculation appears once, at its newest period" (src/aer/agents/red_team.py:175-181), telling the adversary nothing about the facts being a digest too.

options.name: Mirror the calculation treatment
options.change: One row per concept at its newest period plus the full series for any concept a draft claim cites, its own larger cap sized to the distinct-concept count rather than to the row count, and a prompt rule saying the fact index is a digest exactly as rule 4a says of calculations.
options.cost: A session. Token cost is the honest question: sixty-odd distinct concepts times five periods is a few thousand tokens, not a few hundred.
options.risk: Pushes the red-team input toward the role's cap on a filer with many concepts; needs a measured bound, not a guessed one.

options.name: Show only what the draft actually used
options.change: Index the facts and calculations the run's claims cite, plus their same-concept neighbours across periods, and nothing else. The adversary attacks the evidence the draft stood on.
options.risk: Blinds the adversary to evidence the draft ignored — which is a real category of challenge ("you had this and did not use it") and arguably the most valuable one.

options.name: Leave the cap and fix the language
options.change: Keep 40 rows; make the prompt forbid any challenge of the form "no such fact exists" and require "not shown in my index".
options.risk: Prompt-only, and F-27 already tried the prompt half; an adversary reasoning from 0.96% of the evidence will keep concluding the draft is unsupported, in whatever words.

items.recommendation: Mirror the calculation treatment, and additionally include the cited-fact neighbours from option two — the two are complementary, not alternatives. The third option alone repeats F-27's mistake of fixing with wording what is a defect in what the adversary is shown. Measure the resulting token cost against the role's cap before merging; this is the one item here with a real spend consequence.
items.tests: Extend `tests/test_red_team.py::TestTheAdversarySeesTheFigureTheDraftWasWrittenFrom` with a fact half: plant 300 facts across five periods including a five-year revenue series, and assert the index carries revenue for every period, one row per concept per period, and that no concept the draft's claims cite is absent. The test must fail against today's 40-row cap.
items.acceptance: On the next live run, no published challenge asserts the absence of a fact the report itself prints. Measured by grepping the run's challenges for absence language and cross-checking against `financial_facts`.
items.challengeNote: Restate the defect as '40 of about 218 consolidated facts, undeduplicated, ordered newest-period-first' and drop the 0.96% framing. The consequence is that the open question about token cost and the claim that this is 'the one item here with a real spend consequence' both collapse: 150-220 facts with periods is a few thousand tokens, so the honest first move is simply to raise the fact cap to cover the work order's consolidated fact set and measure, with per-concept dedup only if a filer overruns. Separately check red_team.py:313's `work_order_id == request.id` filter — facts an earlier run of the same company wrote are invisible to the adversary, which may be a larger part of the starved index than the cap.

items.title: A challenge whose arithmetic is void still raises the banner and still buys four redrafts
items.problem: AZN #2's four material challenges — severity 5 on profitability, 5 on balance sheet, 4 on growth, 4 on valuation — were all built on the period mismatch. All four were counted material, all four raised the §2.4 banner, and all four provoked redrafts: seven revisions across `executive_summary`, `earnings_quality`, `balance_sheet_liquidity` and `growth_outlook`, at £1.22 and ten minutes of the run. The two challenges that were actually sound — the governance one about three overlapping `share_repurchases` facts, and the competitive-position one about a constructive stance with no exclusivity data — were severity 3, bought nothing, and were published beside the six false ones where a reader could not tell them apart.
items.rootCause: Materiality is a straight read of a model's self-scored integer: `material=challenge.severity >= MATERIAL_SEVERITY` (src/aer/services/red_team.py:457, MATERIAL_SEVERITY=4 at :83), and the revise loop uses the same line (src/aer/services/revision.py:291). ADR 0039 states the rule as "Materiality follows severity". Nothing between the model's 5 and the platform's response asks whether the challenge's premise holds.

options.name: Materiality requires a surviving premise
options.change: Compute material as `severity >= 4 and not premise_void`, where `premise_void` is the deterministic adjudication from `period-blind-figure-comparison`. The challenge is still recorded, still escalated, still published; it just stops claiming the thesis is in danger and stops buying a redraft.
options.cost: An hour, once the adjudication exists.
options.risk: Amends ADR 0039's "materiality follows severity" — needs the ADR. A bug in the adjudicator would silence a true material challenge, which is the failure direction that matters; the adjudicator must be conservative by construction (only same-name, different-period pairs).

options.name: Rank rather than threshold
options.change: Order challenges by severity and revise the top N regardless, dropping the integer threshold.
options.risk: Changes nothing here: the false challenges were the highest-scored ones. Solves a different problem.

options.name: Leave it and rely on the operator
options.change: Keep materiality as it is; the operator sees the banner and settles.
options.risk: The audit run shows what happens: the operator's own decision aid leaned 'accept' on all eight, and the redrafts had already happened before the operator saw anything.

items.recommendation: Materiality requires a surviving premise. This is the item that stops the damage rather than describing it, and it is cheap once the adjudicator exists. It belongs in the same ADR as `period-blind-figure-comparison`.
items.adrSubject: Same ADR as `period-blind-figure-comparison`: materiality follows severity and a surviving premise, and a challenge code has shown to be comparing unlike periods raises no banner and buys no redraft.
items.tests: A run with one severity-5 period-mismatch challenge and one severity-5 same-period challenge: the first is recorded, published, non-material and provokes no revision; the second is material and provokes one. Assert on the `disagreements.material` column and on `revision_notes` rows, both.
items.acceptance: No revision on the next live run is provoked by a challenge whose cited calculation is on a different period from the claim it attacks. Checkable from `revision_notes` joined to the challenge's cited ids.
items.challengeNote: Scope the claim to 'three of AZN #2's four material challenges'; the growth one is only answered by the fact-index item, which makes this item depend on `fact-index-shows-forty-of-four-thousand` as well as on the adjudicator. Also note in the item that materiality is read twice from two places (the `disagreements.material` column and revision.py:291's independent read of detail.severity), so a premise gate must be written into the recorded detail, not just into the column, or the revise loop will keep firing.
items.invariantRisk: ADR 0039:36 'Materiality follows severity' is amended by this change; the item already says so and asks for the ADR, which is correct.

items.title: The false challenges did not stay in the appendix: they rewrote four sections, and the published body now contradicts itself
items.problem: Because the four material challenges were false, the redrafts they bought made the report worse. `balance_sheet_liquidity` — revised for the severity-5 balance-sheet challenge — now says "Interest cover is not established by the figures available, and no view is offered on it here; the leverage read rests on balance sheet multiples alone and is not evidence that earnings cover finance costs." Five other places in the same document assert the figure confidently: "interest is covered 8.1 times" (Cash Flow Analysis), "interest cover of 8.11 times" (Valuation, Scenarios), "Interest cover of 8.11x relates EBITDA of $18,829m to interest expense of $1,694m" (Earnings Quality), and three Figures tables print 8.11. `growth_outlook` gained a paragraph headed "Where the funding read is contested" instructing the reader to "Treat balance-sheet capacity to sustain R&D and business development as an open question". The correct figure was withdrawn in one place, hedged in another and asserted in four. This is a self-contradiction the platform created in answer to an accusation that was itself wrong.
items.rootCause: ADR 0091 routes a material challenge to the section that made the attacked claim and redrafts that section alone, at most four sections, once each (src/aer/services/revision.py:148-252). Nothing propagates the consequence: a figure withdrawn in one section stays asserted in five others, and no check compares them. `check_report_consistency` (src/aer/services/consistency.py:49) compares facts by concept and period; it does not compare a section that asserts a calculation against a section that disclaims the same calculation, and in any case it runs at `validate`, one step before the red team and two before the revise loop (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:578-602).

options.name: Fix the cause and add a withdrawal check
options.change: Land `void-premise-still-material` so false challenges buy no redraft, then add a deterministic pass after `revise` that flags any calculation asserted in one section and disclaimed in another, as a `disagreements` row the operator sees at gate 3.
options.cost: A few sessions — the withdrawal check needs a way to recognise a disclaimer, which is the hard half.
options.risk: Recognising "is not established" as a disclaimer of a specific calculation is prose analysis; the honest deterministic version is narrower — a section whose claims no longer cite a calculation other sections still cite.

options.name: Revise the whole document or nothing
options.change: When a challenge is accepted as material, redraft every section carrying the attacked calculation, not just the one that made the claim.
options.cost: A few sessions, and materially more model spend — four sections became seven revisions at £1.22; a figure-wide sweep could double that.
options.risk: Blows the £10 budget on a bad run, and multiplies the blast radius of a false challenge instead of containing it.

options.name: Do not revise at all; leave the challenge for the human
options.change: Revert ADR 0091's draft loop, publish challenges beside an unmodified draft.
options.risk: Discards a decision with a record behind it, and the loop is right when the challenge is right — the ADR was written after a section published a number contradicting its own citation.

items.recommendation: Fix the cause and add the narrow withdrawal check. The wide-revision option makes the failure worse and costs money; reverting ADR 0091 answers the symptom by removing a good feature. The narrow check — a calculation cited by some sections' claims and conspicuously absent from a revised section that used to cite it — is deterministic and catches this exact shape.
items.tests: A fixture where `balance_sheet_liquidity` is revised and drops its `interest_cover` citation while three other sections keep theirs: the post-revise pass records one disagreement naming the calculation and the sections on each side. A run where every section keeps its citations records none.
items.acceptance: The next live run's report does not both assert and disclaim the same recorded calculation. Checkable by comparing each section's cited calculation ids before and after the revise step.
items.challengeNote: One thing the item missed and should carry: the same revise step recorded `over_bound: [historical_financial_analysis, investment_thesis, scenarios_sensitivities, valuation_dcf]`. Four further challenged sections were never revised because of the four-section bound, so the published body already mixes answered and unanswered sections for the same challenge — which is a second, independent route to the same self-contradiction and is not addressed by fixing materiality.

items.title: The one exit a challenge has — a person settling it — never reaches the report
items.problem: Every one of the eight challenges prints "Resolution: Escalated for human decision at approval." The reader judge called it "the same non-answer" eight times over. Worse than the non-answer is that it is unconditional: if the operator had opened gate 3, weighed each challenge, chosen a side and written a reason — the whole point of the settle control — the published document would still say "Escalated for human decision at approval" on all eight, because the appendix was written before the operator saw it. There is no state the reader can observe between "the adversary said this" and "a person considered it and decided".
items.rootCause: `validation_disagreements` is a `SectionStage.VALIDATE` builder (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:364), filled at `validate`, refilled after `red_team` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1737) and after `revise` when anything was revised (:1841-1846). The settle route calls `settle_by_hand` then `reseal_final_gate` (src/aer/web/pages.py:1616-1630) and never refills the section; `reseal_final_gate` only moves the payload hash (src/aer/services/gates.py:83-145). The render step assembles from the stored section rows (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3703-3735). Two further defects sit behind this one: if the section were refilled, `_disagreement_blocks` would render a hand-settled challenge as "Resolved by rule 'thesis_conflict': position A selected." (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:322-327) — wrong on both halves, since a person resolved it and "position A" means nothing to a reader — and the operator's reason would still be dropped, because `resolution_rationale` is rendered only on the non-challenge branch (:330-340) and in any case carries the operator's email address (src/aer/services/disagreements.py:284-286), which must not reach a shareable artefact.

options.name: Refill inside the settle path
options.change: Between `settle_by_hand` and `reseal_final_gate`, call `fill_deterministic_sections(..., stage=VALIDATE)`. The reseal then captures the changed section content — which is already inside the gate-2 hash (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3577-3583) — so the operator approves the appendix that records their own decision. Add a settled wording to `_disagreement_blocks` and render the operator's reason with the actor identity stripped.
options.cost: A session including the wording and the redaction.
options.risk: None to the hash discipline: the settle route already refuses settling after a decision and already reseals. The redaction must be a positive strip, not a hope — F-22 was a leaked identifier in a rendered table.

options.name: Render the appendix at render time from live rows
options.change: Move `validation_disagreements` out of stored section content and build it during `_render`.
options.risk: Breaks the property that what was approved is what was rendered — the section content is inside the gate-2 hash, and a document assembled from rows that moved after approval is exactly what ADR 0014 draws a line against.

options.name: Require every challenge to be settled before approval
options.change: Refuse a final-gate approval while any thesis conflict is open.
options.risk: Makes eight challenges eight mandatory written rationales — the operator has already asked for the reason box to be optional (src/aer/web/pages.py:1638-1655). Turns a review into a chore and would have blocked the AZN #2 run outright.

items.recommendation: Refill inside the settle path. It is small, it keeps the approval hash honest, and it is the difference between a control that exists in the code and a control the reader can see the result of. Do not require settling — the operator has already pushed back on rationale friction, and with the adjudicator in place most challenges will not need a person at all.
items.tests: Settle one red-team challenge by hand, then render: the appendix says the operator kept the draft's position (or accepted the challenge) and prints their reason, with no email address and no "Resolved by rule" phrasing anywhere in the output. Assert the rendered markdown contains neither the actor's address nor the string "position A".
items.acceptance: On a run where the operator settles three of eight challenges, the published report shows three settled and five open, and a reader can tell which is which without opening the platform.
items.challengeNote: adrNeeded should not be false. The behaviour is a recorded intention, not an oversight: the builder's docstring (deterministic.py:150-155) says the appendix states what the run did and 'The decision itself is recorded in `approvals`, not rewritten into this content'. And ADR 0091:68-69 makes `revise` 'the new last step that can change what the operator is shown' — repeated in three code comments (vertical_slice_v1.py:585-587, 1735-1736, 1856-1858) — which a web route that refills section content after that seal amends. Ship it with a short ADR note stating the new rule (the operator's own settlement may change the appendix, and the reseal is what keeps the approval honest), rather than silently reversing a documented one.
items.invariantRisk: ADR 0091:68-69 and deterministic.py:150-155's recorded intent; neither is breached in substance, but both are amended and the item marks adrNeeded false.

items.title: A challenge quoting five recorded figures carries one footnote, so the reader must do forensics
items.problem: All three judges refuted the accusations the same way — by chasing footnotes — and all three said so. The sceptic: "I traced the footnotes: [^143] is FY2021 interest cover, [^145] FY2021 gross margin, [^146] FY2021 free cash flow, [^148] FY2022 ROIC, so the red team compared across periods and the body is probably right. That took footnote forensics, not minutes, and no reader should have to do it." And it only half worked: the balance-sheet challenge quotes five recorded values and carries one footnote, so for net debt, debt-to-equity and the two EBITDA figures "no citation resolves the period at all".
items.rootCause: `_disagreement_blocks` attaches at most one source footnote and one calculation footnote per challenge, taking the first id in each list: `opening[key] = str(ids[0])` (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:345-349). The challenge schema allows six calculation ids, six fact ids and six source ids (src/aer/agents/red_team.py:88-97), and the detail record stores all of them (src/aer/services/red_team.py:479-484). Separately, the period is nowhere in the challenge's prose — it exists only in the footnote text the render composes from the calculation row.

items.recommendation: Footnote every cited id and print the period beside each figure. It is an hour of work that directly removes the forensics all three judges had to perform, and it is the difference the sceptic explicitly asked for. items.challengeNote: Effort: a session, not an hour, and name which route is taken. The cheap route (one small prose block per cited id, each carrying the row's name, period and value composed by code) is close to the item's own second option, so the 'evidence table' alternative is nearer than it looks; the expensive route changes a rendering convention shared by every section and should not be started casually.

items.title: The operator's only decision aid leaned 'accept the challenge' on all eight, including the six that were wrong
items.problem: ADR 0095 added a per-challenge brief at gate 3 so the operator compares consequences rather than paragraphs. On AZN #2 it produced eight briefs and leaned `challenge` on eight of eight. On the profitability challenge it told the operator that accepting means believing "the recorded calculations (0.668–0.721 gross, 0.028–0.085 operating, 0.003–0.074 net, 0.203–0.208 EBITDA, 0.003–0.089 ROE) are the true margins for the period" — those are FY2021 and FY2022 values, and the brief presents them as the alternative truth for FY2025. The platform's own advisory surface, built to help the operator, pointed at the wrong answer eight times and cost £0.011 to do it.
items.rootCause: The briefer reads the two positions and nothing else; it has no access to the periods and no deterministic adjudication to read (src/aer/agents/challenge_brief.py). ADR 0095 argues the brief cannot carry a figure because "the schema has no field for either" — but `keeping_assumes`, `accepting_assumes` and `because` are free text, and the model wrote the figures straight into them. `ChallengeSide` has deliberately no third value ("A brief that could decline to lean would reliably decline", src/aer/agents/challenge_brief.py:41-52), so a uniform 8-of-8 lean is indistinguishable from an informative one.

items.recommendation: Brief only what code could not adjudicate. It respects ADR 0095's reasoning exactly — the briefer speaks where no rule could choose — and it removes the case where the lean was wrong, without reopening the decided question about a third value. Note for the record that ADR 0095's structural argument ("the schema has no field for a figure") is unsound as written: free-text fields carry figures, and this run proves it. That sentence should be corrected in a superseding note whether or not the behaviour changes.
items.adrSubject: A short amendment to ADR 0095: a brief is written only for a challenge the platform could not adjudicate, and the claim that the schema structurally excludes figures is withdrawn — the exclusion is a prompt rule and a check, not a type property.
items.tests: A run with one adjudicated and one surviving challenge briefs exactly one of them, and the review page shows the adjudication in place of the lean on the other. Assert on the `brief_challenges` step output and on the rendered review page.
items.acceptance: On the next live run, no brief leans towards accepting a challenge whose cited calculation is on a different period from the claim it attacks.
items.challengeNote: Split the item. The correction to ADR 0095's structural claim is free and independently evidenced — the briefs quote '(0.668-0.721 gross...)' straight into free-text fields — and should ship as a superseding note now. The adjudication-gating half inherits `period-blind-figure-comparison`'s weakened premise and should be re-costed after that item is re-baselined. A briefer that could read the evidence would be a second validator', agents/challenge_brief.py:114-121).

items.title: The report tells the reader eight sources disagreed, when what happened is that an adversary ran
items.problem: The Validation & Disagreements summary reads: "8 disagreement(s) between sources were recorded, of which 8 were escalated for human decision at approval." Not one of the eight is a source conflict; all eight are red-team thesis conflicts. A reader is told the evidence base contradicts itself eight times, which is a much worse statement than the true one, and it stands directly above a table showing every validator passing. The review page fixed this exact confusion — it splits the two and says so in its own comment — and the report never got the same fix.
items.rootCause: `_summary` hardcodes "between sources" for every disagreement kind (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:253, 261) and `_validation_disagreements` renders one undifferentiated list (:145-179). The review page separates them by kind with a comment recording why — "A source conflict is a fault … A red-team challenge is the adversary doing its job, and seven of them listed under 'unresolved' read as seven problems with the run rather than as the review the run paid for" (src/aer/web/pages.py:1165-1194). That reasoning applies at least as strongly to a shareable document read by someone who cannot ask.

items.title: An investor and a sceptic need opposite things from the adversarial record, and both are handed the same eight blocks
items.problem: The brief asked what a sceptic should see and what an investor should see, and they are not the same. Today both get the identical wall: eight severity-scored accusations, the evidence as prose figures, one footnote each, and "Escalated for human decision at approval". The investor judge called it the weakest paragraph in the document and said it "destroys the reader's ability to rely on any number in it". The sceptic judge said "A's provenance mechanism is better in kind" and still preferred the console, for this reason and no other. Meanwhile the two challenges that were genuinely good — the governance one about three overlapping `share_repurchases` facts contradicting a zero-buyback narrative, and the competitive-position one about a constructive stance built on company self-description — are the platform's actual advantage, and they are buried at severity 3 among six false severity-4-and-5s.
items.rootCause: There is one surface and no editorial model behind it. The body carries no adversarial prose at all — the revise loop changes sections silently (src/aer/services/revision.py:148-252) and the report never says a section was redrafted in answer to a challenge, despite `revisions_for_job` holding exactly that record and putting it in the gate-2 payload (src/aer/services/revision.py:256-278). The appendix carries everything, ordered by `created_at` (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:159-165), material and immaterial alike, with no separation between what code settled, what the writer answered and what stands open for judgement.

options.name: Three states in the appendix, one paragraph in the body
options.change: The appendix groups challenges by what happened to them: *settled by code* (the period adjudication, with both periods shown), *answered in the draft* (the section was redrafted — name it, and say so), *open for judgement* (published as now, with the operator's settlement when there is one). options.risk: A new model-written paragraph is a new place for an unsupported sentence. It must go through the ordinary claim rules and evidence policy, exactly as ADR 0091 requires of a revision; nothing about the adversary earns it an exemption.

items.recommendation: Three states in the appendix, one paragraph in the body. The severity floor is actively harmful on the evidence available. The body paragraph is the item that could move a judge's verdict rather than merely stop losing points: the sceptic already rates the platform's provenance above the console's, and an argued bear case in the body is what the console note has and this one does not. It is also the operator's call how far the body paragraph goes towards a stated view — that framing question belongs with the wider "no view reached" decision, not to this area alone.
items.adrSubject: What the adversarial record owes each reader: the body carries the argument in prose under the ordinary evidence contract, the appendix carries the record in three states — settled by code, answered in the draft, open for judgement — and a severity score never decides what is published.
items.tests: A run with one code-settled, one answered and one open challenge renders three labelled groups, and the answered one names the section that was redrafted. A body paragraph drafted from challenges passes the same claim and citation validation as any section — assert that a paragraph citing nothing is refused.
items.acceptance: A repeat blind judging of the next AZN run: no judge names the disagreement appendix as the weakest passage, and at least one names the adversarial record among the reasons to prefer the platform. The audit's own instrument, re-run at roughly £7 for the platform run plus the judging.
items.challengeNote: Add the workflow constraint to the item: the body paragraph is written before the revise step's seal (vertical_slice_v1.py:1850-1858) or ADR 0091's seal rule is amended in the same ADR; add vertical_slice_v1.py and a section_definitions migration to filesTouched. 'A few sessions' survives that, but only if the paragraph is folded into an existing section's contract rather than given a section key of its own. Also tighten the acceptance criterion: 'no judge names the appendix as the weakest passage' is one noisy sample of three free-text reads — pair it with something countable from the same rubric, e.g. that the adversarial record appears in at least one judge's reasons to prefer the platform across both compared documents.
items.invariantRisk: ADR 0091:68-69 (revise is the last step that can change what the operator is shown) constrains where the new writing pass may run; invariant 3 and the ordinary claim/citation contract must bind the new paragraph, which the item states.

items.title: The validation table published beside the accusations was measured before four sections were rewritten
items.problem: The Validation Metrics table is the sceptic's warrant — eleven metrics, ten passing — and it sits immediately above the eight accusations it silently refutes. But it was measured at the `validate` step, which runs before `red_team` and before `revise`. On AZN #2 four sections were rewritten after that measurement, so `cited_figure_agreement` (population 81), `numerical_consistency` (population 831), `presentation_integrity` (population 18 sections) and `source_coverage` describe a document that was not published. The appendix's own eight challenge blocks, full of unlabelled figures, were also not in the document `presentation_integrity` scanned, because the section was still empty of challenges when it ran.
items.rootCause: Step order: `validate` (which computes every metric and then fills `validation_disagreements`) precedes `red_team` and `revise` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:578-602, 1658-1705). The comment at :1685-1688 explains the fill ordering deliberately — "the metrics above were measured before this fill, so a section recording the validators never sits in its own denominator" — which is a good reason for the fill order and not a reason for the metrics never to be recomputed after the draft changes. ADR 0091 states that a revision's "contract, evidence policy, claim rules and validation are exactly the first draft's", and the per-section validation inside `execute_builtin_section` is indeed the same; the run-level metrics are not re-run.

items.recommendation: Re-measure after revise. The table is the sceptic's reason to trust the document and it must describe the document. Take the late-stop risk deliberately: a revision that breaks a validator is exactly the thing the operator should be told about before approving, and ADR 0091 already accepts that the revise step is the last thing that can change what they are shown.
items.tests: A run where a revised section introduces a claim whose figure disagrees with its cited calculation: `cited_figure_agreement` fails on the second measurement, the gate shows it, and the published table reports the failure. Today the metric is measured before the revision and passes.
items.acceptance: On the next live run with revisions, the published Validation Metrics table's populations match the published document's claim and calculation counts.
items.challengeNote: Rewrite the acceptance criterion against the evaluation rows or the run export — 'on the next run with revisions, each metric row's `details.population` matches the counts in the rendered document, and the row's measured_at follows the revise step' — or add the population to the published table as part of the item. Re-measure inside the revise step before the payload hash is sealed (vertical_slice_v1.py:1850-1858), which removes the late-stop risk entirely and keeps the approval honest; then update escalation.py:8-13's 'frozen once the red-team step has run', which is already stale after ADR 0091.

items.title: The adversary's own statement of what it could not test, and every challenge the platform threw away, reach no surface at all
items.problem: AZN #2's red team wrote a coverage note that diagnoses this whole finding in its own words: "almost none of the draft's ~150 numeric claims can be traced to the evidence shown me. The fact index holds only share counts, capex, taxes paid, debt balances, SBC and buybacks … The recorded calculations are unlabelled by period or entity … I cannot tell whether the draft used an evidence set I was not shown or whether the figures are unsupported; that ambiguity is itself the finding and should be resolved before a reader sees this." It also says what it could not test at all: "segment mix, LOE timing, litigation quantum or peer comparison". None of that reaches the report, the review page or the operator. Nor does the list of challenges the service rejected for citing ids the run does not hold — a sceptic's first question about any adversarial process is what it discarded and why.
items.rootCause: `RedTeamOutcome.coverage_note` and `RedTeamOutcome.rejected` are returned, logged and stored in the step output (src/aer/services/red_team.py:124-140, 249-268) and then read by nothing. `_validation_disagreements` reads `Evaluation` and `Disagreement` rows only (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:151-165); the review page's red-team block renders challenges and briefs and no note (src/aer/web/templates/runs/review.html:375-464). The note is the adversary's honest statement of its own limits, and the platform treats it as a log line.

items.recommendation: Publish the note and the rejections in the appendix, and show the note at gate 3 as well — they are the same hour of work twice. Publishing the coverage note is also the cheapest possible early warning that the evidence index is starved: had it been on the review page, the operator would have seen the diagnosis of F-27 before approving the run, in the adversary's own words.
items.tests: A run whose adversary returns a coverage note and two rejected challenges renders both in the appendix and on the review page; a run whose adversary rejected nothing renders no rejection line and does not change shape.
items.acceptance: The next live run's report states what the adversary could not test and how many of its challenges the platform refused, without anyone opening the run export.
items.challengeNote: One thing to settle before publishing: the coverage note is unvalidated model prose entering a shareable document, so it must be framed as the adversary's own testimony rather than as a finding of the run, and checked for figures — this run's note carries none, but nothing stops the next one carrying some, and invariant 3 governs the document it lands in. A one-line label and a numeral refusal on that field are part of the hour.

items.title: Eight challenges is the schema's ceiling and the run hit it, and nothing selects, orders or bounds what the reader meets
items.problem: Every judge counted them: "eight unresolved red-team accusations", "all eight disagreements are left 'Escalated for human decision at approval'", "the eight 'Red team' entries". The number itself did work — a reader meeting eight numbered attacks on a document's own figures concludes the document is broken before reading one of them. The schema's ceiling is eight (`challenges: list[RedTeamChallenge] = Field(max_length=8)`), and the run produced exactly eight, which is the shape of a bound being hit rather than a judgement being exercised. They are then printed in recording order, so the two sound challenges landed fifth and sixth among six false ones.
items.rootCause: `RedTeamReport.challenges` is capped at 8 (src/aer/agents/red_team.py:120-125) and the prompt asks for honest scoring but sets no target count (src/aer/agents/red_team.py:152-190, rule 5). The appendix renders every recorded row ordered by `created_at, topic` (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:159-165). There is no selection step between "the adversary produced N" and "the reader meets N", and no ordering by anything the reader would care about.

items.title: No run can state a view: the rating column is written once, as None
items.problem: Every report ever rendered carries the header line "**Non-binding view:** no view reached". Judges named this first and unanimously: audit §4.1 records "the platform's header says 'Non-binding view: no view reached', so there is no thesis to act on", and the msft1 sceptic wrote "for a note asked for a 12-month view, that is a non-delivery". A document with no destination cannot argue toward one, so every section describes instead. The reader is also lied to: on azn2 the Investment Thesis says in prose "We therefore hold a constructive but low-confidence view" while the header five inches above says no view was reached.
items.rootCause: `report.rating = None` and `report.confidence = None` are literal assignments in the render step (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3765-3766). No other line in src/ ever assigns `.rating`; every other reference reads it (src/aer/render/markdown.py:162, src/aer/services/history.py:164/470, src/aer/web/pages.py:2773, src/aer/api/routes/reports.py:65, src/aer/obsidian/export.py:298). The schema supports it (src/aer/db/models/report.py:73, nullable String(32)) and the planner is even shown prior ratings as hypothesis material (src/aer/agents/planner.py:319), so the whole pipeline is plumbed for a value nothing produces. The `verdict` role that could author one is forbidden to: ADR 0087 scopes it to "never a figure, never a fact, never a recommendation, and never evidence" (src/aer/agents/registry.py:348-360), and its sentence reaches only the web review page (src/aer/web/pages.py:1148, 1309-1331) — never the exported Markdown or PDF.

items.recommendation: Build the stated view as three separately-typed pieces so the one rule is never touched: (a) a **rating word** from a closed vocabulary, authored by a model over the frozen draft, which asserts no fact and states no figure; (b) a **target**, which is not authored at all — it is the existing `value_per_share` calculation row, rendered through the same footnote door as every other figure; (c) an **implied return**, a new traced calculation over `value_per_share` and the last close, which the 2026-08-09 licence determination already permits as a derived figure (src/aer/services/price_acquisition.py:21, src/aer/services/comps.py:20). The model never computes (b) or (c) and never sees a figure it may restate. Where the run has no per-share output, the type carries no target field at all — ADR 0034's shape — so the header degrades to "view withheld: no valuation output" rather than to "no view reached", which reads as an abstention rather than a failure.
items.adrSubject: A stated view is a closed-vocabulary word authored over a frozen record, a target that is a calculation row, and an implied return that is a calculation over it — and it amends ADR 0087, which today forbids the verdict role any recommendation and keeps it off every shareable surface.
items.tests: A test that renders a report whose run holds a `value_per_share` row and asserts the header carries a rating word, a target footnoted to that calculation, and an implied return footnoted to a new calculation; the same test with the valuation withheld must assert the target field is structurally absent (no `None`, no field), in the shape `tests/test_report_document.py` already uses for withheld comps. A containment test that a skill file cannot set the rating (the rule is already stated at src/aer/core/schemas/skill.py:11 and must now have teeth). Both must fail on today's code, where the first assertion cannot pass because no producer exists.
items.acceptance: On a live run of MSFT (the subject where a market capitalisation is present), the rendered Markdown header carries a rating, a target and an implied return, each resolving to a footnote that names a calculation row; `aer replay` re-derives both figures; and three fresh blind judge reads answer "yes" to view_stated where msft1's answered "no" 3 of 3.

options.change: New ADR amending 0087; verdict role gains a rating field over a closed vocabulary; two new traced calculations; header and one-pager render all three.

But it does not make the *prose* argue, because the sections are drafted long before the gate, so it must be paired with the synthesis item to have any effect on the document.

options.name: Calculated view only, no word
options.change: Render target and implied return, and let the reader infer. No ADR, no model opinion.
options.risk: Cheapest and safest, and probably insufficient: the judges asked for a thesis to act on, not a number to interpret. Worth doing first as the floor.

Reorder the recommendation: option 3 (calculated view only) cannot be the floor either while `value_per_share` is unreconciled, so the first session's work is settling which case produced the headline per-share figure, not rendering it. Prefer option 2 (operator-set rating at gate 2) as the first shipped half — it is the operator's own judgement, it fits the personal-tool framing, and it needs no figure the document cannot defend. items.invariantRisk: ADR 0087 ('never a recommendation', 'never evidence', 'reaches no shareable surface') — the item names this. It also runs into ADR 0074 ('a judgement is never a source reference') and the reserved-field rule at src/aer/core/schemas/skill.py:73-91, which reserves `rating`, `recommendation`, `target_price`, `price_target`, `fair_value` and `valuation_range` for precisely the reason the item proposes to render them: 'a view somebody holds is not a figure at all... no holder, no time, no stated basis, and nothing to check'. The new ADR must say why a model-authored rating reaching the report through the workflow step is permissible when the same word reaching it through a section contract is structurally refused. The item does not name this.

items.title: Each section sees 40 rows of an 831-row record, and the slice is chosen so the valuation never appears
items.problem: Sections contradict each other and the front page about what the run holds. msft1's Executive Summary states "it holds no valuation output, no discount rate and no peer multiple, so we take no view" while the At a glance table three inches above prints WACC 9.3% and Value per share $485.29. azn2's Executive Summary states "No discount rate, terminal growth assumption, invested capital, return on invested capital, share price or share count is available" while its own Investment Thesis two pages later cites "a 15.6% return on invested capital" on "$72.6 billion of invested capital". A judge cannot argue with a document that cannot agree with itself, and the msft1 sceptic said exactly that: "A's deeper problem is that it contradicts itself on exactly the load-bearing points."
items.rootCause: `gather_evidence` caps calculations at `EVIDENCE_ITEM_CAP = 40` (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:97) ordered `period_end DESC NULLS LAST, sequence` (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:580-588). azn2 holds 831 calculation rows of which 667 carry no period — every DCF output, `wacc`, `cost_of_equity`, `value_per_share`, `enterprise_value` among them — so they sort last and are cut every time, while the 40 slots fill with FY2025's 34 ratios plus 6 of FY2024's. The code names the trade-off and accepts it ("Sorting them first would fill the cap with grid cells and cut every period"), but the consequence is that no section can ever discuss the valuation, and the sections with the smallest token budgets get the smallest slices: `executive_summary` is seeded at 2,000 tokens (migration 0023 line 529) against `valuation_dcf`'s 5,000, and the listing share is 0.45/0.6 of that (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:116-117). Measured: azn2's Executive Summary was dealt 12 facts, 9 calculations and **1** excerpt; the Investment Thesis 18/13/2; the valuation 31/20/6. `evidence_truncated: true` on 48 of 48 section executions across azn2, msft2 and mtb.

items.title: The deterministic layer computes levels, not movements, so the writer has nothing to argue from and is rightly forbidden to derive it
items.problem: Every judge comparison turned on decomposition the platform cannot do. The msft1 reader wrote that the console "proves it from segment arithmetic a reader can redo by hand ('The premise is wrong: cloud margin is not expanding' — IC gross margin −420bp, cost of revenue +44.1% on revenue +29.7%), then quantifies the capitalisation flattery ($72–92bn/yr not yet in the P&L)", against which "A's Earnings Quality calls useful lives 'unverifiable' and declines to estimate". The azn operator judge chose the console for "a reverse DCF that tells me exactly what I have to believe to justify the market price". The platform's own approved plan asked for both — azn2's `historical_financial_analysis` focus reads "Identify the cost lines driving the gap between gross and operating margin", and its `valuation_dcf` focus reads "Run the valuation primarily as a reverse DCF" — and the run delivered neither.
items.rootCause: `src/aer/calc/bridge.py` implements exactly the missing analysis — `margin_bridge`, `bridge_contribution`, `bridge_residual`, `margin_movement` — with a docstring that says it "is the difference between a report that describes a company and one that explains it". It has **no production caller**: `src/aer/services/analysis.py:36-41` imports ratios, quality, cash_uses, statements and units, and nothing else in src/ imports `aer.calc.bridge` (the only other reference is the replay allow-list at src/aer/eval/replay.py:65). It is fully tested (tests/test_bridge.py) and was mutation-hardened (audit F-20 / gap-analysis A26: "every sign in the margin bridge"). Beside it there is no contribution-to-growth calculation and no market-implied solve: `implied_terminal_growth` and `implied_exit_multiple` (src/aer/calc/dcf.py:786-830) invert the platform's *own* terminal value, not the market's price. With none of these recorded, prompt rule 1 binds correctly and absolutely — "You never produce a figure of your own — no sum, difference, growth rate or share worked out from the figures you were shown, however simple the arithmetic; where the figure you want is not in the listing, describe the direction in words and give no number" (src/aer/agents/section_writer.py:104-107) — and the writer does the only thing left: it recites levels and describes direction in words.
