items.title: The summary and the thesis are written in parallel with the sections they summarise, and nothing ever concludes
items.problem: The Executive Summary and Investment Thesis are the report's argument, and they are written before — in fact alongside — every section whose findings they are meant to weigh. So they summarise the evidence pack rather than the report, which is why msft1's summary says "no prior-period comparatives sit here to test durability" while the same document's Revenue history table prints FY2022–FY2026 and footnotes [^42]–[^56] carry a five-year margin series. There is also no conclusion: the eighteen-section spine puts the thesis at position 110, second, and ends on Prior Research Comparison and Validation & Disagreements. The argument is asserted at the front, never revisited, and the last thing a reader meets is the platform attacking its own figures.
items.rootCause: The draft step fans out concurrently under `asyncio.Semaphore(DRAFT_FAN_OUT)` with `DRAFT_FAN_OUT = 4` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:299,3288-3317), and the step's own docstring states the design: sections "share the research wave's shape — each depends on the evidence pack and on **nothing another section produces**" (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3336-3339). The azn2 log confirms the interleaving: executive_summary was refused at 18:20:27 and generated at 18:21:59, between segment_analysis and historical_financial_analysis. No later step reads the finished sections and writes a synthesis — `revise` answers red-team challenges section by section (src/aer/services/revision.py), `verdict` writes one sentence for a web page, and `render` assembles. The eighteen-section order is data (migration 0023 `_SPINE`), so the absence of a closing section is a seed, not a code constraint.

items.title: The report's second-longest section is the platform accusing its own figures, with no answer printed beside it
items.problem: azn2's Validation & Disagreements runs to 1,234 words — longer than every analytical section except the valuation — and consists of eight severity-graded red-team challenges against the report's own headline numbers, each closed by "Resolution: Escalated for human decision at approval." The azn2 reader judge's decisive sentence was "I cannot trust a single headline number in A on A's own account", and audit §4.1 records that the repaired AZN report "carries eight unresolved red-team accusations against its own figures". Four of those sections had in fact been redrafted to answer the challenges (£1.22 and ten minutes of the run), and the reader is told none of it. So the run pays for the critique loop and ships only its accusations.
items.rootCause: ADR 0091 decides, deliberately, that "the challenge's `disagreements` row is never auto-resolved" and "the revision happens *beside* the challenge". `_disagreement_blocks` (src/aer/sections/deterministic.py:307-355) renders the challenge, its basis and one of four fixed resolution sentences; there is no field for the section's answer and nothing records that the section was revised. The revise step writes `revision_notes` rows (src/aer/services/revision.py) that only `aer lessons` reads, and the `challenge_brief` role that reads a challenge as a choice is explicitly barred from the document ("reaches no rendered report", src/aer/agents/registry.py:363-378). Compounding it, the adversary's own index was the defect F-27 fixed — forty rows by `sequence`, oldest period first, with no period label — so on these runs most of the accusations were false and the report shipped them as its own verdict.

items.title: The one-pager and the authored verdict exist, and neither is in the file anybody is handed
items.problem: The document a reader receives — the Markdown and the PDF — opens with an eight-line metadata block, a disclaimer, three small tables and then a 400-word Executive Summary, and runs to 14,000–16,000 words with no route through it. The platform already builds a one-page summary and already writes a sentence of interpretation over the frozen draft, and a reader outside the web interface gets neither. Audit §4.3 use case 9 ("Sharing the result") is scored "partly" for exactly this family of reasons, and §4.1 records that "the platform's verifiability advantage lives in the interface, not in the document it exports".

The authored verdict is read only by `_review_verdict` for the review page (src/aer/web/pages.py:1148,1301-1331). items.recommendation: Add three deterministic run-time metrics — not model judges, which would be a model scoring a model's prose and would cost money every run. (1) `view_stated`: the header carries a rating and, where a per-share output exists, a target and an implied return. (2) `self_consistency_of_absence`: no section's prose asserts the absence of a figure the rendered document prints elsewhere — computed by matching a closed list of absence phrases against the At a glance and per-section figure sets. (3) `explained_figure_ratio`: the share of the report's numerals that appear in a sentence carrying a movement, a decomposition or a comparison, against those that appear only as a level — computed from the claim rows and the calculation names, so it needs no new reading of prose. Set thresholds advisory at first and promote to blocking once two live runs have baselined them. Keep the judge panel as an occasional acceptance harness under `audit/`, not as a gate.
items.adrSubject: A metric may measure the shape of an argument without judging it — which properties of a document are deterministically checkable, why no model scores the prose at run time, and why these three join the run-time set advisory before they block.

items.title: The length salvage removes the last sentence of the longest field and destroys every paragraph break
items.problem: In a research paragraph the last sentence is the conclusion — the "so what". `trimmed_to_word_count` removes trailing sentences, longest field first, until the draft fits, so the platform systematically deletes the payoff of the longest argument in the section and keeps the restatement at the front. The same functions then rejoin what survives with single spaces, so every paragraph break in the edited field is destroyed. azn2's Earnings Quality is the proof: it is the one section marked "Shortened to fit the length allotted to this section", and it renders as a single unbroken 590-word block, where msft1's unsalvaged Earnings Quality renders as four paragraphs.
items.rootCause: `trimmed_to_word_count` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:1094-1140) picks `max(slots, key=len of words)` and drops `_SENTENCES.split(text)[:-1]`, on the stated assumption that "in a section that overruns, both [restatement and narration] sit at the end" — an assumption the documents contradict. All three salvage functions then write `" ".join(kept).strip()` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:981, 1056, 1137), and `_SENTENCES` splits on `\s+`, which consumes `\n\n`; `display.prose` and the Markdown serialiser pass newlines through untouched (src/aer/render/display.py:225-248), so the paragraph structure exists right up to the moment the salvage runs. Only `growth_outlook` and `scenarios_sensitivities` have a structured prose-block contract (migration 0037); every other section's commentary is one flat string, so it is one flat string after the trim too.

items.title: The numeral rule is the commonest cause of a refused draft, and it is refusing product names and disclosed dates
items.problem: Across the three runs with worker logs, drafts were refused 27 times; 16 of those refusals were the numeral rule and 13 the word budget — together 29 of 32 refusal reasons. The refusals are not catching fabrications. azn2's Earnings Quality was refused twice, on the first draft and again on the revision, for the product code "FPI-2059"; Cash Flow Analysis and Catalysts were both refused for "substantially complete by the end of 2030", a date the filing discloses; the Investment Thesis was refused for "AstraZeneca enters the second half of 2026". Each refusal costs a paid retry and, more importantly, teaches the writer to avoid naming specifics — which is exactly the habit that makes prose recite. One refusal even left mangled text in the writer's hands: the log shows "the Fusion FPI-2059 programme, consolidated from , was ful…", the date eraser having removed the anchor.
items.rootCause: `unsourced_numerals` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:605-658) scans erased text and refuses any numeral not covered by a claim or readable as a named figure. The erasers before it — `without_document_references`, `without_product_names`, `without_plain_counts` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:469-604) — implement ADR 0054, 0060 and 0057, and they miss two live shapes: a hyphenated alphanumeric product code (`FPI-2059`, where ADR 0060's "a number inside a name is not a figure" plainly applies) and a bare year anchored by a preposition rather than by a month or quarter ("by the end of 2030", "the second half of 2026"). The prompt already asks the writer to anchor years (src/aer/agents/section_writer.py:110-113), which is a workaround for a gap in the eraser rather than a rule about research writing.

items.title: The one-sentence gap budget catches three sentences per report while roughly a tenth of the prose is about absence
items.problem: The rule exists because "a live report spent a third of its prose describing absent disclosure". It has not fixed that. Measuring the two reports' body prose against the platform's own `_GAP_PHRASES` list, msft1 matches 3 of 277 sentences and azn2 3 of 292 — about 1% each. Measuring against a wider absence vocabulary drawn from what the documents actually say, 28 of 277 and 23 of 292 — 10.1% and 7.9%. The sentences the rule misses are the load-bearing ones: "it holds no valuation output, no discount rate and no peer multiple, so we take no view"; "Exclusivity exposure — unresolved"; "No discount rate, terminal growth assumption, invested capital, return on invested capital, share price or share count is available." Meanwhile the rule did refuse a draft: azn2's Scenarios & Sensitivities lost an attempt to it. So it costs retries without changing the document, and it teaches the writer to reword absence rather than replace it.
items.rootCause: `_GAP_PHRASES` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:760-782) is a closed list of nineteen surface phrases, matched case-insensitively against whole sentences, with `MAX_GAP_SENTENCES = 1` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:828). It is a lexical test for a behavioural property. The prompt simultaneously tells the writer both to "say so plainly in the content" when evidence is thin (rule 3, src/aer/agents/section_writer.py:121) and to do it "in one clause and move on" (rule 6, src/aer/agents/section_writer.py:131-137), so the writer is under two instructions and satisfies the enforced one by choosing other words. Structurally, the absence is real: the sections genuinely have nothing else to say, because of the evidence-pack and movement-calculation items above — which is why a tighter phrase list would only move the problem, not solve it.

items.title: The budgets are flat where the argument is not, and migration 0045's experiment has an answer nobody acted on
items.problem: Budgets are allocated by section type rather than by how much argument a section has to carry, and the writer still overruns. Of the drafts refused for length across three runs, the overrun ratios were 638/508, 639/508, 671/508, 654/508, 466/363 and 484/363 — 1.26 to 1.33, mean about 1.29, against a ceiling factor of 1.25. Meanwhile the sections that judges praised and the sections they missed are budgeted almost identically: `valuation_dcf`, the section with the largest evidence pack (31 facts, 20 calculations, 6 excerpts) and the only augmenter block, produced the prose the msft1 comparison singled out for "candour in the DCF caveats"; `key_risks` carries a 580-word budget and msft1 spent 96 words of commentary on it; `catalysts` carries 362 and spent 167, all of them about absence. The Executive Summary is the only section consistently pressed against its ceiling (368 and 370 against 362) and is the one the reader meets first.
items.rootCause: Budgets were seeded flat by editorial intuition (migration 0034 `_WORD_BUDGETS`) and then multiplied uniformly by 1.45 (migration 0045), whose docstring states the experiment explicitly: "If the overruns vanish, the budgets were below what these schemas can be written in; if they rescale — the model again writing ~1.46x the new number — the prompt's `target_words` does not bind, and the fix is a hard constraint instead of larger numbers. The next complete run answers it." Three complete runs have now answered it — the overruns rescaled, from 1.46× to about 1.29× — and nothing has been decided. `_WORD_CEILING_FACTOR = 1.25` (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:801) sits just below the observed mean, so near-misses are the normal outcome: the writer lands a few per cent over the line, pays for the draft, and is refused or trimmed.

items.recommendation: Answer 0045's question, then reallocate. The experiment's own conclusion applies: since the overruns rescaled, `target_words` does not bind, so stop treating the number as a target the model aims at and make the ceiling the number the model is told — raise `_WORD_CEILING_FACTOR` to the observed mean or state the ceiling itself as the budget, so a compliant draft is not refused for a few per cent. Then reallocate by argument load rather than by section type: the summary and the risks (the two `one_pager` sections) and the synthesis get more, the descriptive sections less; total prose can fall while the argument grows. Do this **after** the evidence-pack and movement items, because a section with more to say will use its budget differently and a reallocation made against today's starved packs would be calibrated on the wrong document.

items.title: The reading ladder discards the scale word, so "$331.8 million" reads as $331.8 billion
items.problem: A report can state a figure with the wrong scale word — "$331.8 million" of revenue where the filing says $331.8 billion, a thousandfold error — and both of the platform's own numeric guards pass it. The draft-time §2.12 numeral rule accepts it, and the `cited_figure_agreement` metric at gate 2 accepts it, because both read the digits "331.8" and neither reads the word after them. This is the one item in my area that puts a wrong number in front of a reader, and it does so in the exact sentence a research note is read for.
items.rootCause: `src/aer/core/figures.py:103-110` defines READINGS as a blind ladder of scale factors (×1, ×100, ×0.001, ×1e-6, ×1e-9) and `reads_as` (figures.py:112-127) returns true if the stored value under ANY of them quantises to the quoted token at the token's own precision. The scanner `NUMERAL` (figures.py:70-76) consumes a glued unit suffix (`bn|mn|m|k|x|×`) inside a non-capturing group and discards it, and never looks at the following word at all. Both callers share the ladder by design: `without_unsourced_numeral_sentences` via `_reads_as_named` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:431-446) and `cited_figure_agreement` (src/aer/eval/runtime.py:383-387). ADR 0097 made this ladder the single definition deliberately, and named as its accepted cost only 'a section quoting a *different* figure that happens to be one of these readings of a figure it did cite, which the excerpt-level citation check and `cited_figure_agreement` still see' — that escape does not hold for the scale-word case, because `cited_figure_agreement` uses the same ladder.
evidence: Audit §5 F-21, guard items: 'The reading ladder discards the scale word, so "$331.8 million" reads as 331.8 billion. Both are in core/figures.py and ADR 0060's territory.'
Audit §8 item 9 puts it to the operator
src/aer/core/figures.py:70-76 (NUMERAL, suffix consumed and dropped)
src/aer/core/figures.py:103-110 (READINGS)
src/aer/core/figures.py:112-127 (reads_as)
src/aer/core/section_output.py:431-446 (_reads_as_named)
src/aer/eval/runtime.py:383-387 (cited_figure_agreement uses the same ladder)
docs/adr/0097-a-numeral-is-checked-against-the-figure-not-its-spelling.md, 'Accepted costs' and 'What is not weakened'
audit/scoring/numerals.py:126-140 (_SCALES, _SUFFIX_SCALES), 599-609 (scale resolution), 266-277 (Numeral.scale / Numeral.scaled) — a working scale-word reader already in this repository
items.recommendation: Option B. The scale reader already exists in this repository, written and calibrated during this audit, and reuses the same `numeral_matches` scanner — `audit/scoring/numerals.py` builds on `aer.core.figures` and adds scale, currency, percent and multiple hints from the neighbourhood. Porting the scale half into `aer.core.figures` as an optional hint, and narrowing READINGS to the readings consistent with that hint when one is present, is a port with a reference implementation and an existing test corpus rather than a design problem. Option A (drop the ladder) is refused: ADR 0097 shows it costs sections. Option C (leave it) is refused: it is the one item here that can publish a wrong number, and it is cheap to close. This amends ADR 0097 and needs a new ADR beside it — the ADR's stated escape hatch is wrong and the record should say so.

options.name: A — refuse a numeral whose scale word disagrees, dropping the ladder
options.change: Read the scale word and require an exact match against the stored value; abandon READINGS entirely.
options.cost: Re-opens roadmap §2.1: ADR 0097 records two sections lost to exactly this strictness.
options.risk: High. Costs sections on every run for a defect never observed live.

options.name: B — carry the scale word as a hint and narrow the ladder when one is present
options.change: Port the scale-word reader from `audit/scoring/numerals.py:126-140, 599-609` into `aer.core.figures`; when a numeral carries a scale word or suffix, admit only the readings consistent with it; when it carries none, keep today's ladder unchanged.
options.cost: One function and one signature change in `core/figures.py`, threaded through its two callers.
options.risk: Low and bounded — a numeral with no scale word behaves exactly as today, so no run loses a section it does not lose now.

options.name: C — leave the ladder and rely on the writers
options.change: Nothing in code; record the gap in ADR 0097 as a known residual.
options.risk: A thousandfold error reaches a reader unguarded, and the audit's own accuracy verdict rests on a scorer the platform does not carry.

items.adrSubject: A figure's scale word is part of the figure: the reading ladder narrows to the readings the writer's own words admit (amends ADR 0097).
items.tests: A test that fails first: `reads_as(Decimal("331.8"), Decimal("331839000000"))` is true today and must stay true for a bare numeral; the new test asserts a section whose content states '$331.8 million' beside a claim naming a fact worth 331839000000 is refused by the numeral rule, and that `cited_figure_agreement` reports it. Plus a regression test that '$331.8 billion' and '331,839' (the millions a table renders in) both still pass, so ADR 0097's two recovered sections stay recovered.
items.acceptance: On a replayed draft (`aer replay-draft`) over an archived reply edited to say 'million' where the run said 'billion', the numeral rule refuses the section and the metric reports the disagreement; and every one of the five audit runs' archived drafts still passes with zero new refusals when replayed under the new rule.
items.challengeNote: Effort: a session is understated by roughly 2-3x; call it a few sessions. The blocker is not the signature of `reads_as` but the plumbing around it: `numerals_in` returns `frozenset[str]` (section_output.py:421-428), `_FoundNumerals.numerals` is a frozenset (:695), and the rule does set arithmetic on it at :641, :973 and :990. A scale hint is per-occurrence, so it cannot ride a token set - `numerals_in`, `_numerals_by_path` and all three set operations have to become position- or match-carrying. That is the work, and it is in `core/`, which is mypy --strict and must stay pure. Acceptance: 'a replayed draft over an archived reply edited to say million' is not executable. Archived replies are content-addressed artefacts and `artefacts` carries a BEFORE UPDATE trigger raising restrict_violation (migrations/versions/0003_artefacts_and_sources.py:63-72, 119-124), so an archived reply cannot be edited; `aer replay-draft` (src/aer/cli.py:1470-1483) reads a run's own archived replies by job id. Rewrite the criterion as a synthetic reply fixture plus a clean replay of the five runs. One narrowing in the fix's favour that the item did not use: `Evidence.figure_values` holds absolute values by design (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:438-440, 'financial_facts.value is absolute and scale is the source's presentation'), so narrowing on a scale word cannot regress a fact stored in millions - the scale-only scope is safer than the item claims, provided percent and multiple hints stay out of it.

items.title: A fact-backed numeric claim is never checked against the fact's value; its own statement lends the cover
items.problem: Two thirds of the platform's numeric claims name a financial fact rather than a calculation, and for those nothing ever compares the sentence to the stored number. Worse, the claim's own statement is what grants cover to the numerals in the section's prose — so a writer that states a wrong figure in the claim and then repeats it in the content satisfies the draft-time rule with its own mistake, and the gate-2 metric that would catch the divergence joins on calculations only and never sees the claim at all.
items.rootCause: Two independent halves. (1) `covered_figures` (src/aer/sections/evidence.py:815-836) returns the claims' `statement` strings as cover, and `without_unsourced_numeral_sentences` (src/aer/core/section_output.py:963-974) admits any content numeral that appears in a covering statement, with no comparison between that statement and the named figure's stored value. (2) `_cited_figures` (src/aer/services/evaluations.py:569-596) builds the observations for `cited_figure_agreement` with `select(Claim, Calculation).join(Calculation, Calculation.id == Claim.calculation_id)` — a claim carrying `financial_fact_id` instead (the check constraint at src/aer/db/models/claim.py:107-112 makes exactly one of the three non-null) produces no row and is never measured.
evidence: Audit §5 F-21, guard items: 'A fact-backed numeric claim is never checked against its fact's value: the claim's statement lends cover to the content's numerals and cited_figure_agreement joins on calculations only.'
Audit §8 item 9
src/aer/services/evaluations.py:577-586 (the join on Calculation.id == Claim.calculation_id)
src/aer/db/models/claim.py:77-112 (exactly one of financial_fact_id, calculation_id, attestation_id)
src/aer/sections/evidence.py:829-836 (statements returned as cover, values only for the named ids)
src/aer/core/section_output.py:968-974 (a token is accounted for if it is in a covering statement OR reads as a named figure)
Audit §5 F-21 also records the live counter-evidence: '0 contradicted of 169 and 165 checkable figures', so the writer was faithful and the guard is absent
items.recommendation: Do both halves, and do the metric half first because it is nearly free. Widening `_cited_figures` to a UNION over `Claim.financial_fact_id` → `FinancialFact.value` is about twenty lines and one extra observation source; `CitedFigureObservation` already carries name/text/value/unit and needs no schema change, and `figure_plausibility` already reads `FinancialFact` in the same module (`_figure_scenes`, evaluations.py:598-610), so the join and the unit handling have a pattern to copy. The draft-time half (checking a claim's own statement against its named figure) is the larger change and is where the invariant genuinely bites — the statement is a model's sentence lending cover to a model's prose, which is the circularity invariant 3 exists to break. Do it as a claim-level check inside `validate_draft`, so it costs the claim rather than the section (ADR 0096's rule), not as a new refusal of the whole draft.

options.name: A — widen the metric only
options.change: Add fact-backed claims to `_cited_figures` so `cited_figure_agreement` measures them at gate 2.
options.cost: About twenty lines in `services/evaluations.py` plus a test.
options.risk: Low. The threshold is already zero and the audit's runs show zero failures, so it should not newly refuse a good run — but it is measured at `validate`, so see the separate item about `revise`.

options.name: B — check the claim's statement against its named figure at draft time
options.change: In `validate_draft`, compare each numeric claim's own statement numerals against the stored value of the fact or calculation it names; a claim that disagrees is malformed and is dropped (ADR 0096's disposition), which removes its cover before the numeral rule runs.
options.cost: One check in `sections/evidence.py` plus the ordering note in `sections/writing.py:_salvaged`.
options.risk: Medium. A claim whose statement legitimately quotes a different related figure would be dropped; the mitigation is to check only when the statement quotes exactly one numeral, and to widen from there.

options.name: C — both
options.change: B at draft time and A at gate 2, so a fact-backed figure is checked where it is written and again where it is scored.
options.risk: Low if B is conservative.

items.tests: A test that fails first: a section whose claim names a fact worth 331839000000 and whose statement says 'revenue of $412.6 billion', with the same numeral in the content — today it drafts and scores clean; after the fix the claim is malformed, its cover is withdrawn, the sentence is removed by the salvage, and `cited_figure_agreement` reports the disagreement if the sentence survives.

items.challengeNote: One figure in the problem statement is unsourced and should be marked a hypothesis: 'two thirds of the platform's numeric claims name a financial fact rather than a calculation' appears nowhere in the audit (no 'two thirds' or 'two-thirds' in docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09.md) and was not measured here. The data to settle it is in the repository (docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/*/replay.json, truth.json) and the ratio drives how much Option A actually adds, so measure it before sizing. Minor: the observation is built from `claim.text`, not `statement` - `statement` is the pre-persistence `ProposedClaim` field - so a reader following the file references should expect both names for the same sentence.

items.title: cited_figure_agreement is measured at `validate`, and `revise` then replaces the claims it measured
items.problem: The gate-2 scorecard the operator approves reports a figure-agreement score for claims that no longer exist. `revise` redrafts the sections the red team attacked, replacing their claims with new ones, and nothing re-measures. A revision can introduce exactly the error the metric exists to catch and the run still shows a clean check at the gate the operator is signing.
items.rootCause: Step order in `src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py`: `draft` (557) → `validate` (578) → `red_team` (582) → `revise` (587). `_validate` (1658-1676) calls `evaluate_run`, which writes every RUN_TIME metric row including `cited_figure_agreement`; `_revise` (1808) then calls `revise_challenged_sections`, which rewrites section content and claims and never re-runs the evaluation. The docstring at 1685-1688 shows the ordering was reasoned about for the validation *section* ('the metrics above were measured before this fill, so a section recording the validators never sits in its own denominator') without the revision case being considered.
evidence: Audit §5 F-21: 'cited_figure_agreement is measured at validate, before revise replaces a section's claims; revised claims are never re-measured.'
Audit §8 item 10, which pairs it with F-22: 'Both are the same question: what re-runs after a late change?'
src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:557, 578, 582, 587 (step order and the comments justifying it)
src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1658-1688 (_validate)
src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1808-1840 (_revise)
src/aer/services/revision.py has no commit and no evaluation call
items.recommendation: Option A, narrowly. Re-measuring only the per-section metrics over only the sections `revise` actually touched keeps the cost at arithmetic over the run's own rows — none of the RUN_TIME metrics make a model call (`evaluate_run`'s assists are advisory and separable) — and it removes a stale number from the page an operator signs. It is the same question as F-22 (§8 item 10) and the operator should take them together, but this half needs no ADR: no recorded decision says a metric is measured once.

options.name: A — re-measure the touched sections at the end of `revise`
options.change: After `revise_challenged_sections` returns, re-run the per-section RUN_TIME metrics over the sections it rewrote and update their rows before the gate-2 payload is sealed.
options.cost: One call in `_revise` before the payload is built.
options.risk: Low, but it can newly refuse a run at gate 2 that would previously have passed — which is the point, and which the operator should be told before it lands.

options.name: B — move `validate` after `revise`
options.change: Reorder the spine so the metrics are measured once, on the final draft.
options.cost: A step-order change plus the gate-2 hash reasoning at 579-591.
options.risk: Higher: the comment at 579-582 says the red team's challenges join the payload and the gate-2 hash is computed at the last step that can change what the operator sees. Reordering touches the approval hash.

options.name: C — say so on the page
options.change: Label the figure-agreement row on the gate-2 scorecard as measured before the revision, when a revision happened.
options.cost: A template line and a flag.
options.risk: Honest but weak — it tells the operator the number may be stale without giving them a true one.

items.tests: A test that fails first: a run whose `revise` introduces a figure disagreement into a rewritten section shows `cited_figure_agreement` passing at gate 2 today; after the fix the row reports the disagreement and the gate shows it.
items.acceptance: On a replayed AZN #2 run (the one with a revision and every check green), re-measurement after `revise` produces the same rows as today — so the fix costs nothing on a clean run — while the constructed fixture is caught.
items.challengeNote: The item asserts 'none of the RUN_TIME metrics make a model call (evaluate_run's assists are advisory and separable)'. That is not established and the code points the other way: `_validate`'s own docstring says 'the LLM assists advise on what it could not settle and their advice lands in the rows' details' (vertical_slice_v1.py:1661-1666), `evaluate_run` takes an AgentContext carrying provider and router, and its signature documents `use_batch: Route multiple advisory questions through the provider's batch path' (src/aer/services/evaluations.py:148). Re-measuring therefore either costs money at the end of `revise` or requires first carving a deterministic-only entry point out of `evaluate_run` - and that carve-out, not the one call in `_revise`, is the work. Effort: a session becomes a few sessions, and the item should say which metrics it intends to re-run and prove they are model-free. Also note `_revise` already re-runs `validate_draft` on each revised section (ADR 0098 is cited in its docstring at :1809-1819), so the draft-time rules are not stale after a revision - only the gate-2 metric rows are. That narrows the claim usefully and should be said.

items.title: The model-route table is a free-text JSON box: an unknown model drops effort silently and prices at the ceiling
items.problem: F-05's four Haiku routes asking for an effort the model has no parameter for are one instance of a general hole: nothing validates a route's model name. An operator editing the routing table on the settings page — a fourteen-row raw JSON textarea — can type any string. Two things then happen silently. The effort they set is dropped if the model is not in the effort table. And if the model is not in the price table, every call is metered at the Fable ceiling ($10/$50 per million), so the per-call guard over-projects, and a run can be paused for spending caps against money that was never spent. Neither failure says anything at the moment of the edit.
items.rootCause: `ModelRoute.model` is a bare `str` (src/aer/config.py:88) with no validator; `Effort` beside it is a `Literal` and is validated (config.py:57). `Router` checks role names and never model names (src/aer/providers/router.py:107-141). `_coerce` in the settings service calls `ModelRoute.model_validate` and nothing more (src/aer/services/configuration.py:244-248). `prices_for` falls back to `unknown_model_prices`, which returns the dearest known model (src/aer/providers/costs.py:100-104, 152-167) — documented as the safe error, and it is, but the cost is a false pause. `_request_payload` drops effort for any model not in `_MODELS_ACCEPTING_EFFORT` (src/aer/providers/anthropic.py:82-93, 732). The two tables disagree with each other by construction: eight models accept effort, five have prices, and only three are in both.
evidence: Audit §5 F-05: four roles route claude-haiku-4-5 at effort='low' against a model the effort table excludes
Audit §5 F-13: the Haiku snapshot id fell through to the unknown-model fallback and was metered at Opus rates on a live run
Audit §8 item 13 puts effort-on-Haiku to the operator

src/aer/services/configuration.py:244-248
src/aer/web/templates/settings/index.html:37-43 (a 14-row raw JSON textarea)
items.recommendation: Option C, which is one change that closes F-05, F-13's residual and the settings hole together. Validating the route's model against the price table at the point of edit turns three silent failures into one refusal with a reason, and it is the same shape as the existing `Router.unknown_roles()` check that already surfaces a typo'd role at startup (router.py:131-137). Then take F-05's own decision separately and prefer retiring the setting over re-routing: §8 item 13 offers both, and the audit's own budget verdict (§3.3, £7.19 average inside a £10 target) gives no reason to move triage roles to a dearer model. A CORRECTION TO THE RECORD: F-05 states that '`agent_runs` records both `effort` and `effort_applied`, so the divergence is auditable'. It does not. `agent_runs` has one `effort` column (src/aer/db/models/agent_run.py:50) and `effort_applied` appears exactly once in the whole of `src/`, as a field on a structured log line (src/aer/providers/anthropic.py:273). The divergence is recoverable from the archived request artefact, which does record the truth (anthropic.py:225-231, 251), and from the worker's JSON logs — but there is no column to query, so 'it is auditable' overstates what a person can actually ask the database.

items.title: Sibling calls in a wave cannot see each other's spend, so the per-call cap can be jointly overshot
items.problem: The per-run budget cap is enforced per call by summing committed `costs` rows. Inside the five-node research wave and the draft fan-out, each node runs on its own session and commits only when it finishes, so every concurrent sibling's guard reads a total that excludes every other sibling's spend. Five calls each individually under the cap can jointly cross it, and the operator sees the breach after the money is gone rather than before.
items.rootCause: `spend_so_far` (src/aer/workflow/engine.py:365-374) sums `costs` by `job_id` on the caller's session, and `_meter` (src/aer/agents/base.py:878-906) only flushes — a flush is visible inside its own transaction and to nobody else. `_run_node` (engine.py:720-793) gives each node its own session and commits at 787; `_draft_one_apart` (src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3136-3171) does the same per section, committing at 3170. The engine's step-level guard already compensates for this at its own level — `_run_wave` (engine.py:651-660) adds `in_flight` to each sibling's projection with the comment 'two siblings each individually under the cap can jointly be over it, and the guard only sees committed spend' — but the per-call guard inside the agents (`base.py:400-480`) has no equivalent, and it is the one that runs per model call.
evidence: Audit §5 F-21: 'Sibling spend is invisible to the per-call guard inside the research wave and the draft fan-out (five and four sessions each seeing only committed rows), so the per-run cap can be jointly overshot by up to (N−1) × one call's worst case'

The fix therefore has to publish the `agent_run` row on that same short-lived session too, which is exactly the objection the item raises against Option B and does not apply to its own Option A. That makes the change larger than stated: a few sessions is the floor, and the ADR has to cover publishing `agent_runs` early as well as `costs`. One point in the item's favour it missed: ADR 0016's 'nothing here does' is already false - `_draft_one_apart` commits inside the draft step and its docstring calls that deliberate ('own session, own commit', vertical_slice_v1.py:3145-3152) - so the new ADR corrects a record that has already drifted rather than breaking new ground.

items.title: A step that poisons its session or dies outright loses the cost rows it flushed — and those rows are the cap
items.problem: Money the platform has genuinely spent can vanish from the ledger, which means it vanishes from the budget cap — the cap reads the `costs` table and nothing else. A run whose step fails in a particular way is then allowed to spend again up to a ceiling it has already partly consumed, and the operator's total for the run under-reports what the provider will bill.
items.rootCause: This needs narrowing from how the audit states it, and the narrowing matters for the fix. `_meter` flushes rather than commits (src/aer/agents/base.py:906), so the rows live in the step's transaction. On an ORDINARY step exception the rows are NOT lost: `_record_node_failure` (src/aer/workflow/engine.py:830-837) sets the step row to FAILED and calls `node_session.commit()`, which commits the pending Cost objects with it. The rows are lost in exactly two cases. (1) The session is poisoned — a flush-time error leaves it in pending-rollback, the commit at 836 raises, and the recovery path at engine.py:846-855 rolls back and rewrites only the step row. The docstring at engine.py:820-824 accepts this explicitly: 'The rollback discards whatever the step had written before it broke, which is the right trade — that work was already unreachable.' That trade was reasoned about for *work*; money is not work, and the docstring does not notice that it is discarding the only record the cap reads. (2) The process dies with no commit at all — a killed worker, which is what the audit observed. `revise` is the worst case because it is a single-transaction step: `src/aer/services/revision.py` contains zero `commit()` calls and `_revise` (vertical_slice_v1.py:1808) runs everything on the node session, so a minute of model calls is one uncommitted block.
evidence: Audit §5 F-21: 'cost rows flushed by a step that dies mid-flight are lost, consistent with AZN's revise attempt 0 (a minute of calls, no rows)' — note 'consistent with', an inference rather than a proof

Separately, the docstring at engine.py:818-828 should be corrected whatever is decided: it states an accepted trade without noticing that the trade includes money, and a reader of this repository will take it at its word.

items.title: Up to 18,706 output tokens a run are paid for and discarded, and no surface adds them up
items.problem: Every run buys replies the platform cannot read — one to five per run across the five audit runs, up to 18,706 output tokens on AZN including the red team's 9,919. The money is metered correctly and the rows are in the ledger, but nothing anywhere sums it. The operator can see what a run cost and cannot see what part of it bought nothing, which is precisely the figure that would tell them whether a schema is too tight, a token ceiling too low, or a role worth re-routing.
items.rootCause: Not a defect in metering — `_meter_a_failure` (src/aer/agents/base.py:716-770) deliberately writes the same two records a success gets and stamps `stop_reason="schema_rejected"` on the `agent_runs` row (base.py:749) so the rows are findable. The gap is that no reader ever asks. `spend_summary` groups by `Cost.category` only (src/aer/services/spend.py:99-121) and `spend_by_role` groups by role and model (spend.py:124-149); neither touches `stop_reason`. The spend page renders role/model/calls/tokens/cache (src/aer/web/templates/spend/index.html:67-76) and the run console shows one total against the ceiling (src/aer/web/templates/runs/console.html:243-244). `stop_reason` reaches a surface only per-exchange, in the run export (src/aer/services/run_export.py:107) and `aer replay-draft` (src/aer/cli.py:2041) — both terminal, both one exchange at a time.
evidence: Audit §3.3: 'Paid replies the platform could not read: 1 (1,431 output tokens) / 3 (7,366) / 5 (18,706, including the red team's 9,919) / 3 (6,903) / 4 (6,888)'

items.title: No non-model acquisition spend reaches the pounds ledger; the `data_api` category is defined and never written
items.problem: The ledger claims to be complete and is not. `CostCategory.DATA_API` exists, the `costs` table's own docstring describes 'a data-provider fee [that] belongs to the job with no step', and nothing creates such a row. Today no user notices, because every source the platform actually fetches from is free at the margin — but the shape of invariant 6 has a hole in it, and the first metered data vendor added will spend outside the cap by construction.
items.rootCause: `CostCategory.DATA_API` is declared at src/aer/providers/costs.py:125 and has no writer: the only two places that construct a `Cost` row are `Agent._meter` (src/aer/agents/base.py:890) and `_meter_search` (src/aer/services/research.py:479), and both price model usage. SEC, FRED, ECB and ONS are genuinely free (a free FRED key, src/aer/sources/macro/client.py:249-250; the ECB's own licence, src/aer/sources/macro/ecb.py:72-73), and EODHD is a flat monthly subscription bounded separately in calls rather than pounds — `WeightedCallBudget` reserves against a daily weighted-call allowance in Redis (src/aer/sources/eodhd/budget.py:16-22, 104-116) and raises `CircuitOpenError` rather than writing a cost row. So the absence is honest about today's economics and dishonest about the code's own documentation.
evidence: Audit §5 F-06: 'CostCategory.DATA_API is defined and never written … The cost.py docstring describes a row nothing creates. State: to document, or to meter. Not closed here — no run's money turned on it (every acquisition in this pass was free), and writing a row per fetch is a schema decision.'
Audit §7: every platform figure is the sum of that run's own `costs` rows; the categories listed are output, input, cache write, cache read and web search — no data_api

items.title: The audit chain is application-writable: UPDATE and DELETE were never revoked, and the app owns its own tables
items.problem: The platform's integrity story rests on an append-only, hash-chained audit log, and the log is append-only by convention only. The application role can rewrite or delete any row, and a rewrite that recomputes every hash as it goes is undetectable by the verifier. Nothing a user does today touches this, and the audit walked all 36 events of the pass with the chain unbroken — but the guarantee on offer is 'nobody did', not 'nobody could', and the difference is the whole point of a tamper-evident log.
items.rootCause: Migration 0001 records the deferral as a TODO in its own docstring: 'revoke UPDATE and DELETE on audit_events from the application role … It needs a separate migration role to exist first, which is why it is not done here' (migrations/versions/0001_core_schema.py:22-25). No such role exists: `docker-compose.yml:19` and `.env.example:94-98` both use one role, `aer`, which alembic runs as and which therefore owns every table — and an owner's privileges can be revoked but also re-granted by the owner. `src/aer/db/models/audit_event.py:1-18` and `src/aer/services/audit_verify.py:1-13` are both candid about it. Two facts materially change the sizing. First, the precedent exists: `migrations/versions/0003_artefacts_and_sources.py:63-72, 119-124` already installs a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger (`artefacts_are_immutable`) that raises `restrict_violation`, so the mechanism is in this repository. Second — and the audit does not record this — a hard block would break the test harness: `tests/db_cleanup.py:99-119` deletes from every table in the metadata, `audit_events` included (it is not in `SEEDED_BY_MIGRATIONS`, db_cleanup.py:51-58), and `tests/test_db_schema.py:414-448` proves the chain detects tampering by issuing a literal `UPDATE audit_events` and `DELETE FROM audit_events`. Both would have to change.
evidence: Audit §5 F-07: 'Migration 0001 notes that UPDATE and DELETE were never revoked … verify_audit_chain documents that a full rewrite with recomputed hashes is undetectable … the guarantee is that nobody *did* rewrite it, not that nobody could.'
Audit §3.1: 'aer verify-audit walked 36 audit events with the chain unbroken'
migrations/versions/0001_core_schema.py:22-25
migrations/versions/0003_artefacts_and_sources.py:63-72, 119-124 (the existing immutability trigger)
docker-compose.yml:19, .env.example:94-98 (one role, which owns the schema)

src/aer/services/audit_verify.py:7-12

Nothing in src/ ever updates or deletes audit_events — verified by grep; ADR 0031 makes erasure an appended event
items.recommendation: Option B now, Option C when the platform leaves one machine. A trigger costs a session, has a working precedent twenty lines away, and converts the realistic threat — a stray UPDATE, an ORM bug, a careless migration — from silent to loud. It does not stop a determined owner, and the ADR should say exactly that rather than overstating it. The full guarantee needs the separate role migration 0001 asked for, which belongs with roadmap A5/A7/A8 ('Before this leaves one machine … treat these as a single gate rather than three tickets'), not ahead of it. Note when sizing: the two chain-tamper tests must be rewritten to disable the trigger explicitly (owner-only, and visible in the test) or to assert the trigger raises, and `tests/db_cleanup.py` needs `audit_events` handled the way `SEEDED_BY_MIGRATIONS` handles migration-seeded tables.

options.change: A migration installing `audit_events_are_append_only()` raising `restrict_violation`, plus the two test rewrites and the cleanup exception.
options.cost: A migration, a test-harness change, two rewritten tests.
options.risk: Low. Honest about its limit — an owner can drop a trigger — and it stops every accidental path, which is the realistic one. Must be stated plainly in the ADR or it reads as stronger than it is.

options.name: C — a separate application role with INSERT and SELECT only
options.change: A migration role that owns the schema and an `aer_app` role granted INSERT and SELECT on `audit_events` and full DML elsewhere; the application connects as `aer_app`.
options.cost: A role, a compose change, a settings change, a bootstrap path, and documentation for the operator's own machine.
options.risk: This is deployment work, and it is the one answer that makes the guarantee real. It belongs with A5/A7/A8 as one gate.

items.adrSubject: Append-only is enforced by the database, and what that does and does not guarantee while the application owns its own schema.
items.tests: A test that fails first: `UPDATE audit_events SET payload = ... WHERE id = ...` succeeds today (it is the body of `test_editing_a_middle_payload_breaks_verification`); after the fix it raises a `restrict_violation`, and the chain-detection tests prove detection through a path that explicitly disables the trigger rather than one that quietly relies on its absence.
items.acceptance: A hand-issued UPDATE and DELETE against `audit_events` through psql as the application role are both refused with the trigger's own message, the full suite is green in both orderings, and `aer verify-audit` still walks the chain.
items.challengeNote: Every load-bearing fact checks out, including the two the item adds beyond the audit. Migration 0001's docstring carries the deferral verbatim (migrations/versions/0001_core_schema.py:22-25). The precedent is real: `artefacts_reject_update()` raising `restrict_violation` behind a BEFORE UPDATE trigger (migrations/versions/0003_artefacts_and_sources.py:63-72, 119-124). The harness consequence is real and is the item's genuine addition: `delete_all` deletes from every table in the metadata order and `SEEDED_BY_MIGRATIONS` names only `section_definitions` and `sector_profiles` (tests/db_cleanup.py:51-58, 99-119), and `tests/test_db_schema.py:414-448` issues a literal `UPDATE audit_events` and `DELETE FROM audit_events` to prove the chain detects tampering - both would break under a hard block. The recommendation is honest about the trigger's limit against an owner, which is the right register for this record.

items.title: The integrity checks behind the platform's single strongest use case live only in the terminal
items.problem: The audit's suitability matrix rates 'checking the work' as the platform's best result and the one thing the console cannot match — and rates it 'yes, in the interface'. That is true of the evidence walk and not of the integrity backstop. `aer verify-audit` and `aer verify-artefacts` — the two commands that answer 'does this record still say what it said' and 'are the bytes still the bytes' — exist only as CLI commands. A competent private investor who never opens a terminal cannot ask either question, and the audit's own journey table already records that 'anything that needed the terminal' was a defect.
items.rootCause: `verify_audit_chain` is reachable from `aer verify-audit` (src/aer/cli.py:720-737, 2132-2138) and `just verify-audit` (justfile:132-133) and from nothing else — grep finds no route, no page and no template referencing it, and the one web mention of a 'chain' (src/aer/web/pages.py:1914) is the evidence chain from a claim to an excerpt, not the audit chain. `verify_store` is in the same position. `src/aer/db/models/audit_event.py:15-18` names the missing half explicitly: 'Chain verification on startup and in CI. The verifier exists … wiring it into a scheduled check comes with the hardening phase.' Nothing schedules it; the only runs of it in the record are the audit's own manual ones.
evidence: Audit §4.3 use case 10: 'Checking the work — yes, in the interface … This is the platform's strongest result, and it is the one the console cannot match.'
Audit §4.2: 'Anything that needed the terminal: yes'
Audit §3.1: the pass ran `verify-artefacts` (559 artefacts) and `verify-audit` (36 events) by hand
justfile:132-133
src/aer/db/models/audit_event.py:15-18 (chain verification on startup and in CI, deferred)
docs/users/troubleshooting.md:257 and docs/users/getting-started.md:157 — both instruct the operator to run it in a terminal
items.recommendation: Option A, and it is small. The services are already written, already read-only, already paged (`DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE`, audit_verify.py:32-33), and already return a typed report with the offending row's id. A page under the existing settings or overview area with two buttons and two result lines is an afternoon, and it converts the platform's strongest claim from 'true if you use a terminal' into 'true'. For issue 2 specifically: a judge reading the document cannot see this, but an operator deciding whether to trust the platform over the console can, and §4.4 check 3 is exactly that act. Option B (a scheduled check) is worth adding once the surface exists, since the model's own docstring asks for it.

options.name: A — a verification page
options.change: A page that runs `verify_audit_chain` and `verify_store` on request and renders the two `ChainReport`/`IntegrityReport` results in plain language, naming the first broken row if there is one.
options.cost: One route, one template, two service calls that already exist.
options.risk: Low. Both are read-only. A long walk on a large store wants the existing paging and a progress state, which `verify_store` may need.

options.name: B — run it on a schedule and surface the last result
options.change: A periodic check writing its result where the overview page can show 'last verified, N events, intact'.
options.cost: A scheduled task and a small result table.
options.risk: Low, and it is what `audit_event.py:15-18` asks for. Better after A, so a failure has somewhere to be looked at.

options.name: C — leave it in the terminal and say so
options.change: Nothing in code; correct §4.3's 'in the interface' claim in the record.
options.risk: Honest, and it concedes the platform's best result is half in the terminal.

items.tests: A test that fails first: no route serves the chain report today. After: the page renders 'N events checked, the chain is intact' on a sound chain, and on a deliberately broken one names the first failing event id — the same two outcomes `tests/test_audit_chain.py` already asserts on the service.
items.acceptance: The operator can answer §4.4's 'checking the work' question, including the integrity check, without opening a terminal.
items.challengeNote: Note when sizing that §4.2's 'yes' is evidenced by `aer resume` and by a refused gate-2 run being re-measurable nowhere (F-22, F-25), not by verify-audit, so the item borrows that row rather than citing it directly; the point survives but should be stated as its own observation. Effort: a session is about right for the chain half, optimistic for the artefact half - `verify_store` re-hashes every stored artefact (559 in this pass) and running that synchronously inside a web request is a design decision the item flags in one clause and does not cost. Ship the chain report first and treat the store walk as its own piece of work.

items.title: The ordering fix landed by hand on two seeds and nothing in CI stops it recurring
items.problem: At the audit's HEAD the suite's answer depended on file order across three modules and the recorded pair — 28 failed, 7 errors under one seed. The fix is in and proved green on two seeds. What is not in place is anything that would catch the next one: CI runs the files in one fixed order, `just test-shuffled` is a manual command with a hand-chosen seed, and the record itself says a third ordering is unestablished and that the widened runner has never been run under a seed. The next fixture that leaks state will be found the same way — by hand, weeks later, in a 35-minute run.
items.rootCause: The fix itself is real and is in place: `db_engine` and `api_engine` empty the database on the way in (tests/db_fixtures.py:167-176, tests/api_fixtures.py:63-74) through `delete_all` (tests/db_cleanup.py:99-119). The gap is coverage. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` has three jobs — `static`, `tests` (`uv run pytest --ignore=tests/e2e -q`, one fixed order) and `browser` — and no shuffled job. `justfile:284-288` defines `test-shuffled` as a manual recipe. `tests/shuffled.py:28-46` was widened in this pass to walk every directory; its own docstring records that the audit's thirty-five tests had never been shuffled at all, and §9 says the widened runner has not itself been run under a seed.
evidence: Audit §5 F-03: 'just test-shuffled 20260811 … fails at HEAD: 28 failed, 7 errors, 6,830 passed, across test_db_schema.py, test_decisions.py and test_thesis_monitor.py's page tests, not only the recorded pair.'
Audit §9: 'What is not established is a *third* ordering; and the shuffled runner was widened in this pass to walk every directory … which has not itself been run under a seed.'
tests/db_fixtures.py:167-176 and tests/api_fixtures.py:63-74 (the fix)
tests/db_cleanup.py:99-119
tests/shuffled.py:28-46 (ordering, and the docstring on the widened glob)
justfile:284-288
.github/workflows/ci.yml — three jobs, none shuffled
CLAUDE.md: 'One pytest process per database' — a shuffled CI job needs its own AER_TEST_DATABASE_URL
items.recommendation: Option B. A nightly shuffled job with a fresh random seed is the honest shape: the seed is already printed and the failure message already tells you how to repeat it (tests/shuffled.py:52, 63-65), so a red nightly is directly actionable. Putting it on every push would add 35 minutes to every build and turn an intermittent class of failure into a flaky gate — which is how people learn to ignore a job. Whichever is chosen, give the job its own `AER_TEST_DATABASE_URL`: CLAUDE.md's own rule is one pytest process per database, and the audit lost a test to exactly that (§6). This has no user-facing consequence today and it is the difference between the platform's claims about itself being checked and being asserted, which is what F-03 was categorised as.

options.name: A — a shuffled job on every push
options.change: A fourth CI job running `uv run python -m tests.shuffled` with a fresh seed.
options.cost: A job block plus a second Postgres service and its own database URL.
options.risk: Adds ~35 minutes and a genuinely intermittent red to every push. The seed is printed, so it is reproducible, but a flaky required check gets ignored.

options.name: B — a nightly scheduled shuffled job
options.change: The same job on a cron, non-blocking for pushes, with the seed in the run's summary line.
options.cost: A job block and a schedule trigger.
options.risk: Low. A defect is found within a day rather than within an audit, and it never blocks a push. It needs somebody to look at a nightly result, which for one operator means a notification.

options.name: C — assert the property instead of sampling it
options.change: A fixture-level check that every engine fixture leaves the database empty, so a leak fails on the test that caused it rather than on the next one.
options.cost: A conftest hook and the cost of one extra `_holds_rows` probe per test (the cleanup already does this cheaply — db_cleanup.py:105-110).
options.risk: Catches leaks through the fixtures and not leaks through module-level state, which is the other half of what shuffling finds (`tests/shuffled.py:1-10` records an `Agent.__subclasses__()` leak of exactly that kind). Best as a complement to B, not a replacement.

items.tests: The job is the test. Prove it fails first by running it against the commit before the fixture fix (the audit records seed 20260811 failing there with 28 failed and 7 errors) and green on HEAD under a seed nobody has run yet — which is the third ordering §9 says is unestablished.
items.acceptance: A fresh, never-used seed runs green on HEAD, and the nightly job is visible with its seed printed, so a red one can be repeated with a single command.
items.challengeNote: The `AER_TEST_DATABASE_URL` emphasis is misplaced for the shape being recommended: CLAUDE.md's one-process-per-database rule bites when two pytest runs share a database, and a separate nightly CI job brings up its own `postgres:16-alpine` service (ci.yml:52-64), so it is isolated by construction. Keep the note for anyone running the shuffled suite locally beside `just test`, and drop it from the CI sizing.

items.title: The documented counts drift from the code, in the docs and now in the docstrings too
items.problem: F-01 and F-02 are closed for the specific numbers the audit named — `ruff format --check .` reports 1,003 files already formatted, and the live docs now say ten blocking metrics, thirty-nine golden calculations and 458 mypy files. But the class of defect is untouched: every one of those numbers is typed by hand into prose, and one of them drifted again inside the audit's own window (410 → 458, commit 7ca1441). Two stale copies are still in the code itself, where a reader of this repository will believe them. The cost is trust in the record, which is F-01's own framing: 'minor as a defect, major as a signal'.
items.rootCause: Nothing derives or asserts any of these numbers. `src/aer/eval/metrics.py:63-72` still opens 'Two overlapping eights share it' and describes BLOCKING as 'the six from Phase 2 plus the two that arrived with task 32' — BLOCKING is ten (metrics.py:94-105) and RUN_TIME is eleven (metrics.py:110-122). `src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1659` says `_validate` writes 'the run's eight §2.10 evaluation rows'; it writes eleven. In the documents, `docs/developers/testing-by-hand.md:348-353` pins '458 source files' as prose and warns the reader to read mypy's count — a number that moves with every added module. Archived plans still carry the old figures (docs/archive/phase-3-plan.md:624, docs/archive/phase-4-plan.md:36), which is defensible for an archive, and docs/plan/acceptance-2026-09-08.md:28 carries 'all eight blocking metrics', which is a historical record of what that pass checked and should probably be annotated rather than edited.
evidence: Audit §5 F-01 and F-02 ('Eight blocking metrics … against ten in aer.eval.metrics.BLOCKING … 353 mypy files against 410')
`uv run ruff format --check .` at HEAD: '1003 files already formatted' — F-01's formatting half is closed

src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:1659 ('eight §2.10 evaluation rows')
docs/developers/testing-by-hand.md:348-353
grep for '458' in tests/ returns nothing — no test asserts any documented count
items.recommendation: Option A for the docstrings (they are wrong now and a reader believes them), plus Option B for the counts that are genuinely checkable. Asserting `len(BLOCKING) == 10` in a test is worth nothing on its own; asserting that the documented count in `docs/developers/testing.md` and the justfile comment matches `len(BLOCKING)` is worth something, because it is the drift itself that is being tested and the fix is one line when it fires. The mypy file count is the opposite case — it moves with every module and should stop being a number in prose at all; 'it should be the number mypy prints, and a run checking materially fewer is a green build over unchecked code' says everything the paragraph at testing-by-hand.md:351-353 is trying to say, without a figure to maintain. Nothing here needs an ADR.

options.name: A — correct the two stale docstrings and the prose
options.change: Fix `metrics.py:63-72` and `vertical_slice_v1.py:1659`; replace the '458 source files' pin with the rule rather than the number.
options.risk: None, and it drifts again in a month.

options.name: B — assert the documented counts against the code
options.change: A test that reads the count out of `docs/developers/testing.md` and the justfile's `eval` comment and compares it to `len(BLOCKING)` and the golden-calculation count; the same for `len(RUN_TIME)`.
options.risk: Low. Parsing prose for a number is brittle; keep it to a single tagged marker per document rather than a general scrape.

options.name: C — generate the counts
options.change: Have the documents include a generated fragment produced by a justfile recipe from the code.
options.cost: A generator, a recipe, and a CI check that the fragment is current.
options.risk: More machinery than the problem justifies for a personal tool, and it puts generated text into documents whose whole value is that a person wrote them.

items.tests: A test that fails first: assert the count named in `docs/developers/testing.md`'s `just eval` line equals `len(BLOCKING)`. Set BLOCKING to nine in a scratch branch and confirm the test goes red — the property being tested is the agreement, not the number.

The drift test should anchor on docs/developers/testing.md:12, which is the line that is currently right and therefore the one worth pinning.

items.title: No open roadmap item closes any part of either issue, and both planning documents point at work already done
items.problem: An operator opening ROADMAP.md to find out what to do next about "not user ready" and "not better than the console" is told that §2.1 is next (:120) and that §3.1 is what an operator is currently blocked by (:391). Both are closed — §2.1 by the audit itself (:56), §3.1 on 2026-08-29 (:37). The only genuinely open entries in the whole document are §2.8 (concept-map curation), §2.9 (report readability, written as a standing instruction rather than a task), the Phase-6 gate A5/A7/A8, and commercial checks 3 and 5. Building all of them changes no judge's answer and removes no dead end. remaining-work.md, the document that holds the running order, still lists "Approve one confirmation run's spend" as operator move #2 (:149) — discharged five times over by the audit.
items.rootCause: The audit landed after the roadmap's last structural edit. `docs/plan/ROADMAP.md` was updated once post-audit, in commit d3c4c1c (2026-09-12), and that commit only rewrote the "What to do next" preamble (:55-63) to point at the audit document; it added nothing to §2, §3 or §4. `docs/plan/remaining-work.md`'s last commit is cb26dd5, 2026-09-04, eight days before the pass reported. So the two documents that govern scope and order both describe a product state that the audit superseded.

items.recommendation: Rewrite. The repository's rule is explicit that ROADMAP.md is the authority on scope and that where it and anything else disagree it wins except the ADRs (ROADMAP.md:3-4). An audit list that lives outside it is a second authority, which is exactly what the roadmap's own framing forbids. The preamble correction is not optional housekeeping either: the two stale pointers are what a person driving an AI coding session reads first, and each one sends a session at work that is already done.
items.tests: None — documentation. The check is that no open roadmap item's state contradicts the audit's §3/§5 record.
items.acceptance: Every item in §2 and §3 is either marked done with a date or is open and traceable to an audit finding or §8 decision; remaining-work.md's phase table has a row whose gating names the audit; neither :120 nor :391 names a closed item.
items.challengeNote: The "fifteen vs sixteen" charge is not a stale figure. §8 numbers sixteen, but item 16 is "The call on 'ready'" — a judgement, not a decision that could "put a wrong number or no answer in front of somebody". Fifteen is the defensible count for the sentence as written; drop this from the evidence list and replace it with the §2.1 self-contradiction (ROADMAP.md:56 against :122-123), which is the real documentary defect.

items.title: Add F-24 (a bank's revenue) to §2 as a numbered item — the roadmap names it only in the preamble
items.problem: The one blocking finding still open has no roadmap entry. It is described in the "What to do next" paragraph (ROADMAP.md:61-63) and nowhere in §2, so it is not ordered against anything, has no owner, and a session working §2 worst-first will not meet it. Meanwhile no bank produces an approvable report: M&T's run reached gate 2 with eleven impossible relations and was refused.
items.rootCause: M&T reports no total-revenue caption after FY2023, so `revenue` resolves to `RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax` — $1,541m and $1,657m of ASC 606 fee income against net income of $2,588m and $2,851m, giving recorded `net_margin` of 1.6794 and 1.7206. Both components a bank's revenue is made of are already mapped (`InterestIncomeExpenseNet` $6,948m, `NoninterestIncome` $2,742m); nothing sums them, because a sum is a calculation and no calculation claims that definition.

Readiness audit §8 item 2 — "the one blocking finding open, and the reason no bank produces an approvable report"

options.cost: Smaller — a rule in concept resolution and the withheld-figure path already exists.

items.recommendation: Derive it, and this is the operator's call rather than mine — each answer is a different statement about what a bank's revenue is, which is why the audit did not choose. What is not the operator's call is that it belongs in §2 with a number: it is the roadmap's own definition of a §2 item (something is wrong and should not be) and the only open blocker. Add it as §2.10 and put it first in §2's worst-first order.
items.adrSubject: A bank's revenue is net interest income plus non-interest income, taken only for a filer the sector gate has confirmed, and used where the total-revenue caption is absent.
items.tests: A property test over M&T's archived companyfacts asserting `revenue` FY2024/FY2025 resolves to $9,157m/$9,690m rather than the ASC 606 component, and `net_margin` lands in 0.28-0.30; a test that the derivation does not fire for a non-bank; `figure_plausibility` at zero on a replay of the MTB run.

items.challengeNote: Effort "a session" is optimistic by roughly two-fold once the item's own gating is honoured: it depends on the sector gate having confirmed the filer as a bank, and F-26 (§8.4, the gate's third answer) is the mitigation the item itself names — so the ADR, the calc function, the ratio-input preference, the non-bank negative test and a `replay-draft`/plausibility replay of the archived MTB run are realistically two sessions plus the ADR.
items.invariantRisk: None if built as stated. Putting the sum in `aer.calc` with a recorded formula honours "deterministic Python owns every number"; it would breach nothing. The breach to avoid is the tempting shortcut of letting the sector-specialist role state a bank's revenue in prose, which invariant 3 and RESERVED_OUTPUT_FIELDS forbid.

items.title: Add a new §3 item: nothing in the codebase ever writes reports.rating, so every report says "no view reached"
items.problem: Five of six judges said no investment view is stated; five of six said the view is not argued; all six blind comparisons cited the header. Every report the audit produced carries "**Non-binding view:** no view reached" — MSFT #1, MSFT #2, AZN, AZN #2 and MTB, all at line 8 of their exported Markdown. This is the single most-repeated reason the console won, and it appears in no roadmap item, in no audit finding number, and in no §8 decision.
items.rootCause: `reports.rating` is a nullable column (`src/aer/db/models/report.py:73`) and nothing writes it. The one construction site is `report = Report(job_id=context.job.id, request_id=request.id)` at `src/aer/workflow/workflows/vertical_slice_v1.py:3761`, with no rating argument; every other reference reads it. The renderers fall back to the literal string — `src/aer/render/markdown.py:162` and `src/aer/render/templates/report.html:158`. That is by design on the model's side: `rating` is the first entry in `RESERVED_OUTPUT_FIELDS` (`src/aer/core/schemas/skill.py:73-81`), so no section, skill or agent may produce one. What is missing is the *operator's* route: no gate form, no service, no column write.

items.title: The one thing that must not be pulled forward: widening evidence scope alongside peer acquisition or the tier ceiling
items.problem: Two of the most attractive ISSUE-2 items — acquiring peer financials, and raising the evidence tier ceiling so news reaches a section — both look like "give the writer more to work with". Done together, or done by relaxing the scope filters rather than by adding a separate labelled channel, they reproduce a failure this codebase has already shipped once: an Amazon note that cited Walmart, Alibaba, eBay, JD.com, MercadoLibre and Target as its evidence.
items.rootCause: `visible_facts` is scoped by company rather than by request precisely because peer acquisition once put eight other issuers' filings under one request, and the two consumers that joined through `source_documents.request_id` handed a section writer an annual pool the subject did not appear in. The comment recording it is at `src/aer/services/facts.py:63-67`, and ADR 0061 is the decision. The section pack repeats the warning at `src/aer/sections/evidence.py:505-509`.

items.title: Add a new §2 item: the document the judges read drops every exhibit, and no roadmap item covers the exported file
items.problem: The judges read `report.md`. Four of MSFT #1's exhibits and three of AZN #2's render as the single line "*Rendered in the HTML and PDF editions of this report.*" — including the Segment mix chart and, per one judge's own words, a five-year gross-margin series that "exist only in footnotes [^42]–[^56] to an unrendered chart". The same export is what use case 9 (sharing the result) scores "partly": a reader outside the interface cannot follow a footnote to `source_document:<uuid>`, which is why judges reading the Markdown alone found the console no slower to check despite the platform's footnotes resolving to hashed bytes. The roadmap's only document item, §2.4, was about the PDF's page geometry and is closed; §3.12 explicitly put the rendered document outside its scope.

Neither changes the conclusion — every judge read Markdown and none opened a PDF — but state it correctly. items.title: Reopen §2.9 as an active item: the coverage notice speaks in code identifiers and raw Decimals
items.problem: §2.9 is written as a standing instruction — "The register is clean … Keep it that way" — and the audit found it is not clean. The bank's report opens with: "the figure_plausibility, presentation_integrity validation checks failed; and … net income 818000000.000000 exceeds revenue 442000000.000000 … net margin 1.720579360290 for FY2025 is above 1". Two internal metric names and three unformatted Decimals, in the first paragraph a reader meets. The validation table beside it prints thresholds as `0E-8`. The audit's journeys row names this directly: "a coverage notice that names metrics by their code identifiers".
items.rootCause: The coverage notice composes from the evaluation metric keys and the raw stored values rather than going through the house-style rendering door that every other figure in the document uses. F-25 fixed one instance of this class (an ADR number in the withheld-figure note) with tests; the class itself — platform vocabulary reaching the reader on any refusal path — is exactly what §2.9's own sentence predicts: "the failure mode returns whenever a new refusal path gets a placeholder written in the platform's voice rather than the report's".

A rule the document states about itself but does not enforce is how all three of the audit's presentation findings happened; F-22 and F-25 were both caught by `presentation_integrity` and both were prose the platform wrote about itself, so the check has the right shape and the wrong coverage.

So the English names exist; the work is to make the render path reach them, and the open question is direction of dependency (the module is deliberately in `aer.web` because "`aer.eval` is a package the interface reads from and must not import back into"). items.title: Add a new §3 item: the diagnosis and recovery tools §3.15 built are CLI-only, and the web has no equivalent
items.problem: ISSUE 1 asks for an operator who can recover without a terminal. The audit's journeys row answers: "Anything that needed the terminal — yes". Three runs were stranded; before F-08's fix the only way on was re-enqueuing a job id, which no surface offers. F-08 fixed the stranded case and put *Continue* on the console, which is the model to follow — but `aer preflight`, `aer diagnose`, `aer replay-draft`, `aer rehearse-section`, `aer step`, `aer lessons` and `aer curation-worksheet` have no web counterpart, and a run refused at gate 2 can be re-measured nowhere at all.
items.rootCause: §3.15 chose the terminal deliberately and said why: the diagnostic is "in the same family as the existing job_id-scoped CLI commands … which is the right shape for something meant to be read by whoever — human or Claude — is sitting at the terminal deciding whether to continue" (ROADMAP.md). That was the right call for a developer debugging a run. It was never a decision about the operator, and the roadmap has no item that makes the operator's half exist. `src/aer/cli.py` carries 27 commands; grepping `src/aer/web/pages.py` and `routes.py` finds `replay_run` (pages.py:1451) and `reseal_final_gate` (pages.py:1623) and none of preflight, diagnose, rehearse or replay-draft.

items.title: Add §8.9's two missing guards to §2 — they are holes in the one thing the audit calls unambiguously good
items.problem: Accuracy is the platform's single unqualified win: 0 contradicted of 779 checkable figures, 259 of 259 citations verified. Two guards that would defend it do not exist. A fact-backed numeric claim is never checked against its fact's value — `cited_figure_agreement` joins on calculations only, so the claim's statement lends cover to the content's numerals. And the reading ladder discards the scale word, so "$331.8 million" reads as the right number. The audit shares the second blind spot with the platform and says so, which means the 779 figure is measured by a matcher that could not have caught this class either.
items.rootCause: Both are in `src/aer/core/figures.py` and are ADR 0060's territory. The live runs show no such error — the writer was faithful — so this is a guard gap rather than an observed defect, which is exactly why it belongs in the roadmap rather than in a bug list: nothing will surface it until it costs a report.
evidence: Readiness audit F-21, fourth bullet — "A fact-backed numeric claim is never checked against its fact's value … The reading ladder discards the scale word … Both are in core/figures.py and ADR 0060's territory"
Readiness audit §8 item 9
